items.title: Creating the Conditions: Empowering Communities in Writing and General Education
items.excerpt: How do writing and general education programs create conditions for communities that empower themselves-sustaining, growing, and often exceeding their original design? This panel invites papers that examine collaborative relationships among students, near-peers, tutors, and faculty that form in and around writing instruction and beyond, with particular in...
items.fullDescription: How do writing and general education programs create conditions for communities that empower themselves-sustaining, growing, and often exceeding their original design? This panel invites papers that examine collaborative relationships among students, near-peers, tutors, and faculty that form in and around writing instruction and beyond, with particular interest in work that attends to the unexpected: encounters, connections, and forms of growth that arise when pedagogy exceeds the transactional to become genuinely communal. Papers might address-for example-embedded tutoring or near-peer mentoring in composition; teaching-and-learning communities (communities of practice) among faculty, tutors, and students; writing or Gen Ed programs at HSIs, HBCUs, or open-access institutions; the relationship between first-year instruction and identity transformation; intergenerational writing communities and alumni engagement; or the challenges that AI poses to authentic intellectual and creative development. Empirical, theoretical, and reflective approaches are welcome, as is work that bridges composition pedagogy, approaches to general education, and literary (or other forms of) community-building.

items.location: Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam · RMIT Vietnam
items.excerpt: About the Symposium The Weight of Mountains (TWOM) Symposium 2026 is an international academic symposium in film and media studies, with a primary focus on Vietnamese and Southeast Asian screen cultures and on how cinema documents, reimagines, and gives form to the region's landscapes, urban transformations, and contested histories. Co-hosted by RMIT Univ...
items.fullDescription: About the Symposium The Weight of Mountains (TWOM) Symposium 2026 is an international academic symposium in film and media studies, with a primary focus on Vietnamese and Southeast Asian screen cultures and on how cinema documents, reimagines, and gives form to the region's landscapes, urban transformations, and contested histories. Co-hosted by RMIT University Vietnam and Fulbright University Vietnam, the symposium brings together scholars from film studies and audiovisual studies, cultural studies, environmental humanities, postcolonial studies, and related fields to examine cinema's engagement with place, memory, and environment in an era of rapid urbanization and ecological change. The symposium underscores the significance of authorial and experimental film practices and of speculative fiction emerging in our region. The symposium is organised in conjunction with the fourth iteration of The Weight of Mountains, a periodic international film residency and research platform whose 2026/2027 program places international filmmakers in residence in Ho Chi Minh City for three months. This urban turn - situating the residency in a city shaped by colonial histories, wartime trauma, ??i M?i transformations, and accelerating development - provides the occasion for a focused scholarly conversation about cinema's relationship to place, history, and environment in Vietnam and the wider Southeast Asian region. The symposium will feature keynote addresses by leading Vietnamese and international scholars, artist presentations by TWOM resident filmmakers, and presentations of selected papers. Partners include: The Weight of Mountains (TWOM) team, RMIT Vietnam (DFV and SCD), Fulbright University Vietnam (Arts & Media Studies), Trigger Film Academy Call for Abstracts: Ho Chi Minh City is a city of layered temporalities - part and contemporary - and Vietnamese cinema has long been one of the most searching instruments for reading those layers. The city itself operates as a cinematic text: its streets and interiors producing divergent spatial imaginaries shaped by who holds the camera and from where they look. Like in Tran Anh Hung's Cyclo, urban space can be a site of the uncanny and memories, the promised land, or the space of autoreflective questions. Drawing on Guy Debord's psychogeography and Timothy Cresswell's understanding of place as practiced and performed, we ask how filmmakers navigate, intervene in, and reimagine the urban and ecological spaces of the region through experimental narratives, tools and future-oriented imaginaries. Contemporary film studies has been decisively shaped by the turn toward critical transnationalism, insisting on interrogating the uneven power relations, industrial infrastructures, and cultural politics that condition the movement of films, filmmakers, and capital across borders. For Vietnamese and Southeast Asian cinemas, this means attending simultaneously to inter-Asian circuits of production and distribution, to festival economies and co-production networks, and to the diasporic communities whose experiences and investments shape what gets made and how it travels. The Weight of Mountains residency operates as what Foucault called a heterotopia - a space of productive dislocation and otherness, deliberately positioned at the margins of dominant film cultures. This symposium extends that heterotopic logic into the academic register, asking what forms of knowledge become possible when international filmmakers and researchers engage seriously with the specific textures of Vietnamese urban life: its soundscapes, its landscapes and ecologies as sites of historical sedimentation and environmental change, and its postcolonial politics of the gaze. The symposium is equally attentive to what cinema can do when it turns toward the nonhuman world - the Mekong Delta, the urban waterways, the forest edges and street ecologies that constitute the lived environment of Vietnam and the wider region, bringing further questions about how film documents landscape, registers environmental change, and attends to the nonhuman dimensions of place. Thematic Strands We invite submissions that engage with one or more of the following strands. Papers should present a clear research question, theoretical framework, and original contribution to the field. STRAND 1. Colonial and Postcolonial Cinemas of Southeast Asia Vietnamese and Southeast Asian cinemas carry the unresolved weight of French colonialism, Cold War intervention, and the ongoing politics of decolonial representation. Papers in this strand might address: • The postcolonial gaze and ethics of representation in Vietnamese documentary and fiction film • French colonial cinema in Indochina and its afterlives in contemporary Vietnamese film culture • Decolonial aesthetics and counter-narratives in Vietnamese, Cambodian, Lao, and Thai cinema • The postcolonial condition of Indochinese cinemas across Vietnam, Cambodia, and Laos, and the shared legacies of French colonialism • Colonial urban space and its cinematic re-inscription in Ho Chi Minh City, Phnom Penh, and Vientiane • The ethics of the outsider filmmaker in Vietnam and Southeast Asia - questions of access, positionality, and the politics of cross-cultural representation STRAND 2. Memory and the Afterlives of 1975 Post-1975 Vietnamese cinema remains one of the most contested sites of historical memory in world cinema. Papers in this strand might address: • Historical voices in post-1975 Vietnamese film • Wartime affect in Vietnamese cinema • Heterogeneous temporalities, colonial haunting, and the fantastic in Southeast Asian cinema • Uncanny urban spaces • Generational shifts in the remembrance of war and revolution across Vietnamese film STRAND 3. Transnational Return Papers in this strand might address: • Transnational desire, mobility, and national belonging • The aesthetics of displacement, longing, and return in film • Insider and outsider representations of Vietnam and the returning gaze • Transnational co-productions and festival circulation • Digital platforms, streaming, and new circuits of Vietnamese film distribution STRAND 4. Urbanism and the Cinematic City Ho Chi Minh City and Hanoi are among the most cinematically rich urban environments in contemporary Southeast Asia, shaped by ??i M?i reforms, rapid development, and the layering of colonial and socialist pasts. Papers in this strand might address: • Ho Chi Minh City as cinematic city-text • Psychogeography, the dérive, and spatial practice in Vietnamese urban cinema • Postcolonial urbanism and the layering of colonial and contemporary temporalities in Vietnamese cityscapes • Rural-urban boundaries and migration narratives in contemporary Vietnamese cinema • Bangkok, Manila, Phnom Penh, and other Southeast Asian cities as sites of cinematic spatial inquiry • Infrastructural development, displacement, and the politics of urban transformation on screen STRAND 5. Independent Cinema and Alternative Exhibition in Southeast Asia Beyond mainstream production, a vital ecosystem of independent and experimental cinema has emerged across the region, creating alternative circuits of production, distribution, and spectatorship. Papers in this strand might address: • Critical transnationalism and the conditions of production, funding, and circulation of Southeast Asian independent film • Alternative film exhibitions • Independent film festivals and independent production circuits across Southeast Asia • The role of digital platforms and transnational funding in enabling independent Southeast Asian filmmaking • Distinct regional independent cinema identities • The sonic and haptic dimensions of place in experimental Southeast Asian films STRAND 6. Landscape, Ecology, and Environmental Cinema This strand invites scholarship on how cinema represents, interprets, and attends to the landscapes, ecologies, and natural environments of Vietnam and Southeast Asia. It encompasses documentary, essay film, and fiction practices that attend to environmental change, rural and riverine life, and the nonhuman world as subjects of serious cinematic inquiry. Papers in this strand might address: • Landscape cinema and ecocinema studies in the Vietnamese and Southeast Asian context - how films document, aestheticise, and bear witness to environments under pressure • The Mekong Delta as cinematic space - rivers, deltas, and rural waterways as subjects of documentary, fiction, and experimental filmmaking • Climate cinema and the Anthropocene in Southeast Asian documentary and fiction film • Sensory and immersive cinema - the use of duration, texture, and ambient sound to render nonhuman environments perceptible • Process cinema and the nonhuman agencies - water, weather, infrastructure, animals - that constitute urban and rural life in Vietnam and the region STRAND 7. Festival Aesthetics, Slow Cinema, and Global Circulation The growing international visibility of Vietnamese and Southeast Asian cinema raises important questions about the institutional and aesthetic conditions of that visibility. Papers in this strand might address: • Transcendental style, slow cinema, and contemplative aesthetics in contemporary Vietnamese film • The construction of "Vietnamese cinema" as a category within global film culture • Co-production networks, international funding, and the shaping of film form for global audiences • The tension between local spectatorship and international festival circuits in Vietnamese and Southeast Asian cinema • Transnational frames for Asian cinema and the risks of Orientalist programming logics • The role of film criticism, academic writing, and scholarly publishing in shaping the international reception of Southeast Asian cinema SUBMISSION GUIDELINES Abstract requirements: - Word count: 300-500 words, excluding references - Language: English Abstracts should include: - Paper title - 3 to 5 keywords - Indication of which thematic strand(s) the paper engages - Author name(s), institutional affiliation(s), bio note and email address(es) should be provided only in the submission form - Please indicate your presentation format: online/face to face in the form Author biography: A short biography of 100-150 words per author should be submitted alongside the abstract Presentation format: A 20-minute academic paper presentation, followed by 10 minutes for questions and discussion Review process: All submissions will undergo blind peer review by an international panel of scholars. Selection criteria include intellectual rigour, theoretical sophistication, methodological clarity, engagement with Vietnamese and Southeast Asian contexts, and relevance to symposium themes. Authors should remove identifying information from the abstract document prior to submission Submission portal: https://cmt3.research.microsoft.com/TWOM2026/Submission/Index Symposium format: The symposium will have a hybrid format. An additional online session will be held for online participants. KEY DATES: Abstract submission deadline: September 15, 2026 Notification of acceptance: October 2026 Full text submission: November 20, 2026 Symposium: December 10, 11, and 12, 2026 Symposium Venues: -December 10, Online -December 11, RMIT Unviersity, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam -December 12, Fulbright University, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam Abstract submissions: https://cmt3.research.microsoft.com/TWOM2026/Submission/Index Please submit the abstracts through the submission system. *Some users encountered problems while using Safari browser. If you have problems with registering, please use a different browser. Registration details to be announced. Please contact the organising committee for queries regarding accessibility requirements. The organizers plan to publish an edited monograph containing expanded, selected articles submitted to the symposium. Details to be announced. Enquiries : dfvhub.staff@rmit.edu.vn Organising Committee Khoa Trong Nguyen, Digital Film and Video Program Manager, RMIT Vietnam Dr. Piotr Wajda, Lecturer, Professional Communications, RMIT Vietnam Dr. Agnieszka Kiejziewicz, Design (Games), RMIT Vietnam Tim Marshall, TWOM, Associate Lecturer, RMIT Melbourne Melody Woodnutt, TWOM, Associate Lecturer, RMIT Melbourne Dr. Linda Chen Zhang, Assistant Professor, Fulbright University Vietnam Trinh Dinh Le Minh, Lecturer/Filmmaker, Fulbright University Vietnam Director Lan Nguyen, Trigger Film Academy Le Binh Giang, Trigger Film Academy

items.fullDescription: Call for Papers NeMLA 2027 Annual Convention Rethinking the Fantastic: Impossibility, Ontology, and Alternative Realities What makes a text fantastic? While traditional definitions often emphasize the supernatural or the uncanny, many literary works generate the fantastic through impossibility itself. Impossible worlds, contradictory realities, unstable identities, infinite spaces, and paradoxical temporalities challenge readers' assumptions about reality and invite new ways of understanding existence. This panel explores the fantastic through the lens of impossibility, examining how literature constructs alternative realities that disrupt conventional notions of ontology, epistemology, identity, language, memory, and time. While the work of Jorge Luis Borges serves as a significant point of departure for these discussions, the panel also welcomes comparative and interdisciplinary approaches that extend beyond Borges to other literary traditions, periods, and media. Possible topics include, but are not limited to: Impossibility as a defining feature of the fantastic Ontological and epistemological uncertainty Borges and the redefinition of the fantastic Comparative studies of Borges and other writers of the fantastic Alternative realities, dreams, simulations, and virtual worlds Labyrinths, infinite libraries, mirrors, doubles, and paradoxes Time, memory, identity, and narrative impossibility Metafiction and self-reflexive narrative The fantastic across cultures, languages, and historical periods Philosophical approaches to the fantastic Contemporary fantasy, speculative fiction, and science fiction in relation to impossibility We welcome proposals from scholars at all career stages and encourage contributions from literary studies, comparative literature, philosophy, cultural studies, media studies, and related disciplines. Submission Information Please submit a 250-300-word abstract through the NeMLA submission portal. Submission deadline: September 30, 2026 CFP page: https://cfplist.com/nemla/ Home/S/22693 Session modality: Remote only This panel seeks to foster conversations on how impossibility reshapes our understanding of the fantastic across literary traditions and theoretical perspectives. We look forward to receiving proposals that reconsider the fantastic beyond conventional boundaries. abeler17@posta.pau.edu.tr Ayse Nur Beler

items.title: It Takes a Village: Building Communities of Learning in Times of Collapse
items.excerpt: This panel invites participants to enlarge on the theoretical, scholarly, and humanistic aspects of community building. Beginning with the idea that the humanities are about nurturing community when so much in our world seeks to drive us apart, we will consider such life-giving functions of humanistic scholarship as fostering joy, facilitating healing, be...
items.fullDescription: This panel invites participants to enlarge on the theoretical, scholarly, and humanistic aspects of community building. Beginning with the idea that the humanities are about nurturing community when so much in our world seeks to drive us apart, we will consider such life-giving functions of humanistic scholarship as fostering joy, facilitating healing, being part of the natural world, and engaging the physical senses and the life of the body. These concerns rarely abide by the expectations of any one academic discipline, field, or department. The more "silo'd" our learning, the less serviceable we are to the actual life of humanity. A wise social-scientist friend of mine recently shared with me that it's considered animal cruelty to own just one duck because they're intrinsically social creatures--a telling reminder that it's not our fault that we ourselves do so badly isolation, yet just the kind of knowledge we tend to foreclose in an average humanities classroom. Likewise, my own training as a woodworker shapes my understanding of the material as well as the intellectual and emotional foundations of my life in queer community. Hence, this panel encourages views of humanistic practice that refuse narrow disciplinary boundaries, and dispensing with limiting assumptions about the potential of academia to take part in a thriving world. For my own part, I will talk about the centrality of reading groups in my own life-not only the well-known sort in which participants discuss something they've all read, but in which we take turns reading aloud to one another, for the sonorous, material, physical, voice-lifting joy of it. (Needless to say, the text has to be worth it; this is not a book-of-the-month kind of approach). Participants will be encouraged to write about and share the sources of wisdom that guide their own efforts to build and sustain community. Suggested topics include ancestral and indigenous wisdom on community relations; pedagogical, philosophical, and poetical approaches to learning in community; performance practices linking music, poetry, and other formally disparate media; liberatory approaches to education; communities of reading and interpretation; the ethics of finance; and the intersection of community and creativity.

items.excerpt: Call for Papers: Geographies of Horror Department of English Studies (University of Zadar) in collaboration with The Society for the Study of the American Gothic (SSAG) Keynote speaker: Jeffrey Andrew Weinstock (Central Michigan University) May 20-21st 2027, University of Zadar (Zadar, Croatia) The study of horror has always been inseparable from the ques...
items.fullDescription: Call for Papers: Geographies of Horror Department of English Studies (University of Zadar) in collaboration with The Society for the Study of the American Gothic (SSAG) Keynote speaker: Jeffrey Andrew Weinstock (Central Michigan University) May 20-21st 2027, University of Zadar (Zadar, Croatia) The study of horror has always been inseparable from the question of space. From the shadowed corridors of Gothic castles to contemporary digital voids, spaces in horror are never just passive backdrops. They function as active agents that shape perception, destabilize subjectivity, and collapse the distinction between interior and exterior, revealing how fragile our sense of spatial coherence can be. This conference seeks to understand how spaces become haunted - materially, symbolically, psychologically, and technologically, and how these hauntings articulate broader cultural anxieties, historical traumas, and epistemological uncertainties. In Gothic and horror traditions, fear unfolds through space, guiding perception, and encounters with the unknown. Early Gothic forms, such as castles and monasteries, establish models of spatial excess, enclosure, and architectural anxiety, while the haunted house transforms domestic familiarity into something uncanny. In modern and contemporary horror, this logic extends to urban environments, where entire cities and infrastructures become haunted. While urban legends and other unsettling narratives embed fear in everyday life, abandoned malls, transit systems, and brutalist structures evoke concepts such as "non-places," characterized by transience and anonymity. At the same time, horror increasingly stages the breakdown of spatial logic itself. Non-Euclidean geometries, infinite corridors, and paradoxical environments destabilize perception and challenge epistemological certainty. In these instances, space becomes fundamentally unknowable, aligning with cosmic horror and philosophical pessimism. These concerns extend into digital and virtual environments, where video games, online narratives, and immersive technologies generate new forms of spatial horror. Phenomena such as The Backrooms exemplify liminal, endlessly reproducible environments that evoke both familiarity and existential dread. Simultaneously, haunted space becomes internalized within the body and mind, as psychological and body horror depict interiority as fragmented and invasive. With all this in mind, we welcome papers from across disciplines and media that examine the spatial dimensions of horror, including but not limited to: Gothic and classical haunted spaces Urban and infrastructural hauntings, including "non-places" Non-Euclidean, paradoxical, and incoherent spatialities Digital and virtual environments (games, online narratives, immersive media) The body and subjectivity as haunted spaces Ecological and environmental horror Spatial storytelling across literature, film, television, comics, and interactive media The keynote speaker for the event will be Professor Jeffrey Andrew Weinstock (Central Michigan University). He is a Professor of English at Central Michigan University, where he teaches a range of courses on American literature and popular culture. He is the founder and president of The Society for the Study of the American Gothic, the founder and general editor of the peer-reviewed journal American Gothic Studies, and the co-founder and past chair of the Modern Language Association Gothic Studies Forum. He also serves as the associate editor in charge of horror for the Los Angeles Review of Books and is currently the general editor for Bloomsbury Publishing's six-volume Cultural History of Monsters series. His research focuses on the "cultural work" performed by the Gothic in its various manifestations - the ways in which Gothic texts and practices give shape to culturally specific anxieties and desires. This interest has led him from considering, for example, how nineteenth-and early twentieth-century American women made use of Gothic conventions as a strategy to express discontentment with their circumscribed roles to thinking about the ways contemporary monsters reflect shifting American fears and aspirations. To date, he is the author or editor of 34 books and more than 100 essays and book chapters on the Gothic, American literature, cult film, and popular culture. Abstracts of 250-300 words, accompanied by a short bio (approximately 100 words) and 3-5 keywords, should be submitted to geographyhorror@gmail.com . The deadline for the abstract submission is October 1st 2026. Selected papers focused on American Gothic and horror themes will also be considered for publication in the American Gothic Studies Journal.

items.excerpt: This ACLA seminar asks what it means to teach the "world" in fields such as world cinema, world literature, comparative literature, and global media studies. items.fullDescription: This ACLA seminar asks what it means to teach the "world" in fields such as world cinema, world literature, comparative literature, and global media studies. Courses organized around the world often promise breadth, diversity, and cross-cultural understanding, but they also face practical and conceptual problems. What counts as the world? How does the nation appear in "world" courses? How do syllabi balance coverage, depth, translation, historical context, aesthetics, and political urgency? How do institutional expectations and restrictions mold the student imagination of the "world"? How does the positionality of the instructor presuppose, structure, or influence the "world" classroom? The seminar invites papers on the pedagogy of world cinema, media, literature, and related fields. We welcome reflections on syllabus design, classroom practice, study abroad programs, canonicity, national, regional, and transnational frameworks, diaspora, migration, colonial and postcolonial histories, language, accessibility, and the politics of curation. Participants might address how a single course constructs the world, how students respond to unfamiliar forms and contexts, how films or texts travel across classrooms, or how teaching the world changes across institutional locations. Through the discussions generated by this seminar, we hope to gather strategies for reimagining "world" courses in film, literature, and new media classrooms. Therefore, this seminar is especially interested in approaches that treat pedagogy as a site of theory. How do teaching practices revise our understanding of the world itself? What models of the world do our classrooms reproduce, and what alternative worlds might they make possible? We welcome both theoretical reflections and concrete case studies, including discussions of specific courses, syllabi, assignments, classroom practices, films, texts, or teaching contexts. Submit your proposal through this link: https://www.acla.org/seminar/6f456f04-ac0e-4024-9daf-ec6a4ca3e277

items.fullDescription: CALL FOR PAPERS / COLLEGE ENGLISH ASSOCIATION ANNUAL CONFERENCE APRIL 1-3, 2027 / ST LOUIS, MO SUBMISSION SITE IS OPEN: https://www.conftool.pro/cea2027 DEADLINE: 11/01/2026 For its 2027 annual conference,the College English Association (CEA) invites proposals for papers and panels that explore the theme of "Gateways" and their significance in literature, criticism, and pedagogy. we also encourage proposals on GENERAL TOPICS, including AMERICAN, BRITISH, AND WORLD LITERATURES. DON'T KNOW CEA? YOU SHOULD! In December 1938, a group of young academics attending the MLA convention in New York took on the biggest name in their field-the MLA. They chose to forge a new path by organizing into the College English Association and offering a voice to "the college English teachers of America." Their aim was to upend the scholar-teacher dynamic by recognizing teaching as paramount. Today, more than eight decades later, the CEA continues in that same spirit. At our core, we strive to meet these goals through two venues: our Annual CEA Conference and our journal, The CEA Critic. With over 400 active members and a collection of regional affiliates, the CEA welcomes teacher-scholars at all levels-from graduate students to emeritus faculty-who share our belief that teaching is central to who we are and what we do. CEA WELCOMES GRADUATE STUDENTS As always, the CEA extends a special invite to students pursuing a graduate degree, not only to attend the conference but to submit their presentations to the CEA Outstanding Graduate Student Paper competition. The award carries a grand prize of $250 and publication of the winning essay in the CEA's flagship journal, THE CEA CRITIC. NEW FOR 2027:UNDERGRADUATE ROUNDTABLES CEA invites undergraduates to enjoy the conference experience by sharing their work in flash-essay roundtable sessions. A flash essay is a highly condensed, high-impact presentation (typically 300-1000 words, or 2-5 minutes) that delivers core research findings, a specific argument, or a compelling narrative. During roundtable sessions, the speakers and audience engage in discussion with each other in more of an open conversation than in traditional panels. Learn more about roundtables here: https://cea-web.org/about-roundtables. LEARN MORE: https://cea-web.org/cea-2027-%2F-st-louis

items.fullDescription: Affiliated with the British Association for Chinese Studies (BACS), the British Postgraduate Network for Chinese Studies (BPCS) is an academic network for postgraduate students and early-career researchers in Chinese Studies in the UK. With over 1,000 members, BPCS is one of the largest postgraduate organisations for Chinese Studies in the UK. We actively promote Chinese Studies by organising annual conferences, seminars, career events, and other academic and professional activities. We also aim to serve as a key source of information on developments in Chinese Studies across the UK and to give members opportunities to connect with peers in their fields. Available Positions We are currently inviting nominations for three committee positions: President: Provides executive leadership for BPCS activities, including the annual conference, and attends BACS meetings as a representative of the community. Internal Secretary: Works with the President to organise BPCS activities, particularly the annual conference, and assumes the responsibilities of the President in their absence. External Secretary: Edits and publishes the weekly newsletter, manages BPCS social media accounts and external communications, and works with the President and Internal Secretary to promote BPCS events and activities. We warmly invite you to nominate yourself for one of these positions. If you would like to nominate someone else, please feel free to share this email and the link https://forms.gle/4Fp34qN9pbwFnZEGA with them. Application Procedure Members are invited to nominate themselves or other candidates by completing the https://forms.gle/4Fp34qN9pbwFnZEGA by 04 October 2026. A confirmation email will be sent once we have received your nomination. We will finalise the list of nominees for each position shortly after the deadline, followed by an election. The results will be announced through the BPCS mailing list by October 2026, subject to the election results and confirmation from the successful candidates. The newly elected members will take office on 23 October 2026. Why Should You Consider Joining Us? Joining the BPCS Committee offers more than an opportunity to strengthen your professional experience. It allows you to become part of an academic community committed to advancing Chinese Studies in the UK. As a committee member, you will gain valuable networking and organisational experience, have opportunities to develop events related to your academic and professional interests, and contribute to initiatives that benefit the wider Chinese Studies community. Your participation will help ensure the continuation of the BPCS annual conference, newsletters, seminars, and other regular activities. We warmly encourage you to consider joining the BPCS Committee and helping to shape the future of our organisation. Together, we can build a supportive and collaborative community for Chinese Studies. We look forward to receiving your nominations and working together to further the study of Chinese culture and society in the UK.

items.title: "Frozen" Cold War Narrative
items.excerpt: In Asian context, the Cold War has not ended but became an ongoing structural condition that determines the social, political, and economic dimensions of everyday lives. The unresolved nature of the war has also left traces on a personal level, expressing through one's body, psyche, and their intimate relations. The Korean War (1950-present) as a proxy wa...
items.fullDescription: In Asian context, the Cold War has not ended but became an ongoing structural condition that determines the social, political, and economic dimensions of everyday lives. The unresolved nature of the war has also left traces on a personal level, expressing through one's body, psyche, and their intimate relations. The Korean War (1950-present) as a proxy war between the two global superpowers, for example, has been continuing as manifested on multiple levels, and it keeps bringing back the traumatic past into the present while challenging the authoritarian interpretation of the war as "The Forgotten War". This session will discuss Cold War narratives that are written from the vantage point of those who have been living through the imperialist war violence. The main discussion centers around the unfinished -- "frozen" -- pasts that are still affecting our present lives, oftentimes taking the form of what is seemingly dissociated from the violent history. The narratives range over a variety genre of writings including fiction, memoir, and autofiction, and ultimately question the hegemonic memory politics that see the defining geopolitical conflicts of the twentieth century as a stable, diplomatic standoff, which has come to an end a while ago. Primary questions may include but are not limited to: How is the frozen nature of the Cold War manifested in the present time? How has the manifestation of the proxy wars in Asia been represented in literature? What is the role of literature in (de)constructing the official narrative/memory? https://cfplist.com/nemla/Home/S/22433 (In-person only)

items.excerpt: Addiction is strongly associated with what Jacques Derrida termed "our narcotic modernity," to the point of being synonymous with its ills--even, or especially, as both addiction and modernity flicker between their narrowest and broadest senses. items.fullDescription: Addiction is strongly associated with what Jacques Derrida termed "our narcotic modernity," to the point of being synonymous with its ills--even, or especially, as both addiction and modernity flicker between their narrowest and broadest senses. On one hand, according to an influential Foucauldian line of thought, addiction as an identity and an institutional formation dates to the nineteenth century, when certain kinds of drug use, much like certain kinds of same-sex intimacy, were pathologized by medicine and criminalized by law. At the same time, addiction's challenges to subjecthood and agency--and its extension as a model for everything from shopping to smartphone use--have made it a powerful figure for capitalist modernity's effects on the self. Taken together, these accounts of addiction as specifically modern and modernity as generalized addiction render the two terms at once interdependent and unstable, a problem of definition running parallel to the urgent social problems of addiction and its failed carceral solutions. Building on recent scholarship by Jennifer Fleissner, Rebecca Lemon, and others, we seek to retheorize addiction and its periodization through a wider view of its articulation across different eras and contexts. This seminar seeks to bring together scholars working at the intersection of addiction and literature from the premodern to the postmodern, to reconfigure our understanding of how these concepts are negotiated and narrativized across time. How has the concept of addiction changed over time, and how have these shifting conceptions been represented in literary terms? How can a critical examination of addiction narratives reconfigure our concept of "modernity"? Is addiction literature a distinct mode? What does addiction look like in the present, and in contemporary literature? What norms, histories, and assumptions overdetermine its representation? Crucially, what do these changes mean in practice-that is, how do they impact our cultural understanding of addiction and how our society treats those living with it? The stakes of these questions are particularly high in the context of a society grappling with the ongoing opioid crisis and related debates about harm reduction, who is deserving of care, empathy, and self-determination, and what we owe to one another as members of a human community. Potential topics include (but are not limited to): Free will, self-possession, agency, and self-control Capitalism, consumption, and commodity fetishism Narratives of slavery and enslavement Literary forms and genres associated with addiction: allegory, picaresque, memoir, trip report, confessional, cautionary tale, body horror, etc. Character theory and the "Addict" (character systems and economies, depth and typicality, etc.) The individual body and the social body Shifting narratives of subjecthood and the Self Medicalization and moralization of addiction Shifting approaches to conceptualizing and treating addiction Submit abstracts directly through the ACLA seminar portal: https://www.acla.org/seminar/8d51e4c4-9c0f-4b74-85e5-5d43ca66fdc3

items.location: Houston/Texas · American Comarative Literature Association / ICLA Research Committee on Religion, Ethics, and Liter
items.excerpt: Papers with a specifically comparative focus on the sins of reading (Peccata Lectionis) can examine the topic of the seminar from a theoretical, methodological and thematic perspective. If we speak about the event of reading in a general sense, misreading as an interpretative act should not necessarily be defined as a sin or even as a mistake. At least, t...
items.fullDescription: Papers with a specifically comparative focus on the sins of reading (Peccata Lectionis) can examine the topic of the seminar from a theoretical, methodological and thematic perspective. If we speak about the event of reading in a general sense, misreading as an interpretative act should not necessarily be defined as a sin or even as a mistake. At least, this cannot be done as clearly as in a legal, ethical or psychological discourse about sin or a mistake in the case of a Mozart overture played out of tune. What then is the sin of reading? From a theoretical point of view, it may well be defined as a complement to "the virtue of reading" (Virtus Lectionis, Ambrus 2026). All this creates a connection between the literary canon and canonisation known from the Christian religious tradition, and perhaps the sin of reading lies in non-canonical interpretation. Also, literary critics as professional readers can commit one of the sins of reading when losing their credibility with lay people watching them. However, the most radical theoretical and methodological problem stems from language itself. If we give credit to Nietzsche's philosophical claims on language adopted from Gustav Gerber, we must also consider language itself and hence literature as an accumulation of errors, in accordance with Paul Ricoeur's theory of metaphor, identifying the origin of tropes as linguistic errors. The professional reading of literature, which is considered as a set of mistakes, is already lying when it discusses its subject not as rhetorical errors, but as aesthetic quality. When we study the literary works of different cultures and periods and think about the sins related to reading, we can come to a similar conclusion. The seminar welcomes any comparative and even interdisciplinary paper that wants to take into account the above problems of reading, primarily in association with the Judeo-Christian tradition and sin understood according to Western philosophical concepts. From a literary point of view, special attention may be paid to the works of Aristophanes, Dante, Cervantes, Laurence Sterne, E. T. A. Hoffmann, Henry James, Marcel Proust, Virginia Woolf, James Joyce, Jorge Luis Borges or Paul Auster, and from a religious point of view, to the works of Philo of Alexandria, the Kabbalist thinkers, Origen, Saint Augustine, Hugh of Saint Victor, Ticonius, Rudolf Bultmann, Northrop Frye, Gershom Scholem, and David Tracy.

items.title: Practice Makes (Im)Perfect: Archival Authority, Conflict, and Constructions of Knowledge
items.excerpt: The construction of archives has long been a fraught process that brings dominant ways of knowing, which are often Western and colonial, into conflict with cultural knowledge. Despite recent efforts to decolonize institutions and collections, many archival practices were developed in ways that contribute to this tension while introducing ethical and epist...
items.fullDescription: The construction of archives has long been a fraught process that brings dominant ways of knowing, which are often Western and colonial, into conflict with cultural knowledge. Despite recent efforts to decolonize institutions and collections, many archival practices were developed in ways that contribute to this tension while introducing ethical and epistemological questions that complicate our ability to read archives as authoritative collections. Decisions about selection, description, curation, organization, and exhibition have vital implications for access and the construction of narrative within the archive. By questioning these practices as a series of choices and attitudes, scholars can arrive at a more meaningful understanding of how they enable and frustrate different kinds of knowledge production. This panel invites proposals that explore past and present archival practices to consider how they impact and empower knowledge communities. We invite papers from a variety of disciplinary perspectives, and welcome work that engages with a diverse range of material and digital objects. What kinds of knowledge choices are curators, collectors, and educators making? How are researchers and students interacting with these archival materials in ways that reinforce and challenge Western epistemologies? How do the ways that publics access and interact with archival collections and exhibits shape cultural knowledge and memory? How does a lack of access condition or obstruct agency in ways that constrain social change? Please submit a 250-300 word abstract through the NeMLA portal for consideration. Contact Kristie Schlauraff and Kate Kasten-Mutkus with questions at kristie.schlauraff@stonybrook.edu.

items.fullDescription: Call for Papers: Journal of Global Human Rights - Inaugural Volume The Journal of Global Human Rights invites submissions for its inaugural volume. The Journal of Global Human Rights is an international, interdisciplinary, double-blind peer-reviewed, open-access journal devoted to the study of human rights. It is an initiative of Research Committee 26 on Human Rights (RC26) of the International Political Science Association (IPSA). We welcome original research articles addressing the philosophical, legal, political and social dimensions of human rights. Topics include, but are not limited to: Human rights theory Political philosophy and philosophy of law International human rights law Justice and equality Democracy and the rule of law Freedom of expression Minority rights and multiculturalism Migration and refugee rights Gender and human rights Discrimination, racism and hate speech Digital technologies and human rights Transitional justice International relations and global human rights Global and regional human rights protection We particularly welcome contributions that combine theoretical analysis with contemporary human rights challenges, as well as interdisciplinary research engaging different academic traditions and regions of the world. All research articles undergo double-blind peer review. The journal is fully open access. There are no article processing charges (APCs) or publication fees. Submissions are now open for Volume 1. items.title: Decolonization, Digital Sphere, and Empowered Communities
items.location: Rhode Island · Salve Regina University in Newport,
items.excerpt: The digital infrastructure in today's world mirrors the colonial administrative structure with its control over data, policing user's behavior, and pushing narratives for the majoritarian political power. The global tech giants have as much sway in geopolitics as the global leaders themselves. Previously the conditions of colonization created an unequal e...
items.fullDescription: The digital infrastructure in today's world mirrors the colonial administrative structure with its control over data, policing user's behavior, and pushing narratives for the majoritarian political power. The global tech giants have as much sway in geopolitics as the global leaders themselves. Previously the conditions of colonization created an unequal economic infrastructure that marginalizes the local communities, and even after independence from the colonial power, the trade relations remain that of a colonial appendage. Similarly, the upkeep of the digital sphere is not without its economic and environmental hazards. Anibal Quijano (1928-2018) a Peruvian sociologist, talks about the plight of this expansion for resources in his book, On the Coloniality of Power. He says: …the contemporary scientific community, insists on destroying the conditions for life on the planet. So, both the movement of the most subjugated people in this world, those who would not be able to exist if they sold their means of subsistence, and those who realize that if all this comes to an end no one will be able to survive, come together in a shared analysis. 359 He stresses on the role of the communities who've resisted the colonial and postcolonial measures to protect their land, water, and air over the years. It shows how the communities have more of a lateral structure which allows for debate and discussions as opposed to the hierarchy of the colonial administrative infrastructure. This panel seeks to garner discourse around the digital world's ambivalent nature of enhancing global communications and generating jobs at the cost of endangering local communities. Questions, challenges, and possible solutions for a community-oriented resistance will be among the many concerns discussed at this panel. Submit on NeMLA's website: Submit an Abstract

items.title: Déplacements dans les réseaux transcoloniaux : l'Asie, l’Afrique et l’Europe reliés

Cette période marque en parallèle la rébellion très présente des autochtones de l'île - les Kanak - face à la dépossession territoriale des colons français. Le...
items.fullDescription: Pendant la période de l'Indochine française, les premiers vietnamiens sont acheminés en Nouvelle-Calédonie en tant que travailleurs sous-contrat dans les mines de nickel. Cette période marque en parallèle la rébellion très présente des autochtones de l'île - les Kanak - face à la dépossession territoriale des colons français. Le refus de participer à l'industrie minière d'un groupe favorise l'expatriation de l'autre sur l'archipel en pleine ère de la colonisation française dans plusieurs colonies. Le roi tonkinois Ham Nghi, à l'âge de 18 ans, a été placé en exil en Algérie après des années de mouvements de résistance contre la puissance coloniale française. Son expulsion fait écho à celle de la Reine malgache Ranavalona III, qui a eu lieu après l'annexion de Madagascar par la France en 1896. L'ensemble de l'empire français, étendu de l'Indochine à l'Afrique insulaire, est sujet à la déportation dans la plus grande colonie de peuplement. Ce réseau de déportation des colonies liées met en avant la question des outils de domination employés par le système colonial. Malgré les différentes populations colonisées, la stratégie de domination s'applique d'une certaine façon. **** Dans le cadre académique au sein des études francophones et françaises, nous voyons souvent des pistes de spécialisation distinctes, telles que les études européennes, les études caribéennes, et les études postcoloniales francophones. Les cours d'histoire et de littérature offrent également des réflexions particulières selon une région spécifique ainsi qu'une époque donnée. L'objectif de former les futurs chercheurs dans des domaines précis, faute d'études approfondies sur les caractéristiques transcontinentales, risque de faire oublier qu'au coeur de l'histoire de l'un est tissée celle de l'autre. Cette imbrication transnationale et transcommunautaire, inévitable soit-elle, est due à la fois aux déplacements migratoires, à l'exil d'après-guerre, et à la mobilisation de la force de travail par le système capitaliste et colonial. Lorsque l'on met en évidence ce lien intrinsèque entre des événements, on fait émerger un réseau transcolonial qui lie l'Afrique, l'Asie, et/ou l'Europe. Ce réseau nous oblige à réfléchir à l'interconnexion de l'un à l'autre, d'une communauté spécifique à une autre soi-disant éloignée. Dans le contexte du monde d'aujourd'hui, une telle conscience de l'interconnexion des histoires coloniales peut susciter des réflexions : Peut-on vraiment ignorer le combat de l'autre ? Quels seront les enjeux ? Communications à envoyer soit en anglais, soit en français.

items.title: Thinking in Images: Visualization, Imagination, and Empathy in Reading
items.excerpt: Visualization and imagination have long been recognized as vital to the act of reading. While Russian Formalist Viktor Shklovsky may have denounced the maxim "Art is thinking in images" in his seminal essay "Art as Device" (1917), in favor of strategies of defamiliarization, mental images and imagery are some of the most important ways we engage with a te...
items.fullDescription: Visualization and imagination have long been recognized as vital to the act of reading. While Russian Formalist Viktor Shklovsky may have denounced the maxim "Art is thinking in images" in his seminal essay "Art as Device" (1917), in favor of strategies of defamiliarization, mental images and imagery are some of the most important ways we engage with a text. In Dreaming by the Book , Elaine Scarry describes the function of poetry and novels as "instructions for mental composition" (244). That is, a text encourages readers to fill in the blanks; to reconstruct for themselves certain sensations, emotions, etc. These blanks, according to Wolfgang Iser in The Implied Reader , require readers to draw upon imagination, whereby meaning is created. Ultimately, literature encourages us to envision realities and modalities outside of our own. It is for this reason that reading fiction is considered to be an exercise in empathy--which Marco Caracciolo and Karin Kukkonen conceptualize to be a form of feeling with; of "imagining what we take him or her to be experiencing at a given moment" ( With Bodies: Narrative Theory and Embodied Cognition , 76). This seminar invites papers which attend to the function of visualization, imagination, and/or empathy in reading. In particular, participants are asked to consider how texts across a variety of genres, languages, time periods, cultural contexts, and subject positions, encourage similar or convergent ways of visualization, imagination, and empathy. Can we say reading is "thinking in images"? To what degree do texts encourage the generation of mental imagery and does this necessarily lead us to empathize? How does reading differ phenomenologically from engagement with other arts and mediums? What are the implications of cultivating an embodied and empathetic reading experience, particularly in an era of increasing polarization and automatization? How do certain texts reflect historical and cultural variations in bodily experience? We welcome interdisciplinary approaches drawing from affect theory, narratology, reader-response theory, phenomenology, psychoanalysis, cognitive literary studies, and other related fields. Possible topics may include, but are not limited to: Theories of mind (ToM) and cognitive approaches to reading; embodied models of reading. The impact of genre and form(at): fiction vs. non-fiction, literary vs. genre fiction, nonstandard/"non-literary" texts. Differences across bodies: gender, race, ethnicity, nationality, religion, and/or ability of readers, authors, narrators, and/or characters. Reading in translation or in different languages and effects on the ways we visualize, imagine, and empathize. Theories of imagination, literary imagination, and limits to imagination in reading. Narratological inquiries; impact of perspective and focalization impact on how we visualize and empathize. Reading in the age of Artificial Intelligence. How do AI/LLMs read and how do we read works produced by them?

items.title: Across Borders, Across Texts: Echoes, Revision, and Rewritings in Black Literature
items.location: University of Houston, Houston, Texas. · American Comparative Literature Association (ACLA)
items.excerpt: In the introduction to the Fourth Edition of The Norton Anthology of African American Literature, Henry Louis Gates Jr. and Valerie Smith emphasize the imitativeness of literature-Black literature, specifically. To them, literature begets newer literature. At the same time, readers have traced formal patterns of repetition and imitation in Black literatur...
items.fullDescription: In the introduction to the Fourth Edition of The Norton Anthology of African American Literature, Henry Louis Gates Jr. and Valerie Smith emphasize the imitativeness of literature-Black literature, specifically. To them, literature begets newer literature. At the same time, readers have traced formal patterns of repetition and imitation in Black literature across centuries, dating back to the antebellum. For instance, "Flight to Canada" by Ishmael Reed and "Kindred" by Octavia Butler; Harriet Tubman's "Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl" and Colson Whitehead's The Underground Railroad, published almost two centuries after Incidents; Mark Twain's Huckleberry Finn and Percival Everette's 2024 "James." These examples reinforce the notion that newer Black literature echoes, borrows, and imitates seminal literatures. This seminar thus seeks to investigate how Black literary and cultural productions have imitated other, earlier literary productions, even across genres and geographical boundaries-like what the editors of the anthology The Negro Caravan (1944) called "a sort of literary inbreeding which causes Negro writers to be influenced by other Negroes…" Even Kwame Anthony Appiah recently aver that "the history of art is the history of people borrowing and adapting techniques and tropes from earlier works." We seek papers that-using fictional and non-fictional Black writings and art-connect the past to the present-papers that explore "imitation," "influence," and "intertextuality" as central to Black literature and Black arts. Guiding questions to consider include, but are not limited to: What literary traditions have endured across generations, and how have they survived? What forms of continuity exist across Black literary history-Plantation to post-bellum literary and cultural productions, Africa to the Diaspora, across centuries, etc.? How do Black writers create new meanings from older texts? What role does memory play in Black literary traditions? How do contemporary writers preserve or challenge earlier literary traditions? How does Black literature reinvent its own past? What histories continue to shape Black literary expression? How do questions of race, identity, and freedom evolve across Black literary history? What earlier genres continue to influence Black literature today? How does Black literature balance tradition and innovation? What can earlier Black literature teach us about contemporary Black writing? Submit abstracts here: https://www.acla.org/seminar/defa99b9-6a8d-41ab-835d-2f1281fc3640 Session modality: Strictly in-person. Questions? Email: saadewumi@wisc.edu

items.fullDescription: 2027 National Advanced Writing Symposium "Evolving Possibilities: Futures of Advanced Writing" FREE & ONLINE, Hosted by the University of Southern California Event Date: Friday, January 29, 2027 Deadline to Submit a Proposal: Friday, September 25, 2026 Link to Submit a Proposal: https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSd9dZiyi_mlo-G9bYPmj47EmQg07M_Xv83yap4bkd_q0i73EQ/viewform Context The USC Writing Program is delighted to host the fourth annual National Advanced Writing Symposium! The event is entirely ONLINE and FREE to both speakers and attendees, as we aim to bring together teachers of advanced and/or upper-division college composition courses to discuss innovative methods and effective practices. Our theme, "Evolving Possibilities: Futures of Advanced Writing," welcomes participants to contemplate how Advanced Writing will address emerging needs and conditions in our discipline and beyond. Please join us and share your work in the Advanced Writing space. We hope to include a wide variety of topics, from how you theorize modes of writing beyond first-year composition to how you build your students' confidence and skills as they prepare to write in a rapidly changing, professional world beyond college. Our theme invites analyses of the multifaceted information landscapes that advanced student writers face as they transition from school writers to life writers. If selected to present at the symposium, you will also be invited to submit your work to the NAWS Online Journal , which will publish its inaugural issue in Fall 2027. Topics & Issues We welcome proposals for panels, individual presentations, workshops, and roundtables related to any of the following: The Human: How can we prioritize the humanity of knowledge production in Advanced Writing contexts? Humanist futures; innovations that embrace analog or paper-based practices; reimagining low-tech approaches; the paradox of reclaiming techniques of the past to offset the uncertainties of emerging technologies. The Generative: How is the humanity of writing in conversation with digital generative tools? Human generation versus machine synthesis; generative AI and LLMs, including contrasting views on these technologies and debates over their uses; writing as generative (because certainly, writing was generative before Chat GPT!) The Political: How can Advanced Writing pedagogies resist oppression, increase inclusion, and support social justice? The intersection of Advanced Writing and DEIB; teaching practices that fight fascism, encourage solidarity, or demonstrate "principled refusal"[1]; resisting institutional structures or social forces that estrange students from their work or each other. The Students' Futures: How might we help our students transition from "school writing" to "life writing" as they adjust to their professional worlds? Anticipating the changing needs and expectations of the professions and disciplines students are entering; professional writing; experiential learning; nonfiction genres as a form of social action.[2] The Discipline: How might Advanced Writing spaces serve to do more than rehash the rhetorical essay, but rather serve as a place to innovate pedagogies in a turbulent Higher Ed landscape? Adapting pedagogies to changing conditions; writing instructors and program administrators working in ways that are shaping or innovating our discipline; the future of Advanced Writing within the broader context of higher education. The Multifaceted Information Landscape: As a teacher or scholar of Advanced Writing, how are you playing in the multiverse? Genre as contextual; how identities shift across projects (i.e., multiple registers, voice, meeting audience and genre expectations while maintaining one's identity as an author); complex information landscapes (i.e., assemblages, Deleuze, Complexity; information circulation; alternative ways to access resources). What to Send Us A proposal of 250-450 words, along with a 40-60 word abstract. You can submit: Panel proposals: 3-4 speakers organized around a theme or issue of your choice Individual presentation proposals: 1-2 speakers delivering a single talk/paper Workshop proposals: Sessions focused on workshop activities and/or audience collaboration Roundtable proposals: 4-5 speakers gathering for a roundtable conversation on the issue of your choice For any questions about developing your proposal, contact Tamara Black at tamarabl@usc.edu or Elizabeth Durst at edurst@usc.edu with the subject line "NAWS 2027." 2027 NAWS Website: https://dornsife.usc.edu/the-writing-program/2027-national-advanced-writing-symposium/ [1] The act of rejecting systems-institutional, cultural, or corporate-that reproduce inequalities. For instance, see Tressie McMillan Cottom's "principled refusal" of AI dominance as a foregone conclusion here: https://www.instagram.com/p/DUlNVvmka05/ [2] See Miller, Carolyn R. "Genre as Social Action." The Quarterly Journal of Speech, 70, no. 2 (May 1984): 151-67. https://doi.org/10.1080/00335638409383686.

items.title: “The Real “Tethered”: A Critical Analysis of Double Consciousness, People, and Society”
items.location: Newport, Rhode Island · Northeast Modern Language Association
items.excerpt: Jordan Peele's Us is a critically acclaimed horror original about government-manufactured clones that are forced to mimic the lives of the people who live on the surface like stringless puppets. While Peele focuses more on a physical tethering, there is a psychological tethering that can be gleamed from this piece, specifically as it relates to the idea o...
items.fullDescription: Jordan Peele's Us is a critically acclaimed horror original about government-manufactured clones that are forced to mimic the lives of the people who live on the surface like stringless puppets. While Peele focuses more on a physical tethering, there is a psychological tethering that can be gleamed from this piece, specifically as it relates to the idea of double consciousness. In his work "The Striving of the Negro People," W.E.B. Du Bois describes this idea as "this sense of always looking at oneself through the eyes of others, of measuring one's soul by the tape of a world that looks on in amused contempt or pity. One ever feels his two-ness-an American, a Negro, two souls, two thoughts, two unreconciled strivings; two warring ideals in one dark body, whose dogged strength alone keeps it from being torn asunder." These "warring ideas" can exist in any group as the numerous stereotypes, prejudices, and misconceptions alive and well in the world has convinced many to fashion a Franksteined-version of themselves in the hopes of being accepted or safe. The jerky, uncoordinated movements of the tethered from the movie are the perfect metaphor for this forced reality. People attempting to push themselves to live in ways they were not meant to and should not have to. This panel is asking participants to provide submissions that explore the many ways this "tethering" has manifested in the world and explain the impact had on people's lives or how this knowledge can be used as a way to empower people and bring communities together. In other words, in what ways could we be tethered to unfair or unjust interpretations in the world and/or how could our lived experiences be used to untether us from opinions and views that do not empower us and help us build healthy communities? The chair welcomes essays, critical analysis, creative non-fiction, hybrid works, and excerpts of longer pieces.

items.excerpt: In the United States, our lives are marked by an abundance of convenience. From fresh produce year-round to two-day shipping, convenient choices feel soft, easy, and frictionless, as they have specifically been engineered to feel. Until relatively recently, it has been possible to maintain a cultural and systemic sense of alienation that makes the cost of...
items.fullDescription: In the United States, our lives are marked by an abundance of convenience. From fresh produce year-round to two-day shipping, convenient choices feel soft, easy, and frictionless, as they have specifically been engineered to feel. Until relatively recently, it has been possible to maintain a cultural and systemic sense of alienation that makes the cost of our convenience invisible to us-to localize all of the necessary precarity and exploitation for convenience "somewhere else," (often in the Global South) and then to ignore it. However, the veil is lifting, and "somewhere else" has reached us directly--worker and labor exploitation, droughts and systemic extermination of wild animals, widening class gaps, heat waves, short and snowless winters, floods, wildfires, unprecedented weather patterns, booming microbe populations that alter the very soil we stand on. A sustainable future must be an inconvenient one, and perhaps a precarious one, unless we can remake communities with a focus on outmoded forms of convenience: reciprocity, mutual aid, de-suburbanization, and anti-capitalism. In this panel, we hope to facilitate a conversation about art, in/convenience, precarity, and resistance in community. We also hope to consider alternate views of in/convenience: What can we do to create communities in which the inconvenience of slowness is celebrated rather than derided? How can we utilize writing to grieve futures that didn't materialize? How might we create work that celebrates the pleasure of systemic and interpersonal inconvenience? How can we build resilience to inconvenience and precarity at once, together? In the tradition of scholars and writers like Lauren Berlant, Hanif Abdurraqib, Anna Lowenhaupt Tsing, and Margaret Price, how can we embrace the inconvenient as a site of connection and resistance? We welcome writers of creative nonfiction, poetry, fiction, art pieces, and hybrid works who seek to consider community and in/convenience. We are looking for writing about all forms of convenience and inconvenience, from the granular to the esoteric. After panelists share their work, the chairs will facilitate a conversation between writers and audience members.

items.fullDescription: Call for Papers NeMLA's 58th Annual Convention - "Empowering Communities" March 6-9, 2027 | Salve Regina University, Newport, Rhode Island (Hybrid Conference) Panel Title: Tracing Female Body, Art & Economy in the Global South Primary Area / Secondary Area: Women's and Gender Studies / Interdisciplinary Humanities Modality: Hybrid Chair: Maryam Raza (University of Auckland, New Zealand) This panel explores how the historical treatment of female bodies in the Global South through the patriarchal structures of subjectification, commodification, sexualization and objectification has been reversed by contemporary strategies of resistance and reclamation. The panel examines how the postmodern woman in diverse socio-economic contexts "trains" the masculine gaze (Dixit 2024) over her body, renegotiating agency. Women increasingly reconfigure the female body through carnivalesque, alternative spaces of identity, creativity and skill through embodied forms. The female body evolves from a passive object of desire into an active, expressive, and economically productive site. Thus, women transform spaces of suppression to places of resistance and empowerment. Hussain et al. (2025) note that emancipation precedes autonomy and decision-making in socio-economic spheres. The panel further examines the intersection of bodily narratives with performative femininity, wellness cultures, fitness regimes, and beauty and anti-aging industries. It also restructures the domestic space as a site of culinary entrepreneurship, aided by digital platforms. Consequently, the Global South woman utilizes such arenas to enhance visibility, economic upward mobility, and global networks beyond what Fahmida Riaz termed the "Four Walled Homestead." Drawing on interdisciplinary approaches from cultural, gender, media, literary, and postcolonial studies, this panel foregrounds how women collectively construct bodily identities that both challenge and adapt to tradition. The selected papers will revolve around the following themes: Women and wellness culture Gender, food, and culinary skills Ageing Dance Cultures Women and Performing Arts Fetishizing and infantilizing women within beauty industry Submission Deadline : September 30, 2026 Please submit abstracts via the NeMLA portal: https://cfplist.com/nemla/Home/S/22411 For queries about the panel, prospective participants are warmly encouraged to contact the chair: Maryam Raza mraz655@aucklanduni.ac.nz

items.fullDescription: Abstract : This roundtable explores contemporary directions in life writing, biography, and memoir, with a particular interest in how we narrate the self amidst evolving issues of identity, culture, and power. We welcome both traditional scholarly essays and creative nonfiction/memoir submissions accompanied by a brief meta-analysis. Potential topics include, but are not limited to, autoethnography, digital self-representation, intersectional approaches to life writing, and the emerging impacts of technological shifts-such as generative AI-on authorship and equity. Desctription : How do we articulate, preserve, and present our lived experiences in an era marked by rapid cultural and technological change? Aligning with the conference theme, "Our Ruling Classes: Culture, Power and Conflict," this roundtable invites participants to investigate the shifting landscape of life writing across textual, digital, and visual formats. To foster a vibrant, multi-voiced dialogue, we encourage submissions from a wide range of perspectives, including traditional literary criticism, biographical studies, and creative pieces that feature a reflective or meta-analytical component. Presenters will deliver brief, 10-to-12-minute talks to maximize time for collective discussion. Link for submissions: https://pamla.ballastacademic.com/Home/S/20174 Submission Deadline: June 30, 2026 Conference format: In Person, in Seattle. No provision for virtual presentations If you have any queries, please reach out to the undersigned: Dr. Meghna Gangadharan Presiding Officer, "Narrating the Self Today" Email: phd1901261010@alum.iiti.ac.in

Artistic works offer numerous examples of figures who maintain an ambivalent relationship to their communities. Because of their social or ethnic origins, their...
items.fullDescription: This panel invites papers that examine the agency of marginalized characters in literary, visual, audiovisual, and artistic productions from the French?speaking world across any historical period. Artistic works offer numerous examples of figures who maintain an ambivalent relationship to their communities. Because of their social or ethnic origins, their divergent perspectives, or their transgression of established norms, certain characters find themselves pushed to the margins of social, familial, or professional groups. While such exclusion may appear to weaken those who experience it, this panel asks whether marginalization might also function as a source of strength. Can marginality become a generative position? Do marginalized individuals succeed in forming new communities that enable them to confront stigma and ultimately overcome it? This discussion seeks to shift our understanding of the place occupied by marginalized individuals and groups in fictional narratives. By considering the networks of solidarity that emerge among marginalized subjects, the panel explores what lies beneath their presumed inferiority, inviting critical attention to what is hidden, erased, or rendered invisible within dominant narratives. More importantly, we will examine how marginalized communities may become empowering spaces of resistance, mutual support, and hope. Drawing on approaches from cultural studies, postcolonial theory, sociolinguistics, and intersectionality, this session seeks to understand how literary, visual, audiovisual, and artistic narratives stage the tensions between marginality and belonging, strength and vulnerability. Proposals engaging with environmental humanities, posthumanism, Indigenous studies, as well as diaspora and migration studies are strongly encouraged. We also welcome submissions drawing on gender and queer studies, memory and trauma studies, digital humanities, or other interdisciplinary frameworks within the humanities. We welcome proposals of 250-300 words, in French or English, submitted by September 30.

items.fullDescription: Building Bridges: Preparing for Global Business (39th Annual IATEFL BESIG Conference) When : Friday, November 20, 2026 (13.00 CET / 12.00 UK time) - Sunday, November 22, 2026 (14.00 CET / 13.00 UK time) Venue : Hotel Flemings Wien Stadthalle in Vienna, Austria. Call for Proposals Business English education sits at the intersection of education, professional communication, and global social change. In a world shaped by geopolitical tensions, economic inequalities, technological disruption, and cultural polarization, communication across cultural contexts is both more necessary and more complex than ever. Business English therefore involves more than teaching linguistic skills for the workplace; it also prepares learners to deal with cultural diversity, power structures, and ethical decision-making in international professional contexts. Effective professional communication today requires not only exchanging information but also negotiating meaning, building trust, and collaborating across cultures and perspectives. Business English courses support university students, vocational learners, and professionals in developing communicative competence, intercultural awareness, and confidence in multilingual workplaces. In many contexts, this work involves collaboration with corporate partners and engagement with current workplace practices, while also encouraging critical reflection on whose voices are heard in professional communication. The role of the business English educator is therefore to help learners bridge multiple gaps: between education and professional practice, between various cultures, and between local experiences and global systems. In a fragmented and rapidly changing world, business English education can help create spaces for inclusive, responsible, and effective professional communication. This year's conference invites contributions that explore how business English education can respond to these challenges and build the bridges needed for meaningful intercultural understanding. We particularly welcome contributions that combine practical experience, innovative teaching approaches, and reflective insights from educational and professional contexts. ----------------- Thank you for your interest in submitting a speaker proposal for the 39th IATEFL BESIG Conference. Only members of IATEFL BESIG can present at the conference. You may submit a proposal if you are not a member; however, if your proposal is accepted, you will be required to join IATEFL BESIG in order to be included in the programme. The call for proposals is open until 30 June 2026 at 16:00 (UK time). Click here for more information: https://www.iateflbesig.org/events/annual-conference
