items.fullDescription: Call for Chapters Rhetoric and Communication. Interdisciplinary Studies in the Humanities The intersection of Rhetoric and Communication continues to attract the interest of many scholars, particularly within the fields of the Humanities and Social Sciences. The scope of analysis is wide-ranging, encompassing literature and culture, language studies and advertising, communication studies and politics, among other domains. In this Volume, we aim to bring together a set of studies that focus directly on topics shared by Rhetoric and Communication, from Classical Antiquity to the present, from an interdisciplinary perspective. Scholarly contributions across the Humanities will enhance our understanding of the influence of rhetoric and communication on society, taking into account, on the one hand, there is a vast legacy that merits further study and, on the other, new forms of communication require us to reassess the impact of the rhetorical art. This Volume welcomes contributions of a theoretical or empirical nature, including case studies, from within the field of the Humanities. Possible topics include: · Rhetorical and communication theory applied to discourse; · Treatises on rhetoric and communication; · The presence of rhetorical genres in contemporary forms of communication; · Argumentation techniques and persuasion in literary texts, the media, advertising, or other narrative forms; · The contemporary relevance of teaching rhetoric and communication; · The contemporary application of classical rhetoric in the media; · Rhetoric in political discourse and in literary composition; · Philosophical perspectives on rhetoric and communication; · The role of the audience and the addressee in rhetorical theory and in the communicative process; · Representations of rhetoric and communication in the Arts. Editors: Cristina Santos Pinheiro, Joaquim Pinheiro, Rui Carlos Fonseca, Samuel Mateus, Telmo Reis e Vanessa Cesário Proposals, in Word format, should be submitted by 10 September 2026 to the following email address: retorica.comunicacao@mail.uma.pt The Volume is scheduled for publication in March 2027 by a leading national publisher. All submissions will be subject to scientific evaluation (blind peer review). Authors will be notified of the review decision by 30 November 2026. 1. Accepted languages Submissions will be accepted in Portuguese, French, English, and Spanish. 2. Formatting guidelines 2.1. Length and formatting: main text: maximum of 20 A4 pages and minimum of 12 A4 pages; font: 11 pt, Aptos, 1.5 line spacing; footnotes: 10 pt, Aptos, single spacing. 2.2. Title centred, 12 pt, bold, Aptos. 2.3. Author name(s), affiliation (University, Institute, Research Unit or equivalent), email address, and ORCID should be provided in 11 pt, Aptos. 2.4. Two abstracts (maximum 250 words each) must be included: one in the language of the article and one in English, followed by up to five keywords. 3. General guidelines 3.1. Citations and references should follow APA style (7th ed.); all citations must be properly identified. 3.2. Quotations longer than three lines must be indented 1 cm from the left margin. 3.3. a) Italics should be used for the titles of works, modern monographs, and journals. b) Quotation marks (" ") should be used for quotations from modern texts. c) Italics should not be used for Latin abbreviations (op. cit., loc. cit., cf., ibid., in…). 4. Footnotes Footnotes should be brief. 5. Images/Graphs/Tables 5.1. Any graphical elements must be clearly identified and numbered. 5.2. Images must be submitted in .jpeg format, with a minimum resolution of 300 dpi, be free of copyright fees, and accompanied by official proof of permission or purchase of rights for academic publication. Each submission may include no more than four images (printing will not be in color). 6. Final bibliography The bibliography should be limited to essential works or cited references and must conform to APA style (7th ed.). 7. Publication The Volume will be published by a Portuguese publisher with extensive experience in scientific publishing. It will also be made available as an e-book in institutional repositories. 8. Copyright statement Submissions must be original, and authors grant publication rights upon acceptance.

items.fullDescription: Northeast MLA 2027: March 6-9, 2027 Panel Title: Supporting the Well-Being of Students and Instructors in a Transitional Time Modality: Virtual Only: All presentations will be delivered via Zoom regardless of whether the presenters are in-person Format: 3-4 presentations/papers, 15-20 minutes per presenter The past few years - which could be described as part of a larger cultural, political, and economic flash point -- have created true challenges for higher education. This transitional time has put pressure on all parties of our postsecondary community, as seen in the reported mental health challenges of undergraduates and the high rates of burnout amongst faculty and support networks in the sector (Mowreader; Pourasadollahi and Vincenti; Liu). In addition to these post-pandemic stressors, a host of broader concerns are also impinging on the postsecondary environment (see "The Trends Report" for one discussion). How can we empower our community - defined through instructors, students, and/or support services -- during such a transitional moment? This session will create a dialogue that touches on any of the following: -discussions/studies of interventions and/or articulations of already established practices in supporting the well-being of students and/or instructors; -the reflections of students, instructors, and/or support networks on the challenges of and responses to our contemporary moment. These challenges can include: the impact of budget cuts on postsecondary contexts, the fallout of declining academic freedom in the classroom, the impact (positive or negative) of Gen AI on the well-being of our community, the discord between instructor expectations and the reality of students. References Liu, Adrienne. "Higher Education is Exhausted." The Chronicle of Higher Education, 10 Feb. 2025, https://www.chronicle.com/article/higher-education-is-exhausted. Mowreader, Ashley. "Survey: Getting a Grip on the Student Mental Health Crisis," Inside Higher Ed, 19 Aug. 2024, https://www.insidehighered.com/news/student-success/health-wellness/2024/08/19/experts-weigh-college-student-mental-health-crisis. Pourasadollahi, Khatereh and Michele Vincenti. "Unveiling the Layers of Faculty Burnout in Canadian Private Universities during the post-COVID Pandemic Period." Journal of Education and Learning, vol. 14, no. 2, 2025, pp. 43-52. https://doi.org/10.5539/jel.v14n2p43. "The Trends Report 2026," The Chronicle of Higher Education, March 2026, https://www.chronicle.com/package/trends-report-2026. Submission Details 200-300 word abstract to the NeMLA portal (https://cfplist.com/nemla/Home/S/22639) by September 30, 2026 Please email any questions to Stacy Denton (sdenton@uwaterloo.ca)

items.fullDescription: Poetry is a perfect medium to explore all of the key issues planned for the 58th Annual NeMLA Convention. The focus of this year's convention is Empowering Communities," which is identified on the NeMLA website as evoking the "process of transformation from a state of passivity to being active agents of change. It represents a shift away from authoritarianism and toward a model that values (and solves problems through) local knowledge, collaboration, and collective action," terms which lend themselves well to the emotional expressions within poetry. For the past five years, the Closet Poets sessions have enjoyed many scholars who research and write papers for conferences as well as write poetry. Perhaps those poems are jotted on note pads, in the margins of your papers or in dedicated personal journals. This session is seeking those scholars whose poetry often remains unpublished due to the heavier responsibility of publishing scholarly journal articles, monographs and genre-specific books which demand much time in between teaching, and perhaps, administrating at the university. Even though those scholarly efforts may yield more rewards, such as job retention and hopefully, job promotions; personal poetry, intermittently created, yields a satisfying venue for emotional issues and satisfying creativity. The 2027 Revisiting Closet Poets Creative session is an opportunity to expand and share your poetry by perhaps featuring the key issues of this years' convention. I am pleased to report that MLS published several participants poetic work since 2023 in their online venue. Perhaps you will have an opportunity to have your work published in MLS in future publications of our Closet Poets work. Remember the words of Poet Laureate, Robert Pinsky, who shared his joy of telling poems during a previous NeMLA conference, "Poetry is the breath of humankind, and must be heard." NOTE: This session is hybrid. It will be seated and accessible on Zoom. Please indicate which you prefer when you submit your proposals. Thank you. You do not need to be a NeMLA member to submit a proposal.

items.fullDescription: This seminar proposes to approach William S. Burroughs not simply as a subject of study, but as a problem. We invite provocative papers grounded in comparative methodologies and attentive to less-travelled texts, episodes, affiliations, and cultural encounters. Rather than asking what Burroughs "was," we want to ask what his work does-and to pause over the categories through which we have learned to understand his oeuvre, asking what they illuminate and, perhaps more importantly, what they conceal. What notions of authorship, originality, literary value, sexuality, politics, nationality, identity, language, media, knowledge, or artistic production did Burroughs put under pressure? What happens when his writing is read alongside figures, traditions, media, or intellectual histories with which it is not usually associated? Can Burroughs's experiments still unsettle us? And what do we make of his political views today? We are interested in archival work, but not simply in the recovery of origins or the reconstruction of authorial intention. Archives can instead be approached as contested sites of selection, mediation, myth-making, and afterlife. We are equally interested in familiar Burroughsian techniques-cut-up, collage, montage, sampling, recording-when they are placed in unexpected comparative contexts. What do these techniques actually do? How have they travelled beyond Burroughs? How are they being used today, and by whom? We also welcome papers willing to be unfriendly to their subject. Is Burroughs overrated? Is he politically embarrassing, historically compromised, or aesthetically exhausted? Is he already "cancelled"-or has cancellation itself become another way of making cultural icons safe? Can Burroughs be restored, and if so, to what? Or is he damaged beyond repair? What might we gain by taking seriously the possibility that some of his work should be rejected rather than rescued? Possible approaches include, but are not limited to: Burroughs and writers, artists, or intellectual traditions with which he is rarely compared Burroughs and competing theories of authorship, originality, and literary value Archives, censorship, canonization, and the production of literary authority Burroughs and the politics of race, gender, sexuality, class, empire, and nationality Burroughs's relationship to religion, esotericism, anthropology, science, medicine, and alternative forms of knowledge Literary and non-literary media: sound, film, photography, visual art, performance, television, and digital culture Adaptation, appropriation, influence, imitation, and misreading The contemporary uses and abuses of Burroughs Critical reception, including hostile, skeptical, and revisionist readings We especially welcome proposals that are comparative in more than name: papers that put Burroughs into genuine friction with another author, tradition, medium, language, archive, or conceptual framework. We are less interested in proving that Burroughs anticipated everything than in discovering where he fails, contradicts himself, becomes strange, becomes ordinary, or becomes impossible to classify.

items.fullDescription: The Centre for Research on Language and Culture Contact invites you to submit an abstract for Resisting Abandonment: Language, Culture, and Ecology, an interdisciplinary conference that will explore the ways in which ecology intersects with language contact, cultural transformation, and pedagogical practice. Conference Dates: October 15-16, 2026 Location: Glendon College -York University (Toronto, Canada) Keynote Speaker: Daniel Frost, Professor of Spanish and of Latin American, Latinx, and Caribbean Studies, College of the Holy Cross Abstracts Due: June 15, 2026 - - - - - - - - - - - - - Le Centre de recherche sur le contact des langues et des cultures vous invite à soumettre un résumé pour Résister à l'abandon : langue, culture et écologie, un colloque interdisciplinaire qui explorera les liens entre l'écologie, le contact linguistique, la transformation culturelle et les pratiques pédagogiques. Dates du colloque : 15-16 octobre 2026 Lieu : Collège universitaire Glendon - Université York (Toronto, Canada) Conférencier principal : Daniel Frost, professeur d'espagnol et d'études latino-américaines, latinx et caribéennes, College of the Holy Cross Date limite de soumission des résumés : 15 juin 2026 - - - - - - - - - - - - - International Conference Resisting Abandonment: Language, Culture, and Ecology Centre for Research on Language and Culture Contact Glendon College, York University (Toronto, Canada) October 15-16, 2026 The Centre for Research on Language and Culture Contact invites you to an interdisciplinary conference that will explore the ways in which ecology intersects with language contact, cultural transformation, and pedagogical practice. Resisting Abandonment is inspired by Sunaura Taylor's groundbreaking book Disabled Ecologies: Lessons from a Wounded Desert (2024), which challenges dominant environmental narratives by centring disability, care, and interdependence. The conference aims to build on Taylor's theorization of abandonment - material and ideological - which manifests in polluted landscapes, dispossessed communities, endangered languages, and marginalized bodies. Ecological degradation and linguistic erosion often unfold together, shaped by colonialism, extractivism, migration, and neoliberal restructuring. In Ecolinguistics: Language, Ecology, and the Stories We Live By (2020), Arran Stibbe articulates the ways in which ecolinguistic inquiry - including language-contact studies - reveals how knowledges of living sustainably in the local environment are embedded in endangered languages and are vulnerable to the global spread of dominant languages. Threats to linguistic diversity can be correlated to diminished biodiversity. Resisting Abandonment will foreground the idea that languages, like ecosystems, are sites of relationality and care. When communities are displaced by climate crises, economic dispossession, or other factors, their linguistic practices shift, hybridize, or face erasure. Yet contact zones also generate creative survivance: new vernaculars, embodied knowledges, and solidarities across difference. The conference convenes scholars, educators, translators, artists, and community advocates to examine how practices of naming, storytelling, teaching, and translating can resist ecological, linguistic, and cultural abandonment. How do metaphors of purity and contamination shape both environmental and linguistic policy? What can disability justice teach us about sustaining multilingual ecologies of access? How might translation function as a form of environmental care work? Participants will explore the ethical and political stakes of attending to fragile ecologies - human and more-than-human - without reproducing narratives of loss that justify further neglect. Resisting Abandonment invites collective reflection on care as method, contact as creativity, and interdependence as a framework for ecological and linguistic futures. Examples of subtopics by discipline: Cultural Studies : analyzing representations of ecological and linguistic wastelands - including their recuperation and adaptation - in media and literature of former and current power sites and/or in post/neocolonial texts. Linguistics : examining how ecological loss accelerates language endangerment or, conversely, how language erosion facilitates ecological loss; reflecting on whether documentation practices themselves risk reproducing extractive models Sociolinguistics : studies of language contact in climate-displaced communities; examining codeswitching as ecological adaptation Translation Studies : translating environmental knowledge across Indigenous and minoritized languages without epistemic extraction Pedagogy : designing care-centred, place-based curricula that link environmental justice with multilingual education Communication Studies : analyzing how environmental crises and linguistic marginalization are framed across media, policy discourse, and digital platforms; probing how choice of language used in the media influences how communities think about ecological issues and/or manufactures consent Second-Language Teaching : incorporating local ecological narratives into L2 classrooms to foster environmental and intercultural care Minority-Language Advocacy : examining how environmental policy, urban planning, and disaster response frequently neglect linguistic accessibility, thereby compounding abandonment or proposing strategies for integrating language justice into climate-resilience planning Those interested in contributing to the conference with a 20-minute paper should send a title, 200-word abstract, and short biography to crlcc@glendon.yorku.ca by June 15, 2026. Keynote speaker: Daniel Frost, Professor of Spanish and Latin American, Latinx, and Caribbean Studies, College of the Holy Cross Scientific Committee: Sibo Chen, Associate Professor & Associate Chair, School of Professional Communication, Toronto Metropolitan University Bruce Connell, Professor of Linguistics, Language, and Society, York University's Glendon College Maryanne L. Colloque international Résister à l'abandon: langue, culture et écologie Centre de recherche sur le contact des langues et des cultures Collège universitaire Glendon, Université York (Toronto, Canada) 15 et 16 octobre 2026 Le Centre de recherche sur le contact des langues et des cultures vous invite à un colloque interdisciplinaire qui explorera les manières dont l'écologie interagit avec le contact entre les langues, avec les transformations culturelles et avec les pratiques pédagogiques. Résister à l'abandon s'inspire de l'ouvrage marquant de Sunaura Taylor, Disabled Ecologies: Lessons from a Wounded Desert (2024), qui remet en question les récits environnementaux dominants à la lumière du handicap, du respect et de l'interdépendance. Le colloque vise à approfondir la théorisation de l'abandon, à la fois matériel et idéologique, proposée par Taylor, qui se manifeste dans des paysages pollués, des communautés dépossédées, des langues en voie de disparition et des corps marginalisés. La dégradation écologique et l'érosion linguistique évoluent souvent conjointement, façonnées par le colonialisme, l'extractivisme, les migrations et les restructurations néolibérales. Dans Ecolinguistics: Language, Ecology, and the Stories We Live By (2020), Arran Stibbe met en lumière la manière dont les approches écolinguistiques, y compris les études sur le contact entre les langues, permettent de mieux comprendre les liens entre langue et environnement. Les menaces qui pèsent sur la diversité linguistique peuvent ainsi être reliées à l'appauvrissement de la biodiversité. Résister à l'abandon mettra en avant l'idée que les langues, à l'instar des écosystèmes, constituent des espaces de relation et de respect. Lorsque des communautés sont déplacées par des crises climatiques, la dépossession économique ou d'autres facteurs, leurs pratiques linguistiques se transforment, s'hybrident ou risquent de disparaître. Pourtant, les zones de contact engendrent également des formes créatives de survie: de nouveaux vernaculaires, des savoirs incarnés et des solidarités au-delà des différences. Le colloque réunit des chercheur·e·s, enseignant·e·s, traducteurs/trices, artistes et militant·e·s communautaires afin d'examiner comment les pratiques de nomination, de narration, d'enseignement et de traduction peuvent résister à l'abandon écologique, linguistique et culturel. Comment les métaphores de pureté et de contamination influencent-elles les politiques environnementales et linguistiques? Que peut nous apprendre la justice du handicap sur le maintien d'écologies multilingues accessibles? De quelle manière la traduction peut-elle fonctionner comme une forme de soin environnemental? Les participant·e·s réfléchiront aux enjeux éthiques et politiques liés à l'attention portée aux écologies fragiles, humaines et plus qu'humaines, sans reproduire des récits de perte qui justifient davantage de négligence. Résister à l'abandon invite à une réflexion collective sur le respect en tant que méthode, sur le contact comme créativité et sur l'interdépendance comme cadre pour penser les futurs écologiques et linguistiques. Exemples de sous-thèmes par discipline : Études culturelles : analyser les représentations des déserts écologiques et linguistiques, y compris leur récupération et leur adaptation, dans les médias et la littérature issus de centres de pouvoir, anciens ou actuels, et/ou dans des textes post/néocoloniaux Linguistique : examiner comment la perte écologique accélère la disparition des langues ou, inversement, comment l'érosion linguistique facilite la perte écologique; réfléchir à la possibilité que les pratiques de documentation elles-mêmes reproduisent des modèles extractivistes Sociolinguistique : étudier le contact entre les langues dans des communautés déplacées par les changements climatiques; analyser l'alternance codique comme forme d'adaptation écologique Traductologie : traduire les connaissances environnementales dans les langues autochtones et minoritaires sans extraction épistémique Pédagogie et didactique : concevoir des programmes axés sur les soins et ancrés dans le territoire, qui associent la justice environnementale à l'éducation multilingue Études en communication : analyser la manière dont les crises environnementales et la marginalisation linguistique sont représentées dans les médias, les discours politiques et les plateformes numériques; examiner comment les choix linguistiques dans les médias influencent la manière dont les communautés pensent les enjeux écologiques et contribuent à fabriquer le consentement Enseignement d'une langue seconde : intégrer des récits écologiques locaux dans les cours de langue seconde afin de promouvoir le respect de l'environnement et l'ouverture interculturelle Promotion des langues minoritaires : examiner comment les politiques environnementales, l'urbanisme et les interventions en cas de catastrophe négligent souvent l'accessibilité linguistique, ce qui accentue l'abandon de ces communautés, ou proposer des stratégies visant à intégrer la justice linguistique dans la planification de la résilience climatique Si vous souhaitez contribuer au colloque avec une communication de 20 minutes, veuillez envoyer un titre, un résumé de 200 mots et une courte biographie à crlcc@glendon.yorku.ca avant le 15 juin 2026. items.fullDescription: Call for Proposals Transformative Synergies Harmonizing the Future: Interdisciplinary Pathways for a Resilient Society Transformative Synergies brings together faculty, scholars, graduate students and practitioners to explore how disciplines can intersect to address the complex challenges shaping our world. As technology, public health, social policy, education and the arts continue to evolve, meaningful solutions increasingly require collaboration across traditional academic boundaries. This conference invites researchers and creators to examine the connections among arts, business, STEM, health and education and consider how these fields can work together to build a more resilient society. Submit Your Work We welcome proposals that explore innovative ideas, research and creative approaches related to the conference theme, including: Pedagogy for a New Era: Interdisciplinary curriculum design, trauma-informed education and the future of the R2 research institution Creative Technologies: Digital preservation, emerging technologies and the ethics of the human-machine interface Social Equity & Policy: Research addressing systemic health and educational disparities Health-Arts Nexus: Narrative medicine, art therapy and the role of the humanities in public health Sustainability & STEM: Environmental science, Indigenous knowledge and resilient urban design These topics are not exhaustive. Proposals that explore meaningful connections across disciplines are encouraged. Graduate Student Symposium The conference will feature a Graduate Student Panel designed to give emerging scholars an opportunity to share research in progress, completed projects, theses and dissertations. The session will provide a supportive environment for scholarly feedback, interdisciplinary dialogue and networking with scholars from across institutions. Proposal Formats We welcome: Individual papers Panel discussions Poster presentations Creative and multimedia works Workshops and interactive sessions Who Should Submit? Graduate students, faculty, researchers and practitioners from all disciplines are encouraged to submit original work that engages with the conference theme. Proposal Guidelines Proposals should be 300-600 words, depending on disciplinary standards, and address: Title - A concise, descriptive title that engages an interdisciplinary audience. Purpose and Central Question/Problem - The primary aim of the work. Conceptual, Theoretical or Disciplinary Framework - The intellectual foundation of the work. Methods, Materials or Creative Approach - How the work was conducted or developed. Findings, Claims or Scholarly Contribution - The work's intellectual contribution. Interdisciplinary Significance and Broader Impact - The relevance of the work beyond a single discipline. For panels, submit an individual abstract for each paper. How Proposals Are Reviewed All proposals will undergo peer review and will be evaluated based on: Clarity and coherence Scholarly rigor Methodological or interpretive soundness Originality and contribution to knowledge Interdisciplinary engagement and accessibility Relevance to the conference theme Conference Information Nov. 8-10, 2026 The Hotel at the University of Maryland Discounted rates are available for conference attendees. Ready to Contribute? Share your research, scholarship or creative work with an interdisciplinary community exploring new approaches to the challenges of the 21st century. Submit your proposal: graduateschool@bowiestate.edu Transformative Synergies Arts, Business, STEM, Health & Education for a Changing World Bowie State University | The Graduate School

items.fullDescription: Date: October 10-11, 2026 Location: SMU Main Campus, Dallas, TX Theme: Movement & Borderlands Abstract Submission Deadline: August 28, 2026 Keynotes: Dr. Tim Bowman & Dr. Elda María Román Graduate students of Southern Methodist University's Departments of English, History, and Anthropology, in collaboration with the Moody School of Advanced Studies, Dedman College Interdisciplinary Institute, and the department of English, have collaborated to hold the third annual Engaging Research Across the Humanities (ERAH) Conference at SMU from October 10-October 11, 2026. ERAH 2026 will prioritize the development of interdisciplinary connections and aims to foster a supportive environment for both graduate students and advanced undergraduates engaged in strong research. There will be special emphasis placed on creating opportunities for participants with limited or no prior conference experience. The theme for ERAH 2026 is Movement & Borderlands. If you have any questions, please email arundhatig@smu.edu. Borders simultaneously construct and limit meaning. By demarcating entities, we hold the power to define space and identity. In the same manner, those entities are restricted to oppositional definitions. What does it mean to occupy borderlands, to move across them and through them? How is the deconstruction of borders, or reconceptualization of definitional demarcation, itself an act of meaning-making that exists without opposition? How do borderlands complicate cultural conceptions rooted in duality? How does movement across and through borderlands produce opportunity for new forms of meaning-making not rooted in hard lines and limitations? This year's theme asks us to think critically about the roles of both movement and borderlands in our respective disciplines by considering these questions and others. We invite you to consider the roles of both movement and borderlands within the works you study-be it literary works, historical archives, etc.-as well as how pervasive disciplinary paradigms shape the ways in which you approach your scholarship. Possible topics may include but are not limited to: Migration, mobility, and displacement Citizenship and belonging Racial, ethnic, national, religious identity Borders as constructs Frontiers Artistic and embodied movement Indigenous perspectives on imposed borders Nationalism and borderlands Environmental and ecological borders Linguistic borders Tourism and global circulation We invite abstracts of 200-250 words for both individual presentations and fully-constructed panels (3-4 speakers). Papers in STEM fields that clearly articulate relevance to the theme are welcome. Full-panel proposals will be given priority. Panel proposals must include a 200-250 word proposal for the panel in addition to abstracts for each individual participant. A select number of travel grants will be awarded on a competitive basis for those traveling more than 100 miles. To qualify for a travel grant, you must submit your application by August 14, 2026. Further details will be included in your registration sign-up. Please submit abstracts via the following google form link: https://tinyurl.com/2026ERAH

items.title: Academic Freedom Now: Rights, Classrooms, and the Future of Democratic Knowledge
items.excerpt: This panel examines academic freedom not only as an individual right, but as a collective condition necessary for the production, circulation, and contestation of knowledge within democratic societies. In alignment with the theme of Empowering Communities, we consider how academic freedom enables communities-within and beyond the university-to participate...
items.fullDescription: This panel examines academic freedom not only as an individual right, but as a collective condition necessary for the production, circulation, and contestation of knowledge within democratic societies. In alignment with the theme of Empowering Communities, we consider how academic freedom enables communities-within and beyond the university-to participate in processes of inquiry, critique, and meaning-making. The panel is structured around three interconnected vantage points. First, it addresses academic freedom as a legal and institutional framework, tracing its historical development and examining contemporary challenges, including policy restrictions, political pressures, and shifts in governance. Second, it considers the classroom as a site where academic freedom is enacted, negotiated, and sometimes constrained, focusing on pedagogical practices that foster open dialogue, critical engagement, and the capacity to navigate disagreement. Third, it explores the future of academic freedom in a changing political and technological landscape, asking how institutions, educators, and communities might work to sustain and rebuild conditions for intellectual autonomy and democratic participation. Across these perspectives, the panel foregrounds the role of academic freedom in supporting not only scholarly inquiry, but also broader forms of social engagement and collective agency. Participants are invited to consider how academic freedom can be understood as a shared responsibility and an evolving practice, rather than a static or purely individual entitlement. Possible Topics• Academic freedom and democratic institutions • Legislative and policy challenges to higher education • The classroom as a space of risk, dialogue, and dissent • Student voice, participation, and vulnerability • Pedagogies of disagreement and difficult conversations • Academic labor, precarity, and speech constraints • Institutional governance and autonomy • Rebuilding trust in higher education • Academic freedom in digital and platformed environments • Global perspectives on academic freedom

items.fullDescription: Thomas Mann, who would have been 100 in 2025, left readers a number of critical challenges. For one, the coded way in which Mann writes about his most dangerous subjects (homosexuality; knowledge of German guilt) still can fool by a credulous reader, meanwhile his essentializing treatment of race, gender, ethnicity, and class is shockingly unabashed. Then, there is the problem of Mann's reversal of political attitudes as the Nazis drove him-the loyalest of native sons-from Germany. As a young reactionary during the First World War, Mann wrote Reflection of an Unpolitical Man, showing such sympathy with the German politics of expansion and aggression in it that he famously considers whether perhaps the sinking of the Lusitania was a reasonable price to pay for the special German destiny. In the aftermath of World War II, under pressure from his children, Mann publicly denounced the Third Reich. Today, he is widely celebrated as a champion of democracy and opponent of Nazism on the global stage. This panel invites responses to the many contradictions of Mann's personality, which permeate his novels, diaries, and essays with remarkable consistency. Responses need not attempt to resolve these discrepancies, but rather interpret them. How do you relate to Mann as an authorial figure? Are there works by him you find troubling but love anyway? This is an opportunity to practice approaching an author's style with sympathetic care and moral scrutiny in equal part. In addition to Mann's queerness and biraciality (both of which he handled with discomfiting ambivalence), topics mights include such Thomas Mann favorites as music, medicine, language, philosophy, and even cinematography. Comparisons with other authors, artists, and theorists also welcome.

You can submit your abstracts here: https://www.acla.org/cfp/70fe7418-c14a-468d-be1d-809e878f2e00/submit-paper/46d872df-9512-49a7-89f7-8bc710370693 Abstract from the ACLA CFP: Since the rise of World Literatur...
items.fullDescription: Please consider submitting to the ACLA seminar titled "South-South Literary Relations and the Remaking of World Literature" by September 21, 2026 . You can submit your abstracts here: https://www.acla.org/cfp/70fe7418-c14a-468d-be1d-809e878f2e00/submit-paper/46d872df-9512-49a7-89f7-8bc710370693 Abstract from the ACLA CFP: Since the rise of World Literature as a major field of inquiry, discussions of literary circulation have often privileged routes that pass through metropolitan centers, emphasizing translation into dominant European languages, global publishing networks, and institutions located in the Global North. Yet literary works have long traveled through alternative circuits that connect regions of the Global South directly, producing histories of exchange that challenge center-periphery models of cultural transmission. This seminar invites papers that examine literary relationships among Africa, Asia, Latin America, the Caribbean, SWANA, Oceania, and other locations within the Global South. Such relationships may emerge through translation, political solidarity, migration, anti-colonial movements, publishing networks, educational institutions, shared aesthetic projects, or indirect forms of influence. They may also involve moments in which Northern institutions, languages, or markets facilitate, mediate, redirect, or constrain South-South encounters, raising questions about whether these exchanges can ever be understood as entirely autonomous. Rather than treating the Global South as a unified category, the seminar seeks to explore its internal heterogeneity, asymmetries of power, and competing visions of solidarity. How do texts travel between Southern contexts? What historical, linguistic, and political conditions make these encounters possible? What role do translators, publishers, periodicals, archives, and digital media play in creating or sustaining South-South literary networks? How might these circulations reshape concepts such as influence, comparison, translation, reception, or worldliness? We especially welcome papers that interrogate the implications of South-South literary exchange for the study of World Literature itself. If literary circulation is not exclusively organized through Northern centers, what alternative maps of World Literature become visible? Can South-South networks offer different ways of imagining literary value, canon formation, and global comparison? By foregrounding overlooked routes of circulation and exchange, this seminar aims to reconsider how World Literature is conceptualized and to illuminate the multiple worlds through which literature moves. Possible topics include, but are not limited to: South-South translation; comparative studies across the Global South; Cold War and Non-Aligned literary networks; postcolonial and decolonial approaches; migration and diaspora; publishing and periodical cultures; digital literary circulation; transregional modernisms; indigenous and vernacular exchanges; reception studies; archives of literary solidarity; and new theoretical approaches to World Literature.

items.excerpt: Transatlantic Connections and the 'Special Relationship[s]': BAAS Postgraduate Symposium, 2026 V&A East Storehouse, London 9th November In 1946, Winston Churchill declared the need for a "special relationship between the British Commonwealth and Empire and the United States" in order to maintain world diplomacy, citing our shared language and cultural val...
items.fullDescription: Transatlantic Connections and the 'Special Relationship[s]': BAAS Postgraduate Symposium, 2026 V&A East Storehouse, London 9th November In 1946, Winston Churchill declared the need for a "special relationship between the British Commonwealth and Empire and the United States" in order to maintain world diplomacy, citing our shared language and cultural values as connecting the two countries. Although this 'special relationship' has continually been called into question by scholars, there is undoubtedly a channel of cultural and political exchange between the US and the UK, as well as with other countries, which has become even more urgent for discussion in recent years. The 2026 BAAS Postgraduate Symposium invites proposals from postgraduate researchers at all levels and across all disciplines on the topic of Transatlantic Connections and the 'Special Relationship[s]'. By using the term 'Special Relationship[s]', we intend to explore the relationship between not only the US and the UK, but also between the US and other countries. We invite panels and individual papers on this theme and encourage you to interpret it as broadly as you wish, including any aspect of the US's transnational cultural, political and literary connections, influences or contrasts. We welcome contributions from all realms of American Studies, including, but not limited to: literature and film studies, postcolonial and decolonial analysis, science and visual culture, and urban and environmental history. As this year's symposium will be held at V&A East Storehouse, the site of the David Bowie Archive, we are particularly keen on hearing from scholars exploring the etymologically and culturally rich prefix of the term 'Transatlantic' itself. This one-day symposium will involve not only academic panel discussions, but other activities such as a career development session, an introduction to the archives at the Victoria and Albert Museum, and a keynote address by Professor Mark Ford. The intention is to foster a strong postgraduate community in American Studies and to learn from both our peers and from leaders in our field. The symposium will be catered, hosted primarily in-person at V&A East Storehouse, but with a digital attendance option for those only able to join online. There will be time in the day to explore V&A East Storehouse and the David Bowie Centre. V&A East Storehouse is a working museum store with a rich archive for students to use in their research. The building is designed to allow visitors to get closer to objects held in the V&A collections and to the work of the museum itself. We welcome the submission of individual papers as well as proposals for complete panels of three researchers. Applications from groups of three or four researchers for roundtable discussions are also welcome. For panel and roundtable proposals, please also include a statement of up to 200 words on the aims of the collective submission, alongside the individual papers. Papers should be around 15-20 minutes long , and roundtables will consist of five-minute introductions by each researcher followed by 45 minutes of discussion. Interdisciplinary paper, panel and roundtable proposals are encouraged. Suggested paper and roundtable topics include, but are not limited to: - Case studies or broader comparisons between literary texts from the US and other nations - Case studies or broader comparisons between films from the US and other nations - Comparative political or historical analyses concerning the US and other nations - Comparative economic, scientific or environmental analyses concerning the US and other nations. Although the symposium will centre on 'Transatlantic Connections', we welcome proposals making any transnational comparisons rooted in American Studies. We especially encourage researchers from across Europe and beyond to submit and attend, as part of ongoing efforts to expand the EAAS community of postgraduates. We want to make this symposium as accessible as possible; we will be working to ensure a relaxed academic environment and we encourage anyone attending to email us with any access needs. Bursaries will be available from BAAS on a limited basis for students requiring financial support for attendance. The deadline for submissions is? 15th September 2026 .?Please send proposals including a title, an abstract of no more than? 250 words ?and?a short biography of no more than 200 words ?to Claire Watt at?claire.watt@baas.ac.uk. If you have any questions about the symposium, big or small, please get in touch and we will be happy to help. We look forward to hearing from you!

items.fullDescription: REMINDER: SEPTEMBER 22 SUBMISSION DEADLINE American Comparative Literature Association 2027 Annual Meeting University of Houston May 20-23 The Poverty of Literature Organizer: Gabriel Quigley, University of Victoria (gabrielquigley@uvic.ca) How does literature represent poverty? Is poverty available for representation? The title of this seminar is taken from Marx's The Poverty of Philosophy, which, in turn, subverts Proudhon's The Philosophy of Poverty. In it, Marx critiques the approach taken by Proudhon and other anarchist, communist, or socialist "theoreticians" who assume that economic categories exist independently of history. According to Marx, "so long as they look for science and merely make systems, so long as they are at the beginning of the struggle, they see in poverty nothing but poverty, without seeing in it the revolutionary, subversive side, which will overthrow the old society." A similar critique might be leveled at today's writers and critics: when literature and literary criticism engage with poverty at all, do they merely reduce it to an ahistorical economic category? What forms of reification, alienation, and exploitation does the literary assumption that poverty is available for representation produce? This seminar asks what literature owes to people experiencing poverty. At a time when 847 million people live in extreme poverty-95% of whom are in the Global South-it seeks to bring together research on the representation, history, and ontological status of poverty. Unlike Marx's "theoreticians," who "see in poverty nothing but poverty," scholars analyzing poverty through other frameworks-such as ethical demand, affective complexity, geopolitical disparities, aesthetic fetishization, and state failure-are strongly encouraged to submit abstracts. Papers may respond to such questions as: how should poverty be represented, if at all? Beyond an economic category, can poverty be conceived as an aesthetic, metaphysical, or phenomenological category? How is the concept of poverty entangled with conceptions of lack, deprivation, or destitution? How does the global distribution of poverty reflect the ongoing injuries of imperialism, colonialism, neocolonialism, globalization, and ecological catastrophe? Possible topics: - Poverty and realism; poverty and genre - The ethics of speaking for the poor - Testimony, life writing, and first-person accounts of poverty - Poverty and racial capitalism - Postcolonial and decolonial frameworks for poverty - Poverty and ecological catastrophe; climate precarity - Poverty and intersectionality (race, gender, sexuality, disability) - "Poverty porn," sentimentality, and voyeurism - Working-class literature and labor - Poverty in the Global South; imperialism and uneven development - Urban and rural poverty as literary landscapes - Homelessness and houselessness - Poverty and the archive - Poverty and affect: shame, solidarity, rage - The literary canon and class; institutional gatekeeping - Austerity, welfare, and the state in literature - Migration, displacement, and border crossing - Literature and human rights - Poverty as aesthetic, metaphysical, or phenomenological category - Poverty and ontology; being, lack, and deprivation - Bare life and destitution ACLA Seminar Description can be accessed here: https://www.acla.org/seminar/63e1eb87-fe99-49c9-aac0-517ccf904102. ACLA Paper Submission link: https://www.acla.org/cfp/2b603883-5d9b-44ae-a485-c732ba80d4bf/submit-paper. Papers can be submitted until September 22, 2026 .

items.title: Beyond Hegemony: Masculinities in World and Comparative Literature
items.excerpt: This panel examines how literary and cultural texts from diverse global traditions imagine masculinity not merely as an individual identity but as a relational and communal practice. In an era marked by migration, political polarization, social fragmentation, environmental crisis, and renewed struggles for collective empowerment, narratives of masculinity...
items.fullDescription: This panel examines how literary and cultural texts from diverse global traditions imagine masculinity not merely as an individual identity but as a relational and communal practice. In an era marked by migration, political polarization, social fragmentation, environmental crisis, and renewed struggles for collective empowerment, narratives of masculinity have become central sites through which communities negotiate belonging, responsibility, vulnerability, and resistance. While dominant models of masculinity have often been associated with hierarchy, authority, nationalism, and exclusion, contemporary world literatures increasingly depict alternative masculinities grounded in care, ethical responsibility, emotional openness, solidarity, and collective survival. Such representations challenge inherited structures of power while opening new possibilities for community formation and social transformation. This panel invites comparative and transnational approaches that explore how literary texts, films, cultural narratives, and other expressive forms construct, critique, or reimagine masculinities within local and global communities. Particular attention may be given to how gender intersects with race, class, migration, coloniality, religion, ecology, technology, and cultural memory in shaping collective identities and practices of empowerment. Situated within the broader concerns of World Literature and Comparative Literature, this session seeks to foster dialogue across regions, languages, and traditions while investigating how masculinities participate in the creation-or disruption-of empowered communities. We welcome papers addressing, but not limited to: Comparative constructions of masculinity across world literatures Masculinity and migration, diaspora, or displacement Literary representations of fatherhood, mentorship, and communal responsibility Masculinities in Global South literatures Masculinity and environmental or ecological communities Masculinity, memory, and post-conflict reconstruction Queer and non-hegemonic masculinities in world literature Masculinity and cultural resistance under authoritarian regimes Masculinity, religion, and collective belonging Masculinity and affect in contemporary global fiction

items.fullDescription: EchoForum 2026 Conference: Disability as Radical Interdisciplinary Practice 26-27 November 2026 Organised by: Lucian Blaga University of Sibiu NEW Submission deadline: 10 October 2026 Working languages: English, French, Romanian Confirmed Keynote Speakers: Jonathan Meth // Goldsmiths University of London Maria Bucur // Indiana University Petra Kuppers // University of Michigan EchoForum: Conceptual Framework Lucian Blaga University of Sibiu and the members of the EchoCamp project are delighted to extend an invitation to the upcoming conference on disability arts, EchoForum 2026: Disability as Radical Interdisciplinary Practice, taking place between November 26-27, 2026 , in Sibiu, Romania. EchoForum constitutes the research and dialogue component of EchoCamp, the first artistic camp dedicated to disability arts in Romania. Paying homage to Camp Jened and to other similar undertakings, EchoCamp aims to radically shape the way in which we think about the intersection of disability, arts, inclusion, and representation in the East-European cultural space. Hence, at its core, the EchoForum conference is conceived as an interdisciplinary crossroad. We believe that disability does not exist in a vacuum, but is shaped by politics of space, care, law, aesthetic frameworks, and broader social organization. Consequently, we seek to move beyond the siloed approach to disability studies, inviting a convergence of knowledge from across the humanities, social sciences, and professional practices. Therefore, we invite contributions that intersect across the following academic and professional domains: The Artistic and Media Humanities: Including Performing Arts, Visual Arts, Film and Media, Literature and Literary Studies, Theatre and Performance Studies, and the field of Artistic Research. The Social and Cultural Sciences: Including Sociology and Social Work, Anthropology, Cultural Studies, Critical Theory, Disability Studies, and the intersectional frameworks of Gender, Sexuality, and Queer Studies. Spatial and Infrastructural Studies: Including Architecture and Spatial Practices, Accessibility and Inclusive Design, and the fields of Curatorial Studies and Cultural Management and Policy. Health and Care Humanities: Including Healthcare/Health Humanities, Psychology, and Education/Pedagogy. Applied Practices and Advocacy: Including Community-based Practice, Political Activism, and Human Rights Advocacy. Since we believe that all knowledge is created equal, we welcome proposals from both academic and non-academic contexts. We invite contributions in a variety of formats: Theoretical and practice-based research (including work-in-progress and case studies). Artistic research and presentations of cultural practices or projects. Interdisciplinary panels and roundtable discussions. Hybrid formats, such as performance-lectures or workshops. We invite both individual and collective proposals. Abstracts may be submitted in English, French, or Romanian. However, presentations may be delivered only in English or Romanian. As a general guideline for programming and scheduling, we suggest a duration of 20 minutes for individual presentations. However, we emphasize that this timeframe is a suggestion and not a strict requirement. In alignment with our commitment to accessibility and inclusive practice, we recognize that different modes of communication, the use of assistive technologies, and various cognitive or physical needs may require alternative timing or pacing. We encourage applicants to propose a duration and format that best ensures their ability to present their work comfortably and effectively. Submit your proposal via the following online form: https://forms.gle/pyVsovHeu3yDkpDeA Practical Information Dates: 26-27 November 2026 Deadline: 10 October 2026 Notification of Acceptance: 15 October 2026 Venue: Lucian Blaga University of Sibiu, Sibiu, Romania Fees: No registration fee. Access: EchoCamp is committed to full accessibility. Please detail your requirements in the application form. EchoFestival: The Forum is followed by EchoFestival, the public programme featuring performances and artistic events. Selected contributors are warmly invited to stay and participate. Contact For questions or support with the application: echocamp2026@gmail.com We're looking forward to welcoming you to Sibiu! EchoForum is committed to accessibility in all its dimensions. We prioritize the voices of disabled artists, researchers, and practitioners and welcome your feedback on how to make this Forum truly inclusive.

items.fullDescription: Silences as Resistance in Public Narratives Silence is generally seen as something to surmount: we break silence; we give voice to silenced stories; we speak out against injustice. But silence can be a powerful mode of expression in its own right. There is a history of silent protest. Silence can reject dominant expectations or refuse to offer up a story for voyeurism, appropriation, or commodification. It can push reader-listeners to listen for something wordless, to play an active role in striving to understand, and simultaneously to recognize the limits of their ability to understand another person's trauma. Silence is rarely ever singular. This seminar, building on successful past seminars about the roles and limits of narrative silences, examines how silences function as forms of resistance to injustice and trauma. It asks: how can we use silences (as creators or as audiences) to create new spaces-spaces of care, of resistance, of justice? How do we listen to what silences have to say-in fictions, testimony, activism, artistic forms of witness, our classrooms and institutions? How can audiences attend to silence in ways that promote structural change? Participants may choose to address some of the following questions: How do the forms of silence change between public narratives (e.g. testimony or activism) and works of art and literature? How can we theorize silence as a narrative framework? How do we hold the tension between listening to silence, on one hand, and the necessity of speaking out against injustice, on the other? How do historical and geographical contexts change the types or effects of silences that strive to oppose injustice? How can we keep from homogenizing silences and attend to them in their specificity and situatedness? Papers on all genres, media, geographical contexts, and languages welcome. Please submit 200-word abstract and bio through the NeMLA portal at https://cfplist.com/nemla/Home /login to Kelly Minerva and Lisa Propst.

items.fullDescription: CALL FOR PRESENTATION PAPER ABSTRACTS "Are Karl Marx's 'Perpetuum Mobile' and/or Max Weber's 'Machine State' Dominating Labor Today? Why or Why Not?" Students, researchers, faculty members, and scholars working in sociology and related social sciences are invited to submit conference presentation paper abstracts for an open conference session entitled "Are Karl Marx's 'Perpetuum Mobile' and/or Max Weber's 'Machine State' Dominating Labor Today? Why or Why Not?" The session will be part of the XXI International Sociological Association (ISA) World Congress of Sociology, from July 4-10, 2027, at Chonnam National University in Jeonnam-Gwangju Special Metropolitan City, Korea. Karl Marx and Max Weber both thought about a time when machines would dominate labor. Marx wrote of a "perpetuum mobile" to describe the unceasing turnover of money by a machine of indestructible materiality, circulating a repeating and alternating flow of sale and purchase. Max Weber's "Sociology of Domination" theory warned that the power to coerce markets endlessly would cause endless conflicts. For Marx social change entailed communist revolution, while Weber, who was not a Marxist, worried that social change would be constricted to political coups to control the government's informational infrastructure. Social problems of alienation and rationalization, capitalist wealth and inequality, abuse of power and authority, coerced markets, money hording and social stratification are as alive today as when Marx and Weber set down theories about these social problems over a hundred years ago. What can we say about our AI dominated world using the concepts and writings of Marx and Weber today? Do their economic and historical comparative concepts help us understand our digital world? Why or why not? Submit presentation abstracts by October 14, 2026, through the ISA Congress Submission System link below. ISA XXI World Congress of Sociology Call for Abstracts: https://www.isa-sociology.org/isa-events/xxi-world-congress-of-sociology/call-for-abstracts Watch the 2025 ISA abstract submission tutorial here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p_dRzY4k_o4 Current Session Participants: Session Chair, Dr. Ece Kocabicak, The Open University Co-Chair, Dr. Pravat Ranjan Sethi, Central University of Himachal Pradesh, India Discussant, Proshant Chakraborty, University of Vienna, Austria Session Organizer, Dr. Noel Packard, Independent Scholar, USA Questions? Contact Dr. Noel Packard at npac825@aucklanduni.ac.nz. Further information available via Sociology Group interview with Dr. Noel Packard on Marx, Weber, and machines dominating labour: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/414162540_An_Interview_with_Dr_Noel_Packard_- Karl_Marx_and_Max_Weber_on_Machines_Dominating_Labour

items.title: Proposed Volume: Teaching without GenAI in the Age of AI
items.excerpt: Since the widespread emergence of Generative AI a few years ago, educators across disciplines have been reconsidering how technology shapes teaching, learning, writing, and assessment. While some departments and faculty have leaned into these new Large Language Models and the technological "advances" they offer, others have worked just as diligently to ke...
items.fullDescription: Since the widespread emergence of Generative AI a few years ago, educators across disciplines have been reconsidering how technology shapes teaching, learning, writing, and assessment. While some departments and faculty have leaned into these new Large Language Models and the technological "advances" they offer, others have worked just as diligently to keep AI out of their classrooms. In light of the recent ban on GenAI in K-8 classrooms by New York City Public Schools, it is possible that the tides in education are going to shift away from AI and back to the uniquely human approach to education. As institutions and educators continue to debate the role of GenAI in education, questions about how to teach effectively without these technologies have become increasingly important. I am currently seeking contributions from interdisciplinary teachers and scholars for a proposed collection on "Teaching without GenAI in the Age of AI." This volume aims to explore pedagogical strategies for instructing without AI. While recent publications look at how to incorporate AI into writing instruction or discuss the complicated nuances of AI in writing classrooms, there is a gap in the field regarding practical approaches on how to instruct without AI in the classroom. Questions to consider include: - How have you structured assignments to prevent AI from being used? - How has your discipline been affected by AI, and how have you worked to keep it out of your classroom? - What pedagogical, disciplinary, ethical, or learning goals motivate your decision to teach without generative AI? - What are your success stories, or failures, of teaching without AI? - How are your students responding to work without AI? - What policies, structures, or pedagogical practices have you used to discourage or prohibit unauthorized AI use? - Have you faced disciplinary contexts that make AI counterproductive? - What role does technology now play in your classroom? - Have you designed any pedagogical experiments or studies to assess your students' learning within a no-AI context? I invite contributions from teachers and scholars across disciplines and educational contexts, including K-12, higher education, and professional education. I am particularly interested in contributions that offer concrete strategies and resources for other educators to implement in their classrooms. Because this volume is intended to be a practical resource as well as a scholarly contribution, submissions that provide example assignments, lesson plans, classroom policies, assessment strategies, or other teaching materials are especially welcome. In order to make this resource available in a timely fashion and respond to existing publisher interest, please send an abstract of no more than 500 words and a brief biographical statement by October 15, 2026 to teachingwithoutgenai@gmail.com. Completed essays will be approximately 4,000 - 5,000 words and will be due by January 31, 2027.

items.fullDescription: Plastic / Plasticity Literature and Culture and the Material of a (Bygone?) Era Plastic is a defining material of our era. Its properties—plasticity, durability, the ability to imitate any shape, its toxicity, and indecomposability—are also properties of contemporary culture and literature. The proposed thematic issue begins with the premise that plastic can be read simultaneously as a historical substance and as a "theory machine"—a tool for understanding cultural texts and the experience of contemporary times. "My approach, in this paper, is one of thinking with plastic through its metaphoricity and materiality, its relationality and gestationality; in short, a material mediality.” [R. Gosh]

items.fullDescription: Call For Paper Women And Art: Representation, Creativity, And Resistance Open Access | Maurer Press, Frankfurt am Main, Germany Edited by Habib Tekin & Ay?enur Özkan I??k Art has long served as a powerful space in which gender identities, social roles, cultural expectations, and forms of resistance are constructed, questioned, and reimagined. Across different historical periods and cultural contexts, women have participated in artistic production as creators, performers, patrons, critics, and subjects of representation. Yet their contributions have frequently been shaped by unequal access to artistic institutions, dominant aesthetic traditions, and gendered structures of visibility and recognition. The conference "Women and Art: Representation, Creativity, and Resistance" invites scholars, researchers, artists, and postgraduate students to explore the complex and changing relationship between women and artistic production. The conference seeks to bring together interdisciplinary perspectives on how women create, experience, interpret, and transform art, as well as how femininity and gender are represented within different artistic forms. We particularly welcome contributions that examine the ways in which art can function as a space of memory, identity formation, cultural negotiation, political intervention, and resistance. Papers may address historical or contemporary contexts and may focus on individual artists, artistic movements, particular works, comparative perspectives, or broader theoretical questions concerning women, gender, and aesthetics. The proposed book seeks to examine the representation, production, and experience of women in art from gendered, cultural, and interdisciplinary perspectives, including but not limited to the following areas: Women artists in historical and contemporary contexts Representations of women in art Women and literature Women in painting, sculpture, and visual arts Women in photography and film Women in theatre, performance, dance, and music Feminist art and feminist aesthetics Gender and artistic representation The female body in art Self-representation and female subjectivity Women, creativity, and authorship Women and artistic institutions Gender inequality and exclusion in the art world Women artists and cultural memory Art, trauma, testimony, and memory Women, war, migration, exile, and displacement Art and resistance Women and political art Women and censorship Queer and intersectional approaches to women and art Race, ethnicity, class, and gender in artistic production Postcolonial and decolonial approaches to women and art Women and indigenous artistic traditions Women and popular culture Digital art, social media, and new forms of female creativity Artificial intelligence, technology, and women in art Women as patrons, collectors, curators, and critics Gendered spaces and artistic production Comparative and interdisciplinary approaches to women and art The book particularly encourages contributions that offer close readings of literary works, films, visual artworks, photography, theatre, performance, music, digital media, or other artistic forms, as well as theoretically grounded analyses that advance current debates on women, gender, and art. We look forward to receiving proposals that critically engage with the intersections of women, creativity, representation, identity, memory, and resistance across artistic and cultural contexts and contribute to ongoing scholarly discussions within Gender Studies, Art Studies, Cultural Studies, Literary Studies, and related fields. Submission Guidelines Abstracts of 200-250 words with 5 keywords. A short biographical note (not more than 150 words), including institutional affiliation and key publications. Please include full contact details. The subject line of the email should state: Submission of Abstracts for the Edited Volume on "Women and Art: Representation, Creativity, and Resistance." Authors selected for inclusion will be invited to submit full chapters (approximately 6,000-7,000 words, including references) following acceptance of the proposal by the publisher. Abstract Submission Deadline: 15 October 2026 Full-Text Submission Deadline: 15 February 2027 Eligibility Contributors are required to hold a PhD. Alternatively, submissions may be co-authored, provided that at least one co-author holds a PhD. In addition, PhD candidates are welcome to submit contributions within their own field of research, particularly if the proposed chapter is directly related to their doctoral project and falls within the thematic and conceptual parameters of this book. Publisher The volume will be published by Maurer Press, Frankfurt am Main, an established publishing house with 35 years of publishing experience. Publication Fee The publication fee for accepted contributions is 115€. Abstracts and inquiries should be sent to: women.art.literature@gmail.com

items.title: Eating for a Green Future : Literature, Culture, and the Politics of Food in Contemporary India
items.excerpt: CALL FOR CHAPTER PROPOSALS Eating for a Green Future: Literature, Culture, and the Politics of Food in Contemporary India Edited by Dr. Manisha Mohanty (Assistant Professor, S'O'A University & Fulbright-Nehru Fellow) Dr. Shashibhusan Nayak (MLA Bibliography Fellow, MLA) Dr. Sonali Das (Assistant Professor, S'O'A University) This edited volume begins from...
items.fullDescription: CALL FOR CHAPTER PROPOSALS Eating for a Green Future: Literature, Culture, and the Politics of Food in Contemporary India Edited by Dr. Manisha Mohanty (Assistant Professor, S'O'A University & Fulbright-Nehru Fellow) Dr. Shashibhusan Nayak (MLA Bibliography Fellow, MLA) Dr. Sonali Das (Assistant Professor, S'O'A University) This edited volume begins from a single premise: food cannot be discussed apart from the politics that surround it. Questions around production and consumption are inseparable from issues of hunger, malnutrition, social inequality, and ecological crisis. The concept of 'food culture', understood as the cooking and eating of food, must be reexamined in the light of sustainability and structural violence. Industrial agriculture, multinational food corporations, and extreme disparities in access have made eating an exercise of power as much as of nourishment. In India, the evidence is stark. Farmer suicides, shrinking biodiversity, corporate-controlled food systems, and climate-induced crop failures expose the systemic inequalities that run through the country's foodways. The volume gathers essays on literature, film, digital media, and everyday food practice, investigating how contemporary texts address climate change, agribusiness, land dispossession, toxic labour, and food scarcity. One question threads through the whole collection: how much of what we eat still comes from traditional, community-based knowledge, and how much is determined by global agribusiness, whose interest lies in maximizing profit rather than social welfare or universal nourishment? This leads us to explore how corporate food systems blur the distinction between inherited culinary practices and their commodified imitations. The result is a food culture in which authenticity itself becomes a marketing strategy. This volume works across food studies, environmental humanities, and popular culture, and its ambition is both practical and critical: to propose justice-oriented frameworks for rethinking consumption, appetite, and sustainability. Proposed Themes: • Food and sustainability: How can food culture foreground sustainability and ecological concerns rather than mere novelty or elitist pleasure? • Culinary knowledge and agribusiness: How much of what we eat today emerges from traditional ecological knowledge, local seed cultures, and community foodways, and what is shaped by agribusiness, multinational food corporations, and algorithmically curated "choices"? • Rethinking consumption: How can we rethink everyday modes of eating, cooking, and appetite to bring about positive ecological change and more equitable food systems? • Power and intersectionality: How does the intersection of food studies and environmental studies illuminate caste, class, and racial hierarchies, gendered labour, and entrenched social inequalities? • Food justice: How do literary texts, films, digital campaigns, and social media food cultures imagine or fail to imagine food justice, and how might these imaginaries inform public policy and activism? Proposed Structure: Part I: Food, Ecology, and Justice · Food politics, food justice, and environmental humanities · Traditional ecological knowledge and culinary/cultural memory · Rethinking appetite and taste in times of climate crisis Part II: Literature, Film, and Visual Culture · Novels and memoirs centred on famine, scarcity, or ecological degradation · Regional food literatures · Films that foreground drought, crop failure, farmer suicides, or agrarian distress Part III: Digital Foodscapes, Social Media, Influencers, and Algorithms · Hashtag activism around hunger, food waste, land rights, and seed sovereignty · Corporate influence in online food marketing · Online recipe cultures as spaces of resistance (low-waste cooking, foraging, veganism, zero-waste influencers, etc.) Part IV: Politics and the Future of Food · Analysing policy texts, food security laws, and welfare schemes through a cultural lens · Grassroots food sovereignty movements, community kitchens, seed banks · Frameworks for sustainable and just food futures grounded in local knowledge systems · Pedagogy: teaching food-environment issues in classrooms, community settings, and online spaces Part V: Special Section India/Odisha · Indigenous and Adivasi food knowledge · Cyclone-prone ecologies and coastal food insecurity · Temple food cultures · Gendered kitchen labour in rural and urban India/Odisha · Caste-based food taboos and community food practices · Land, mining, and displacement affecting food systems Submission Guidelines: We invite scholars, independent researchers, and practitioners working in literary and cultural studies, environmental humanities, food studies, media studies, and related fields to submit original, unpublished chapter proposals. Interdisciplinary and comparative approaches are especially encouraged. Proposals should include: • An abstract of 300-350 words outlining the chapter's argument, methodology, and primary texts or case studies • 5-6 keywords • A short biographical note (75-100 words) with full name, institutional affiliation, and contact details Full chapters should be: • 5,000-8,000 words in length, inclusive of notes and references • Follow MLA style (9th edition) • Original, previously unpublished, and not under review elsewhere Timeline: • Abstract submission deadline: 15 October 2026 • Notification of acceptance: 20 November 2026 • Full chapter submission: 28 February 2027 Submission: Please send abstracts and biographical notes as a single Word document to: Dr. Shashibhusan Nayak: shashienglish@gmail.com and Dr. Manisha Mohanty: manishamohanty@soa.ac.in Publication: Following the review of abstracts and full chapters, the completed manuscript will be submitted to Bloomsbury for consideration. All chapters will undergo peer review as part of the standard editorial and publisher review process.
