items.title: The Human Cost of Migration? Case-Studies From Britain and China
items.excerpt: Social Inclusion, peer-reviewed journal indexed in the Social Sciences Citation Index and Scopus, welcomes new and exciting research papers for its upcoming issue "The Human Cost of Migration? Case-Studies From Britain and China," edited by Robert Walker and Rachel Murphy. Submission of Abstracts: 1-15 October 2026 Submission of Full Papers: 15-30 April 2...
items.fullDescription: Social Inclusion, peer-reviewed journal indexed in the Social Sciences Citation Index and Scopus, welcomes new and exciting research papers for its upcoming issue "The Human Cost of Migration? Case-Studies From Britain and China," edited by Robert Walker and Rachel Murphy. Submission of Abstracts: 1-15 October 2026 Submission of Full Papers: 15-30 April 2027 Publication of the Issue: June/December 2027 About the issue Internal and international migration are often discussed in different intellectual and political spaces which obscures important common features. Internal (or domestic) migration, typically referring to movement from rural to urban areas, is frequently construed as an important mechanism-sometimes planned, although often not-that facilitates economic development, urbanisation and the more effective utilisation of the factors of production. Equally migration has regularly been blamed for escalating housing costs, causing over-crowding, and resulting in the development of slums and criminality. International migration is simultaneously viewed as a cornerstone of global development, necessary according to the UN International Organization for Migration for the achievement of Sustainable Development Goals 1, 3, 8,10, 13 and 16, while others portray it as 'invasion' and a mechanism of 'civilizational erasure'. While most international migration is economic and legal, governed by work permits and quotas and driven by demand for workers and people's aspirations for career development and a better life, political attention tends to focus on illicit migration, asylum seekers and refugees. Much political discourse is framed from the perspective of host communities establishing rules that limit the right of migrants to enter cities and countries and/or to enjoy services available to natives. Academic research has tended to be disproportionately quantitative focused on stocks, flows and spatial concentrations. Where the aspirations and experiences of migrants have been considered, often they have been dissected into variables that lose connection with the people whose experiences they index. What has frequently been neglected is the story of the migrant experience told from the perspective of migrants themselves. The suspicion is that, examined through this lens, international and domestic migrants share many salient characteristics with respect to motivations, work experience, achievements, challenges, exploitation, humiliation and resilience. It is possible, too, that for some, the costs of migration outweigh the benefits. Therefore, this thematic issue is structured as a natural experiment adopting a maximum difference design. Divided into two sections, the first will contain articles invited to focus on the experience of domestic migrants in China, the second section will comprise articles on the experience of international migrants into the United Kingdom. The editorial will present an analysis of the articles drawing attention to similarities and differences in the experiences of internal and international migrants. It will equally explore the trade-offs that migrants make when seeking to migrate and in accommodating to the place of destination and their success in ensuring that benefits of migration outweigh the costs. Over the last 45 years, China has experienced the largest internal migration in history. This has transformed China from a mostly rural society to an urban one, facilitated unprecedented industrial and commercial growth and China's emergence as the world's second largest economy, and contributed to lifting 800 million people out of extreme poverty. There is evidence, though, that China's economic success has been achieved in part by personal and familial sacrifices made rural-urban migrants that go largely unrecognised in public discourse. Britain, its culture shaped over millennia by waves of inward migration, has nevertheless been transformed into a multicultural society since the 1950s, notably in the last 45 years. In 1951, the foreign-born population comprised 4.3 percent of the total. This proportion was still only 6.6 percent in 1981 but, by 2021, it had risen to 77 percent. In 1951, 99.9 percent of the population was white as was 96 percent in 1981. In marked contrast, by 2021/2 29.4 percent of the population was not white. Although migrants have been largely absorbed into Britian's labour market, sometimes undertaking work shunned by the host population, migration has nevertheless become a toxic political issue. Internal migration intensity has declined over this period despite high mobility for certain age groups. Research articles are invited dealing with the life experiences of (1) internal migrants and their families in China or (2) international migrants and their families into the United Kingdom. There are no constraints on the research methodologies employed provided that they seek to capture the lived experiences of migrants. Articles that discuss the challenges confronted by migrants and report on how migrants maximise the benefits accruing from migration are particularly welcome. Instructions for authors: Authors interested in submitting a paper for this issue are asked to consult the journal's instructions for authors and submit their abstracts (maximum of 250 words, with a tentative title) through the abstracts system: https://www.cogitatiopress.com/app/socialinclusion/abstracts When submitting their abstracts, authors are also asked to confirm that they are aware that Social Inclusion is an open access journal with a publishing fee if the article is accepted for publication after peer-review (corresponding authors affiliated with our institutional members do not incur this fee). Open access: Readers across the globe will be able to access, share, and download this issue entirely for free. Corresponding authors affiliated with any of our institutional members (over 100 institutions worldwide) publish free of charge. Otherwise, an article processing fee will be charged to the authors to cover editorial costs. We defend that authors should not have to personally pay this fee and encourage them to check with their institutions if funds are available to cover open access publication costs. Further information about the journal's open access charges can be found here: https://www.cogitatiopress.com/socialinclusion/about/editorialPolicies#publicationFees

items.fullDescription: The rise of the superhero is one of the most significant cultural developments of the twentieth and twenty-first centuries. Since the debut of Superman in Action Comics #1 (April 18, 1938), superheroes have evolved from colorful comic-book figures into powerful global symbols that shape conversations about politics, morality, identity, technology, gender, race, mythology, trauma, and resistance. What began with the imaginative vision of Jerry Siegel (writer) and Joe Shuster (artist) has expanded into a worldwide phenomenon spanning comics, film, television, literature, gaming, digital media, and academic discourse.

items.excerpt: Call for Chapters Proposals Submission Deadline: July 17, 2026 Full Chapters Due: October 30, 2026 Submission Date: October 30, 2026 Introduction This edited collection features scholarly voices with attention to horror in its transmedia representations, including film, literature, comics, art, branding, and more. items.fullDescription: Call for Chapters Proposals Submission Deadline: July 17, 2026 Full Chapters Due: October 30, 2026 Submission Date: October 30, 2026 Introduction This edited collection features scholarly voices with attention to horror in its transmedia representations, including film, literature, comics, art, branding, and more. Chapters give attention to the ways that fans take up the realities and ideas presented in horror, the affordances of the genre, and participation in this network of storytelling. The reactions of readers/viewers/fans, the decisions of creatives, the presentation of ideas within particular forms of media, and more form elements of the researched conversation in this volume. Objective This collection seeks to advance conversation about the theoretical functions of horror across media including notions of adaptation and literary/literacy-based choices in the work. This includes, but is not limited to, design structures, cultural influences, the role of lore, (re)considerations of the monstrous, embodiment in the genre, sub-genre considerations, and more. Target Audience This book is intended for academics in media, literacy, literature, communication, and interdisciplinary fields. Students enrolled in courses in these fields can benefit from this knowledge as they pursue courses of study and further academic work in these disciplines. Recommended Topics Emotional and Philosophical Reactions to Horror Media Themes and Interactions across Media Representations in the Genre Adaptation Processes/Decisions/Designs in Horror across Media Studies of Narrative and Response/Interpretation Recent Trends/Movements in Horror Theoretical Approaches to Horror Composition/Representation Analysis of Race, Gender, Class in Horror Considerations and Reconsiderations of the Monstrous Author/Creator Decisions and Purposes in the Genre/across Media Horror Character and Author/Director Studies Critical and Analytical Work on Embodiment in Horror Critical and Analytical Examinations of Cultural Stories in the Genre The Role of Lore/Mythology in Horror Studies of Writing/Creating Processes in the Genre Fandom Communities, Fan Fiction, Cosplay, and Other Responses Submission Procedure Researchers and practitioners are invited to submit on or before July 17, 2026, a chapter proposal of 1,000 to 2,000 words clearly explaining the mission and concerns of his or her proposed chapter. Authors will be notified by July 31, 2026 about the status of their proposals and sent chapter guidelines.Full chapters of a minimum of 10,000 words (word count includes references and related readings) are expected to be submitted by October 30, 2026, and all interested authors must consult the guidelines for manuscript submissions at https://www.igi-global.com/publish/contributor-resources/before-you-write/ prior to submission. All submitted chapters will be reviewed on a double-anonymized review basis. Contributors may also be requested to serve as reviewers for this project. Note: There are no submission or acceptance fees for manuscripts submitted to this book publication, Theory and Practice in Horror Transmedia Fandom and Creation. All manuscripts are accepted based on a double-anonymized peer review editorial process. All proposals should be submitted through the eEditorial Discovery® online submission manager. Publisher This book is scheduled to be published by IGI Global Scientific Publishing, an international academic publisher of the "Information Science Reference", "Medical Information Science Reference", "Business Science Reference", and "Engineering Science Reference" imprints. IGI Global Scientific Publishing specializes in publishing reference books, scholarly journals, and electronic databases featuring academic research on a variety of innovative topic areas including, but not limited to, education, social science, medicine and healthcare, business and management, information science and technology, engineering, public administration, library and information science, media and communication studies, and environmental science. For additional information regarding the publisher, please visit https://www.igi-global.com. This publication is anticipated to be released in 2027. Indexing Information for Prospective Authors IGI Global Scientific Publishing meets the criteria for inclusion in major indexing services such as Scopus; however, it is important to note that all indexing decisions are made independently by these services. IGI Global Scientific Publishing books are selectively indexed by the indexing organization after publication. Indexing cannot be guaranteed for any book prior to publication, and the indexing organization has complete control over the final selection and timeline. Important Dates July 17, 2026: Proposal Submission Deadline July 31, 2026: Notification of Acceptance October 30, 2026: Full Chapter Submission January 1, 2027: Review Results Returned February 12, 2027: Final Acceptance Notification February 26, 2027: Final Chapter Submission Inquiries Jason DeHart University of Tennessee Knoxville dehartjason33@gmail.com Classifications Education; Library and Information Science; Media and Communications; Social Sciences and Humanities

items.fullDescription: About the book: Human machine interfacing can be as simple as pressing a button or as complex and entangled (also entangling) as inserting a brain chip into the skull. science fiction. Humans with implants, prosthetic and hybrid humans with electronic and mechanical extensions are yet another level are no longer science fiction. Yet, human-machine interfacing has started long before the invention of these technologies. Machines did communicate with us and tell us about themselves even before chatbots were invented. The clanking of a hammer on the anvil tells us that it is old and dull. The whistle of a microwave tells us that dinner is ready. The process of interfacing is not a one-way process.

items.fullDescription: Folklore is having a moment in South Asian writing, and it isn't a nostalgic one. items.fullDescription: What is the real difference between speaking with nature and speaking for it? Is eco-centric thought a universally shared ideology, or does it develop in reaction to historical, philosophical, and socio-cultural contexts? In what way do the fundamental principles of Indian ecology vary from prevailing Western structures? These essential inquiries delineate the parameters of Ramachandra Guha’s Speaking with Nature: The Origins of Indian Environmentalism (2024), which effectively contests the notion that environmentalism is a unidirectional phenomenon dictated by Western influence. This view posits that the rest of the world, particularly the Global South, lacks eco-conscious awareness because it is ‘too poor to be green’.

items.fullDescription: John Steinbeck once remarked that fellow-Californian Robinson Jeffers wrote some the "greatest poetry since Whitman." Steinbeck kept a significant collection of Jeffers work both in his personal library and Ed Ricketts' Lab, where Jeffers was an influential topic in their endlessly varied conversations. When asked about possibility of meeting the poet, Steinbeck declined with a telling degree of reverence: "His poetry is perfect to me, and I don't think one should get the man mixed up with his work." Although they did eventually meet-notably when Steinbeck lived in Monterey in 1944-their relationship was one of distant, though friendly, mutual respect. Although these two writers rarely crossed physical paths, their work maintains a wide concurrence of concern. They both deeply engaged with Californian geography and history; they both emphasized the influence of the natural world upon the individual and society; they both had social circles that revolved around the Monterey Peninsula; they both were interested in psychoanalytical theory; they both were students of classical literature and philosophy; they both experienced extraordinary recognition at the peak of their literary fame (at one point, Jeffers was on the cover of Time magazine); they both were deeply uncomfortable with such a cultural spotlight; they both admonished personal humility in the face of environmental forces. Intersections such as these (and many more) deserve to be explored with more depth and significance. The editorial staff at the Steinbeck Review invites submissions for a special edition, "John Steinbeck and Robinson Jeffers." We are particularly interested in perspectives which put these authors into conversation in productive and even unexpected ways. Although submissions are not required to examine both authors, we strongly suggest that they engage (even if briefly) both Steinbeck and Jeffers. We welcome all critical and theoretical perspectives. Please see the full guide for submissions here and submit your paper to the Steinbeck Review's online submission system, found at www.editorialmanager.com/Steinbeck, no later than October 31, 2026. Decisions will be made by December 1, 2026. Submissions should be accompanied by an abstract and key words.

items.fullDescription: Call for Papers - Siren! Magazine Second Issue: Disciplined Bodies, Transgressive Bodies, Transformed Bodies Link to the call: https://penn.manifoldapp.org/page/siren-current-call-for-proposals Bodies are shaped by the worlds we inhabit, the stories we tell about them, and the institutions through which we learn what a body is, what it should look like, how it should behave, and what it is permitted to become. Yet bodies are often treated as merely biological facts: fixed, self-evident, and prior to politics. This distinction matters because once something is understood as natural, the expectations attached to it can begin to appear inevitable. For this issue, we invite work on disciplined, transgressive, and transformed bodies. We are interested in work that reflects on how bodily norms are produced and enforced, what happens when bodies exceed or destabilize those norms, and how bodies are remade through political, social, technological, medical, aesthetic, and cultural processes. The question, then, is not only who tells bodies what to do, but how we come to understand what bodies are for in the first place and how we may challenge the constraints imposed over them. How do medicine, law, media, family, religion, workplaces, markets, states, and digital platforms make particular kinds of bodies appear normal, desirable, healthy, productive, legible, or valuable? What happens when a body does not fit the meaning assigned to it; when it refuses, cannot comply, fails to conform, or becomes something else? We are especially interested in moments when bodily categories begin to break down, when the meanings attached to bodies no longer hold, or become further reinforced and are resisted, and when bodies become sites of contradiction, refusal, negotiation, and possibility. Key terms For the purposes of this issue, we understand the three terms broadly and provisionally: Disciplined bodies are shaped by the norms, institutions, and expectations that surround them. They may be expected to reproduce, perform gender recognizably, be deemed healthy and desirable, remain productive and self-optimizing, regulate themselves, and stay intelligible to others. We welcome work on how these norms are produced, enforced, negotiated, and unevenly distributed. Transgressive bodies make those expectations difficult to sustain. Transgression need not be intentional: a body may refuse, fail, exceed, disrupt, or simply be unable to comply. Nor are particular bodies inherently transgressive; they are often rendered so by institutions and cultural frameworks that mark some forms of embodiment as abnormal, excessive, threatening, or unintelligible. Transformed bodies ask what happens when embodiments become a site of remaking. Bodies may be altered through medicine, technology, disability, transition, reproduction, labor, aging, artistic practice, environmental exposure, or political violence. Transformation may be desired or imposed, liberatory, or coercive. We are interested in what bodies become, what histories they carry, what forms of power shape them, and what futures they make imaginable. We welcome submissions that interpret one of these categories, bring two or more into conversation, question the distinctions between them, or propose other ways of thinking about bodily discipline, transgression, and transformation. Proposals should identify the term that most strongly connects to the submission while noting any significant intersections with the others. Possible topics may include, but are not limited to: -Bodily autonomy and reproductive rights -Disability and debility -Gender and sexuality -Race and racialization -Beauty and aesthetic labor -Health, illness, and wellness -Medicine and biomedical technologies -Aging -Death -War and militarization -Sport and physical performance -Embodiment and mediation (digital or otherwise) -Surveillance -Cyborg subjectivities -Body modification -Bodily aesthetics -Migration and borders -Carcerality -Labor and productivity -Environmental harm -Colonialism and its afterlives -Speculative or imagined forms of embodiment Who can submit We welcome work from scholars, students, artists, activists, independent researchers, and public intellectuals working in communication, media studies, feminist studies, cultural studies, disability studies, queer and trans studies, critical race studies, the humanities, and related fields. Submissions are open to contributors at all career stages, but we particularly encourage work from early-career scholars and those whose work may sit outside conventional academic publishing structures. Formats Submissions may be written, visual, audiovisual, audio, or hybrid. We welcome experimental forms alongside conventional scholarly approaches. Across formats, submissions should engage the issue's broader commitments to critical feminist inquiry, transnational solidarity, feminist world-making, and transformative social change. Timeline For full consideration, abstracts are due by October 31, 2026, with decisions made by December 10th. Completed submissions will be due by February 10th, 2027, with a projected publication date in September 2027. Guidelines for proposal types -Paper: Please send the title and a 250-word abstract outlining the argument for a full paper featuring an original contribution. Full papers are long-form (3000-5000 words) analytical essays that connect to the current topic of the issue. Please use the APA citation system for references. -Escalator Paper: Please submit the title and a 150-word abstract for a short analytical piece (500-2000 words). Research escalator papers are works-in-progress on novel ideas related to the issue theme; they will be published as submitted and paired with an expert mentor to develop into a full analytical or empirical work. Please use the APA citation system for references. -Multimedia and Hybrid Submissions: Please submit the title and a 200-250-word description explaining how your piece relates to the current issue's theme. For multimedia works, explain how text and other elements interact. Finished pieces should include a link to a sample. For works in progress, add a brief (up to 100 words) outline of the concept, your process, and the timeline for completion. Experimental submissions are encouraged. Important dates Abstract due: October 31, 2026 Acceptances: December 10, 2026 Final submission: February 10, 2027 Peer-review process and mentorships: February - June 2027 Expected publication date: early September 2027 All proposals should be sent as a .docx or .pdf document, and include a brief bio (up to 150 words) introducing yourself and your background. Please submit proposals to asc-sirenmagazine@asc.upenn.edu, using the subject line "Siren Magazine - Bodies." Direct any questions regarding the call or submission process to the same address.

items.fullDescription: Call for Papers Taylor Swift & Swiftie Studies Southwest Popular / American Culture Association (SWPACA) 48th Annual Conference, February 17-20, 2027 Marriott Albuquerque Albuquerque, New Mexico https://swpaca.org Proposal submission deadline: October 31, 2026 Proposals for papers and panels are now being accepted for the 48th annual SWPACA conference. One of the nation's largest interdisciplinary academic conferences, SWPACA offers nearly 70 subject areas, each typically featuring multiple panels. For a full list of subject areas, area descriptions, and Area Chairs, please visit https://swpaca.org/subject-areas/. The Taylor Swift & Swiftie Studies area invites paper proposals on topics related to Taylor Swift and/or Swifties from multiple vantage points. Since her debut in 2006, Taylor Swift has become a fixture of popular culture. Her career has been marked by incredible record-breaking highs and infamous tabloid-fodder lows. Known for her sharp lyrics, her evolving cross-genre musical styles, and her dedicated, creative fanbase (the Swifties), Swift's influence has been noted within music, fashion, economics, politics, and other cultural spheres of power. As an interdisciplinary area, we invite papers from multiple perspectives and disciplines. Topics might include, but are not limited to: • Critical interpretations of Swift's lyrics, eras, and/or personas • Considerations of Taylor Swift and politics, feminisms, activism and social justice • Interrogations of Swift and gender, race, class, and other identities/identifications • Analyses of Swift's connections to business, law, psychology, philosophy or other academic disciplines • Arguments about fandom, belonging, relating, creating and other Swiftie concerns • Examples of Taylor Swift's pedagogical relevancy All proposals must be submitted through the conference's database at https://swpaca.org/app. For details on using the submission database and on the application process in general (including submitting proposals for roundtables and preformed panels), please see the FAQS & Resources tab on https://swpaca.org/. Individual proposals for 15-minute papers must include an abstract of approximately 200-500 words and a brief summary of 100 words or less. For information on how to submit a proposal for a multi-paper panel, please view the above FAQs & Resources link. The deadline for submissions is October 31, 2026. SWPACA offers monetary awards for the best graduate student papers in a variety of categories. Submissions of accepted, full papers are due January 1, 2026. More details are here: https://swpaca.org/graduate-student-paper-awards/. SWPACA also offers travel fellowships for undergraduate and graduate students as well as contingent faculty: https://swpaca.org/travel-awards-students-faculty/. Registration and travel information for the conference is available at https://swpaca.org/albuquerque-conference/. In addition, please check out the organization's peer-reviewed, scholarly journal, Dialogue: The Interdisciplinary Journal of Popular Culture and Pedagogy, at https://digitalcommons.unl.edu/dialogue/. If you have any questions about the Taylor Swift and Swiftie Studies area, please contact its Area Chair, Juliette Holder at jholder1@csustan.edu. If you have general questions about the conference, please contact us at support@swpaca.org, and a member of the executive team will get back to you. This will be a fully in-person conference. If you're looking for an online option to present your work, keep an eye out for details about the 2027 SWPACA Summer Salon, a completely virtual conference to take place in June 2027. We look forward to receiving your submissions!

items.fullDescription: The Routledge Handbook of Hip Hop and Sport, Culture, and Activism Call for Chapters Description: The Routledge Handbook of Hip Hop and Sport, Culture and Activism addresses the critical need for a comprehensive academic survey of Hip Hop's connection to sport as a preeminent sociological and political force among Millennials and Generation Z. This handbook maps the emerging critical terrain where Hip Hop intersects with the sports-industrial complex, digital activism, and the persistent structures of racial capitalism and white supremacy. As the culture enters its second half-century, it serves as an emergent space for self-expression and identity formation, both to hegemonic and counter-hegemonic ends. The leading objectives of this volume are to delineate how Hip Hop's relationship with sport provides narrative resources for youth to explore their social realities in the context of late-stage capitalism and its bedfellows: white supremacy and patriarchy. This handbook explores both the route and roots of Hip Hop expression through the lens of the African diaspora and the historical relationship between Black expressive history and social movements. This handbook is also interested in the ways in which Hip Hop's relationship with sport can be oriented both towards liberation and political conservatism, particularly in the context of Hip Hop's historical and presentist embrace of Donald Trump and his representative movements. This project aims to both engage Hip Hop's historical relationship with sports (professional and amateur) as well as its contemporary shifts,such as the institutionalization of breaking in the 2024 Olympics and the rise of representation activism in major sports leagues (NBA, NFL) that create new tensions between cultural authenticity and corporate appropriation. It is intended to define the current state of theory and establish a foundation for future scholarship across the interdisciplinary fields of hip-hop studies, sport management, and Africana studies. Since this project is a handbook and not an anthology, the chapter topics have already been pre-selected by the editors. However, we encourage submissions that engage the specific areas of expertise of each contributor, and the contributor is welcome to interpret the proposed topics according to their own research and experience. The targeted audience for this handbook are advanced high school students and undergraduates, so chapters should be written with this audience in mind. We invite abstract submissions from Hip Hop practitioners, sport sociologists, scholars, graduate students, postgraduate researchers, and early career researchers. Details for Submission: Abstracts of 250-300 words for the chapters listed below must be submitted by October 31st, 2026. Microsoft Word or PDF formats will be accepted. When submitting your abstract, please include your name, affiliation, email address, title of chapter, and short biography (100 words). Authors will be notified of their acceptance by November 30th, 2026. Full chapters of 4,000-6,000 words (including references) are due by April 30th, 2027. For further questions, contact Dr. Micah J. Dobson (mjdobson92@gmail.com ) and Dr. Tyler Bunzey (tylerbunzey@gmail.com). Table of Contents Section 1: Hip-Hop: A Cultural Politic Chapter 1: The Context of Hip-Hop's Roots and Routes in the Early 1970s Chapter 2: Political Movements that Impacted Hip-Hop's Foundation Chapter 3: Hip-Hop's Formal Political Movements like "Rock the Vote" Chapter 4: Hip-Hop and Moral Panic Section 2: Hip-Hop Generating Identity Chapter 5: Hip-Hop and Generational Identity in the "Post-Racial" Era Chapter 6: Obama, Neoliberalism, and Hip-Hop Mainstream Partisan Politics Chapter 7: From "FDT" to Kodak Black: Hip-Hop's Complicated Relationship with Trump Chapter 8: Hip-Hop and the Black Lives Matter Movement Chapter 9: "Alright" and Social Protests Against Police Brutality Section 3: Hip-Hop and the Sports-Industrial Complex Chapter 10: A History of the Relationship Between Hip-Hop and Sport Chapter 11: Subculture to Spectacle: The Evolution of Breaking and Olympic Institutionalization Chapter 12: Ice Cube, The Big Three, and Mogul "Activism" Chapter 13: Jay-Z and the Problematics of the Roc Nation-NFL Partnership Section 4: Representing: Hip-Hop and Sport Chapter 14: The Politics of Aesthetics: Street Fashion, the Tunnel Walk, and Racialized Pleasure Chapter 15: Generational Agency: From Michael Jordan's Brand to LeBron's "Representation Activism" Chapter 16: The WNBA and Queering Hip-Hop Aesthetics Chapter 17: Hip-Hop Dance as Art and Sport

items.fullDescription: THE RISE OF ASIA 100 YEARS AFTER LAI: Is the Imperialism Dying and a New World Order Emerging? INTERNATIONAL AND INTERDISCIPLINARY CONFERENCE Paris, February 17, 2027 Le Havre, February 18-19, 2027 https://bandungspirit.org/ CALL FOR ABSTRACTS AND FOR PARTICIPATION The conference is open to individual and group paper presentations. Those willing to present their papers are invited to submit their abstracts until July 31, 2026 (for a possible publication in an edited volume to be launched during the conference) or October 31, 2026 (for a paper presentation in the conference). The notification of selected abstracts for publication or for presentation will be communicated to their authors progressively according to their availability. The earlier the abstracts are submitted, the sooner the authors will get notified. A certain number of selected abstracts may be published as an edited volume to be launched during the conference. The terms of reference is available at https://bandungspirit.org/IMG/pdf/the_rise_of_asia-2027-cfa-a-with-cover.pdf Abstracts of 200-300 words are to be submitted online at https://forms.gle/2F3dS1QrDNQTugUs8 OFFLINE AND ONLINE PARTICIPATION The conference will be organised offline (physically) with possible online (virtual) participation following the circumstances. The programme will be based on offline (physical) participants on Paris time zone. INTRODUCTION LAI (League against Imperialism and for National Independence) was not a conference, but an international organisation active from 1927 to 1937 bringing together communists, socialists, nationalists, trade unionists, and pacifists in order to coordinate their myriad 'assaults against empire'. Founded with the support of the Communist International, the LAI at its peak had a membership of several hundred people, from every inhabited continent, among them prominent interwar activists and future heads of state. The organization aspired both to become an international movement and to coordinate specific instances of mass struggle. It was inaugurated by the "First Congress against Colonial Oppression and Imperialism" in Palais d'Egmont Brussels on February 10-14,1927. Its initiator, Willi Münzenberg, a German communist and the chair of the Workers International Relief, invited many personalities from European and American Left and anti-colonial nationalists from the colonised world. The Brussels Congress was attended by 174 people representing 134 organizations from 34 countries. The list of attendees and organizations identifies delegates from the following places: the United States, Mexico, Cuba, Puerto Rico, Peru, Venezuela, 'Central America', Colombia, China, India, the 'Dutch East Indies' [Indonesia], Korea, 'Indo-China (Annam)', Persia, the Philippines, South Africa, 'West Africa' [Sierra Leone], 'North Africa' [Lamine Senghor, from Senegal, representing the Comité de Défense de la Race Nègre], Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Germany, England, France, Holland, Czechoslovakia, Austria, Italy, Syria, and Palestine. Among those present in Brussels were emissaries of the Chinese Kuomintang party in Europe, Jawaharlal Nehru of the Indian National Congress, accompanied by Virendranath Chattopadhyaya, Josiah Tshangana Gumede of the African National Congress (ANC) of South Africa, Messali Hadj of the Algerian Étoile Nord-Africaine, and Mohammad Hatta of the Perhimpoenan Indonesia. Moreover, many activists from the European and American Left were present, such as Fenner Brockway, Arthur MacManus, Edo Fimmen, Reginald Bridgeman, and Gabrielle Duchêne, as well as intellectuals such as Henri Barbusse, Romain Rolland, and Albert Einstein. Today, 100 years after LAI, the recent wars in Ukraine and in West Asia (Iran, Israel, Arab countries, USA) raise questions: is the imperialism dying and a new world order emerging? Why? In what way? And what new world order is emerging? Those fundamental questions may be broken down into more specific questions, such as: • Brussels 1927, Bandung 1955, Belgrade 1961, Havana 1966, what ruptures and what continuities? • In what ways colonialism, neo-colonialism and imperialism continue to take place? • What impacts of foreign military bases on socio-cultural, economic, environmental and political life of the hosting countries? • What role NAM, BRICS, SCO and other Non-Western institutions play in the changing world order? • Are Marxism, Leninism, Maoism, Nasserism, Sukarnoism still relevant today? • Is socialism still promising to replace capitalism? • What role played by social movements and other non-state actors movements in the fight for human emancipation? • Is the present UN still relevant to the global challenges today? What is necessary? UN reform or UN replacement by a new structure? It is to discuss those such questions that the 11th edition of the Rise of Asia Conference Series is organised. It encourages the participation of scholars from a wide range of scientific disciplines (area studies, cultural studies, ecology, economics, geography, built environment, architecture, urban studies, history, humanities, languages, management, political and social sciences, international relations…) and practitioners from diverse professional fields (business, civil society, education, enterprise, government, management, parliament, public policy, social and solidarity movements…) as well as artists and writers, based in diverse geographical areas (Africa, North, Central and South America, Australia, Asia, the Caribbean, Europe, Oceania, Pacific…). (Darwis Khudori, Conference Initiator and Convenor)

items.fullDescription: Call for Papers ESOTERICISM, OCCULTISM, AND MAGIC Southwest Popular / American Culture Association (SWPACA) 48th Annual Conference, February 17-20, 2027 Marriott Albuquerque Albuquerque, New Mexico https://swpaca.org Submissions open: September 1, 2026 Proposal submission deadline : October 31, 2026 Proposals for papers and panels are now being accepted for the 48th annual SWPACA conference. One of the nation's largest interdisciplinary academic conferences, SWPACA offers nearly 70 subject areas, each typically featuring multiple panels. For a full list of subject areas, area descriptions, and Area Chairs, please visit https://swpaca.org/subject-areas/. Esotericism, Occultism, and Magic invites proposals relating to magical worldviews, practices, and representations, as well as consciousness transformation, the preternatural, the paranormal, hidden meanings, the power of transmutation, and related phenomena. Characteristic methods, beliefs, perspectives, paradigms and techniques include: arcane symbolism, imagery, and aesthetics; unseen forces, spiritual intermediaries, invisible agencies, nonhuman intelligences; synchronous patterns, non-ordinary causation, and anomalous processes. Examples of ideas and systems include Hermeticism, Gnosticism, Sufism, Tantra, Rosicrucianism, Freemasonry, Satanism, witchcraft, sorcery, demonology, astrology, alchemy, yoga, shamanism, parapsychology, as well as psychic and paranormal phenomena, along with beliefs and practices relating to altered states of consciousness, overlapping with the study of mysticism and New Age spirituality, channeling, positive thinking, manifestation, reality shifting, the power of intention, numerology, guardian angels, and Ascended Masters. Esoteric, occult, and magical concepts, beliefs, and practices appear in every culture and civilization; contemporary media and popular culture have embraced them enthusiastically, yet at times have reacted against them. The impact of esotericism, occultism, and magic on genre formation/content and popular cultural perceptions has been profound. Their themes and tropes continue to become increasingly prevalent throughout all media of popular entertainment, including arts, music, literature, film, television, anime, comics and graphic novels, as well as being nearly ubiquitous throughout interactive gaming of all categories and genres. Beyond entertainment media, esoteric, occult, and magical concepts and content appear in online memes and frequently in fashion accessories and aesthetics. Their popularity continues to inspire and provoke a variety of conspiracisms in reaction, along with various fads, trends, moral panics, witch-hunts, witch-crazes, and conspiracy theories. Examples include demonic intelligences in "AI" chatbots, anti-occult-conspiracism in QAnon; adrenochrome confabulations, Illuminati paranoia, bloodline of the Holy Grail beliefs, Satanic Ritual Abuse scandals. All reactions to, and polemics against, esoteric, occult, and magical content in popular culture, as well as projections concerning its presence, are therefore also suitable topics for this Area, as are political, religious, secular, scientific, and scientistic receptions of esotericism, occultism, and magic, along with instrumentalization of related concepts, beliefs, and practices in propaganda, intelligence, and information warfare. Special themes and topics of interest proposed for 2027: EOM and time, chronology, and anachronism; concepts of the paranormal, preternatural, supernatural, anomalous, weird, etc; conspiracism, the occult state, conceptions of secret government, and esoteric espionage; lies, fakes, frauds, forgeries, counterfeits, duplicates, deception, disinformation, and propaganda; confabulation, fabrication, imitation, and simulation; boundaries of magic, mysticism, and technology; technoccultism, cybermagic, and cosmotechnics; magic and engineering; EOM and hacking; impossibility and Forteana; humor, parody, and satire; EOM and "influencers", EOM and the media; immediatism; consumerism and consumption in and of magic, and also magic as consumption and as commodity/commodifiable; EOM and economics; the bureaucratic occult; legal regulation of EOM; demographics in and of magic; EOM and the personality; EOM and/as genre; EOM and repetition, reproduction, genetics, heredity, ancestry, generational transmission, generational trauma; EOM and radicalism; values, virtues, ethics, and empathy in EOM; EOM and geography, geopolitics, astropolitics, and "space"; egregores; crowd magic, "mass magic", and EOM-concepts of "the masses"; EOM and the mundane/banal; EOM and materialist worldviews; EOM and architecture. All proposals must be submitted through the conference's database at https://swpaca.org/app. For details on using the submission database and on the application process in general (including submitting proposals for roundtables and preformed panels), please see the FAQS & Resources tab on https://swpaca.org/. Individual proposals for 15-minute papers must include an abstract of approximately 200-500 words and a brief summary of 100 words or less. For information on how to submit a proposal for a multi-paper panel, please view the above FAQs & Resources link. The deadline for submissions is October 31, 2026. SWPACA offers monetary awards for the best graduate student papers in a variety of categories. Submissions of accepted, full papers are due January 1, 2026. More details are here: https://swpaca.org/graduate-student-paper-awards/. SWPACA also offers travel fellowships for undergraduate and graduate students as well as contingent faculty: https://swpaca.org/travel-awards-students-faculty/. Registration and travel information for the conference is available at https://swpaca.org/albuquerque-conference/. In addition, please check out the organization's peer-reviewed, scholarly journal, Dialogue: The Interdisciplinary Journal of Popular Culture and Pedagogy, at https://digitalcommons.unl.edu/dialogue/. If you have any questions about the Esotericism, Occultism, and Magic area, please contact its Area Chair, Dr. George J. Sieg, Luna Community College, georgejsieg@gmail.com . If you have general questions about the conference, please contact us at support@swpaca.org, and a member of the executive team will get back to you. This will be a fully in-person conference. items.fullDescription: Nonfiction film and media have played a crucial role in advocating for animal welfare, rights and liberation. Although short videos and a number of documentaries were produced and distributed with activist purposes during the 1980s, it is during the so-called “documentary renaissance” of the early twenty-first century, together with the communicative advances of digital media, that nonfiction moving images emerged as a medium capable of reaching more mainstream audiences, becoming a central cultural tool for instigating transformative change in humans’ speciesist practices and attitudes toward nonhuman animals.

items.title: Watching Cinema Theoretically: Psychoanalytic Perspectives on Film
items.excerpt: The relation between a theory and its so-called “object” always poses the danger of reducing an art form (in this case film) to a mere instance testifying to the validity of the theory. In this way, the theory provides the “genus” of which a given film will be a mere “species”. The application of psychoanalytic ideas or Marxist concepts to film would ther...
items.fullDescription: The relation between a theory and its so-called “object” always poses the danger of reducing an art form (in this case film) to a mere instance testifying to the validity of the theory. In this way, the theory provides the “genus” of which a given film will be a mere “species”. The application of psychoanalytic ideas or Marxist concepts to film would therefore run the risk of depriving the specificity and singularity of the object in favour of the hegemony of the theory. Here, theory would truly live up to its theological vocation (the “theo” in theory refers to God) standing transcendentally above its “object” upon which it would cast its daunting shadow.

items.fullDescription: The figure of the woman traveler has long occupied a distinctive place in the cultural imagination. At once celebrated and contested, she has been represented as explorer, observer, adventurer, ethnographer, journalist, tourist, and pilgrim—but nearly always an antidote to feminine domesticity. We are currently seeking contributors from across the disciplines for a proposed collection of essays on “the woman traveler.” This volume will explore the enduring and evolving cultural figure across genres and media—from travel writing and photography to film, blogs, Instagram, and TikTok.

items.fullDescription: CFP: Red Reading the Modern Novel Society for Novel Studies (Vancouver, BC; 13-16 May 2027) The organizer seeks papers that apply Red Reading to twentieth- and twenty-first century novels. The literary canon has been expanded brilliantly in the last few decades, and literary critical approaches have shifted away from modes of corrosive critique. There remains however, a dearth of work grounded in Indigenous epistemologies and critical approaches. As an initial response to this gap, this panel seeks to test Red Reading’s utility for studies of the novel.

items.title: International Symposium: The Embodiment of Trauma in Artistic Practices
items.excerpt: Call for contributions: International Symposium organized by Nordic Summer University February 24-26, 2027 - Vilnius, Lithuania in collaboration with the Center for Psychotraumatology at Vilnius University,Performative Design Association, Luna16 Community Resource Center & Feminist Art Space ASABA The winter symposium of our NSU study circle is centered o...
items.fullDescription: Call for contributions: International Symposium organized by Nordic Summer University February 24-26, 2027 - Vilnius, Lithuania in collaboration with the Center for Psychotraumatology at Vilnius University,Performative Design Association, Luna16 Community Resource Center & Feminist Art Space ASABA The winter symposium of our NSU study circle is centered on trauma as an embodied and contested concept, and artistic practices as forms of knowledge production. We are particularly interested in how art engages with experiences of trauma beyond representation, and how bodies carry, transmit, remember, resist, and transform individual and collective histories. Theme: The Embodiment of Trauma in Artistic Practices Contemporary art has become an important site for exploring the embodiment of memory, violence, displacement, ecological loss, and collective histories. Across practices, artists increasingly investigate experiences that exceed language and resist fixed interpretation. Rather than merely representing trauma, these practices generate new ways of sensing, remembering, witnessing, resisting, and imagining together. The symposium approaches trauma as a contested concept. While informed by contemporary research in psychology, and neuroscience, it recognizes that no single discipline can fully account for how trauma is lived, embodied, remembered, or transmitted. Clinical and diagnostic frameworks have significantly contributed to understanding traumatic experiences, yet they also exist within broader institutional, political, and economic systems that shape whose suffering becomes visible, whose experiences are legitimized, and which forms of care are recognized. At a moment when concepts such as healing, resilience, and post-traumatic growth are increasingly mobilized within cultures of productivity, self-optimization, and return to normative functioning, the symposium asks what artistic practice can offer beyond narratives of repair. Questions that explore this inquiry include: ? How does trauma become embodied, and what can artistic practices reveal about this relationship? ? How are trauma, memory, and embodiment shaped by colonization, occupation, war, displacement, ecological crisis, extraction, systemic oppression, interpersonal violence, and intergenerational histories? ? How can artistic practices create spaces for mourning, care, resistance, coexistence, and collective imagination beyond dominant narratives of healing and self-optimization? ? What forms of knowledge emerge through movement, performance, ritual, material practices, sound, image, and other embodied forms? ? How can art challenge dominant narratives of pathology and create alternative ways of living with difficult histories? - Call for contributions We invite artists, researchers, filmmakers, performers, scholars, activists, body practitioners, communities of care, psychologists, and people with lived experience to enrich our dialogue. A diversity of formats is welcome and we highly encourage practice-based forms to present and share research. These include: community-based workshops, body movement practices, moving image, sound, socially engaged practices, walks, and experimental or hybrid formats. We particularly welcome perspectives emerging from marginalized, feminist, queer, diasporic, disabled, and community-based practices. Submit to: decolonialstudycircle@gmail.com Title; Format description; Abstract (max. 250 words); Bionote (max. 100 words). Participation & Registration Participation is only in person for participants residing in Europe. Participants outside Europe may present online with a reduced €50 NSU membership fee. ? €60 - Reduced-rate fee (50 euros membership towards NSU, 10 euros towards our study circle)* ? €150 - Standard fee (100 euros membership towards NSU, 50 euros towards our study circle)** ? €250 - Supporting membership (150 euros membership towards NSU, 100 euros towards our study circle)*** *The reduced-rate fee is for individuals with an annual income below €25,000, as well as students, early-career researchers, retired, unemployed, working in precarious or low- income circumstances. **The standard fee is for individuals with an annual income between €25,000 and €50,000. ***The supporting membership fee is for individuals with an annual income above €50,000, as well as institutions or individuals whose membership is funded by their institution, employer, or research grant. Part of the funds from our study circle will go towards printing a participatory glossary on trauma. Key dates Submission deadline: November 1, 2026, 23:59 AoE (Anywhere on Earth). Notification of acceptance: November 15, 2026. Symposium dates: 24-26 February, 2027. Read the full call here: https://www.nsuweb.org/circle-3-re-configuring-colonialities-reforging-knowledges-healing-trauma-and-re-imagining-digital-futures/ Can't join us in person? Contribute a question. If the theme resonates with you but you're unable to attend, we invite you to submit a question for the roundtable discussion. The roundtable will bring together psychologists, researchers, artists, and community-based practitioners, and is open to a range of topics. The roundtable will be broadcasted and recorded. Submit a question here: https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLScA6ahZH8bFdT3HzhjEBHXtZmsMiXTTMjwe1WOqVwiP4xkdmw/viewform

items.fullDescription: Call for Papers: [Children's and Young Adult Literature] at CEA 2027 Apr. 1-3, 2027 | St. Louis, Missouri The Westin St. Louis Hotel https://cea-web.org/the-conference-hotel The College English Association, a gathering of scholar-teachers in English studies, welcomes proposals for presentations on Children's and Young Adult Literature for our 57th annual conference. Submit your proposal at www.cea-web.org Scholars and teachers of children's and YA lit intimately know the transformative power the right story at the right time can have on an elementary, middle, or high school student. We do not need reminding of how words, and how they are communicated, to young learners have the ability to grow cognitive processes and lead to future generations of lovers of the written word and future torchbearers of the significance of those words coming from the minds of human beings. Coalescing around the conference theme, we consider how the influence of diverse sculpted stories opens the door to deeper discernment across the curriculum. Conference Theme: Gateways For its 2027 annual conference, the College English Association (CEA) invites proposals for papers and panels that explore the theme of "Gateways" and their significance in literature, criticism, and pedagogy. Tracing its history back to French explorers in the second half of the 18th century, the great city of St. Louis began as a fur trading post named after King Louis IX of France and was established on the ancestral lands of the Osage Nation, Missouria, and Illini Confederacy. Becoming part of the United States through the Louisiana Purchase of 1803, the city famously came to be known as the "Gateway to the West," serving as a launching point for generations of explorers and settlers expanding the frontier. Yet, we must remember that the city also serves as a gateway to its past as part of indigenous lands transformed through its colonial history into a major river port and trading center that fostered migration both outwards and inwards for centuries. Today, St. Louis invites us to reflect on the continued significance of gateways in our 21st-century lives. GENERAL CALL FOR PAPERS GATEWAYS: For its 2027 annual conference, the College English Association (CEA) invites proposals for papers and panels that explore the theme of "Gateways" and their significance in literature, criticism, and pedagogy. Potential areas of interest: How do gateways expand literary and cultural spaces but also, as access points, mark out boundaries and limits? Do gateways invite gatekeepers to enable and limit access? Is it possible to imagine gateways without gatekeepers? How can we imagine literary and cultural gateways to foster inter-cultural, cross-cultural, and trans-cultural interactions? How do we envision pedagogical approaches to create gateways for our students to new literary vistas, critical thought, and professional opportunities? How can gateways in both their physical and symbolic significances (like the city of St. Louis and the Gateway Arch) connect the territorial to the cultural, imaginative, and spiritual in literary-critical studies? In what ways can we re-imagine our scholarly and pedagogical work to open up interdisciplinary and multidisciplinary gateways? For CEA 2027, we are especially interested topics related to GATEWAYS in texts, disciplines, people, cultural studies, media, and pedagogy. Consider such topics as the implications of political gateways across time and place, cultural gateways of identity, gateways in the media (including social media) and how they impact society, pedagogical gateways of teaching philosophy and their implementation, or personal gateways through autobiography and memoir. GENERAL TOPICS: The CEA Conference encompasses a wide range of areas, including literary studies, creative writing, rhetoric and composition, technical communication, linguistics, and film. We further encourage proposals in areas about our wider role as academics, including student/instructor accountability and assessment, student advising, academic leadership in departments and programs, and the place of the English department in the university. NEW FOR 2027: UNDERGRADUATE ROUNDTABLES CEA invites undergraduates to enjoy the conference experience by sharing their work in flash-essay roundtable sessions. A flash essay is a highly condensed, high-impact presentation (typically 300-1000 words, or 2-5 minutes) that delivers core research findings, a specific argument, or a compelling narrative. During roundtable sessions, the speakers and audience engage in discussion with each other in more of an open conversation than in traditional panels. Learn more about roundtables here: https://cea-web.org/about-roundtables. For additional information or discussion about this topic and its panels, please contact Peter Elliott at pselliott@anderson.edu.

items.fullDescription: The erotic is a point of infinite signification, a navel in humanity’s symbolic circuit. However, despite its resistance to formalization, it is always in the process of not being written. As Octavio Paz insists, the erotic is a metaphor indelible to the human. As such, it is unsurprising that the manifestations of the erotic in subjective embodied experience are variable and correspond to equally plural treatments of it across the academic panorama. This diverse archive is bound by certain distinguishable threads, in terms of the potentiality of the erotic, its singular relation to language, and to the sphere of sexuality.

items.fullDescription: In January 2026, murals of faceless female silhouettes in yoga poses were scratched around the genital area in the Indian city of Gwalior. The figures depicted no identifiable women; they were attacked anyway. In 2024, sexually explicit AI-generated deepfakes of Taylor Swift circulated widely online, demonstrating a very different but related form of image violation. Across a scratched public wall and a fabricated digital image, the same question emerges: what happens when an image of a woman becomes the surface upon which sexualisation, humiliation or punishment is performed? This special issue asks where, if anywhere, a woman’s image can be assumed to be safe.

This international academic event seeks to bring together researchers, academics, artists, educators, and professionals from different disciplines to explore the historical, cultural, social, artistic, scientific, and technological dimensions of healing and well-being. The Congress proposes a dialogue between nineteenth-century traditions and contemporary approaches to health and healing, examining continuities, transformations, exchanges, and tensions across the Hispanic world, Asia, Latin America, and the Caribbean. Particular attention will be given to the ways in which literature, art, spirituality, traditional medicine, bodily practices, digital technologies, and community experiences have shaped understandings and practices of healing. Suggested themes include: Genealogies of Healing in Nineteenth-Century Hispanic Culture Representations of Illness in Nineteenth-Century Literature and the Press Art and Healing: Music, Dance, Painting, and Theatre as Therapeutic Practices Dialogues between Allopathic Medicine and Traditional Healing Systems Spirituality, Religion, and Healing Practices Healing through Words: Narratives, Discourse, and Therapeutic Processes Convergences between Bodily Practices (Yoga, Pranayama, Sports) and Holistic Health Healing Traditions in Asia and the Caribbean: Exchanges with the Hispanic World Digital Health, Applications, Platforms, and Well-Being Monitoring Ethical and Clinical Risks of Chatbots and Mental Health Technologies Social Media, Virality, and Their Impact on Emotional Health Attention, Cognition, and Technology Digital Churches, the Spiritual Economy, and New Forms of Religiosity Education and Well-Being Public Health Policies in Digital and Multicultural Environments Interdisciplinarity in Health: Intersections between Art, Science, and Technology Imaginaries of Good and Evil in Processes of Illness and Healing Community Well-Being and Territorial Experiences Researchers interested in participating are invited to submit proposals in accordance with the Congress guidelines. items.fullDescription: Heidelberg Center for American Studies Annual Interdisciplinary Spring Academy Conference Heidelberg, Germany, April 5-9, 2027 Call for Papers The Heidelberg Center for American Studies (HCA) invites applications for its annual Spring Academy on American Culture, Economics, Geography, History, Literature, Politics, and Religion to be held from April 5-9, 2027. The HCA Spring Academy provides 20 international Ph.D. students with the opportunity to present and thoroughly discuss their ongoing Ph.D. projects. The conference offers a forum for Ph.D. candidates in which they can present their research candidly and receive valuable feedback. We encourage applications that range broadly across the arts, humanities, and social sciences and pursue an interdisciplinary approach. Participants can present thesis projects on any subject relating to the study of the United States of America. Possible topics include American identity, issues of ethnicity, gender, transatlantic relations, U.S. domestic and foreign policy, economics, and various aspects of American religion, geography, history, literature, law, musicology, and culture. We also welcome proposals focused on the North American continent at large, i.e. Canada, Central America, and the Caribbean. Participants are requested to prepare a 20-minute presentation of their research project, which will be followed by a 40-minute discussion. The Spring Academy aims to create a congenial atmosphere for scholarly exchange in order to inspire future collaborations and foster networking opportunities for participants. The Heidelberg Center for American Studies is prepared to provide accommodation during the conference week. Thanks to a small travel fund, the Spring Academy can subsidize travel expenses for participants registered and residing in developing and soft-currency countries. Applicants for the travel fund must document the necessity for financial aid and explain how they plan to cover any potentially remaining expenses. Additionally, a letter of recommendation from their doctoral advisor is required. items.fullDescription: CFP: Queer Mediterranean - Sex, Gender, and Social Change April 1-3, 2027, Smith College (Northampton, MA) Queer Mediterranean: Sex, Gender, and Social Change is a conference that brings together scholars, artists, and thinkers to explore queer cultures across the Mediterranean from a transhistorical and transnational perspective, with particular attention to the experiences, voices, and cultural productions of women. The conference aims to explore how queer subjects have navigated, resisted, or reimagined structures of power and belonging across the Mediterranean. What does it mean to think the Mediterranean queerly? What new frameworks, methods, or archives emerge from this approach? While centering women's experiences, we remain fully open to contributions that explore queer life in all its forms. Queer Mediterranean explores what becomes visible when we shift the center of queer theory away from Anglophone frameworks. How do Mediterranean histories complicate dominant narratives of queer identity and liberation? How do Mediterranean perspectives challenge or expand existing models of queer community, kinship, and belonging? What do transnational approaches to queerness reveal about the relationship between queerness, language, and translation? The conference will take place April 1-3, 2027 at Smith College. Hotel accommodations will be provided for all accepted panelists. --- We invite proposals for papers that highlight the richness and diversity of queer experiences across time and place. We welcome scholarly work from across the humanities, social sciences, and arts and are particularly interested in interdisciplinary and transnational perspectives. Topics might include (but are not limited to): Queer histories, archives and memory Queer kinship, family, and belonging Queer migration and diaspora Language, translation, and queer expression Queer literature, film, and visual cultures Queer bodies & embodiment Queer geographies and spaces Queer ecologies and the more-than-human Mediterranean Queer labor and economies Queer tourism and Mediterranean imaginaries Colonialism, postcolonialism, and queerness Queer art and creative practice as resistance Queer temporality and futurity Teaching the queer Mediterranean Abstracts (250-300 words) should be sent through the following google form by November 15, 2026. We will notify accepted panelists by December 15, 2026. Contact: Adrián Gras-Velázquez (agrasvelazquez@smith.edu) Gianna Albaum (galbaum@smith.edu)

items.fullDescription: In the 2000s and 2010s, social networking facilitated citizen-based activism of enormous significance like #BlackLivesMatter and #MeToo. But in the 2020s, corporate enshittification and government surveillance have restricted the reach of social networking tools. For example, Elon Musk’s purchase of Twitter meant that many users left X rather than adapt their activist practices to the restrictive corporate environment (Tenbarge & Collier 2024). Instances such as the Trump administration’s use of social media posts to target international students during the Gaza protests caused many users to avoid social media altogether (Lonas Cochran 2025).

items.fullDescription: CFP: 28th Southeast Conference for Languages, Literatures, and Film (Feb 27-28, 2027) in St. Petersburg, Florida (on the University of South Florida St. Petersburg Campus) Languages and Cultures in a Changing World: Identity, Responsibility, and Justice Abstracts for papers (and panels) are now being considered. Deadline for abstracts: Nov. 16, 2026 Selected papers will be published in a post-conference anthology. To view prior publication, visit the conference website. The SCFLLF welcomes papers on all aspects of literature, theoretical and applied linguistics, culture, philosophy, cultural history, film, other popular media, second language acquisition, and language pedagogy pertaining to non-English languages (ancient and modern). We would like to encourage (but not limit) submissions addressing our conference theme: Identity, Responsibility and Justice, in its broadest understanding. Selected papers will be published in a post-conference anthology. The humanities and the study of languages are facing changing institutional and social expectations. These changes encourage us to reconsider what work we do and the people and communities our work serves. To whom and to what, are artists, scholars and teachers accountable? How do languages, literatures, films, and other forms of cultural expression preserve or challenge established narratives and structures? How do they engage with different identities? How can they help us understand the present and/or imagine different futures? What responsibilities come with teaching and learning languages as well as with studying, interpreting, and representing other cultures? This conference invites scholars working in non-English languages, literatures, film and media, cultural studies, applied and theoretical linguistics, second-language acquisition, and language pedagogy to explore these and related questions from a wide range of disciplinary, theoretical, historical, and methodological perspectives. The conference theme, Identity, Responsibility, and Justice, is deliberately broad. Responsibility may involve our relationships with students and communities, with texts and their histories, with linguistic and cultural traditions, or with the institutions in which we teach and conduct research. Or responsibility can be interrogated with regard to artists and art, in a broad sense. Justice can also be approached in diverse ways. It may involve social justice, questions of representation and recognition, historical memory, inclusion and exclusion, or access and lack thereof to language learning. Justice may also concern translation and cultural mediation or the ways in which literature, film, language, and other cultural practices engage with conflict, inequality, trauma, discrimination, displacement, and/or social change. The SCFLLF keynote speaker is Adam Schwartz (Associate Professor of Language, Culture & Society, Oregon State University). Dr. Schwartz's research addresses Spanish language education and Spanish-English multilingualisms in the U.S. He takes particular interest in intersections of language, race and racism, wherein questions of identity, responsibility and justice persist. In addition to various articles and chapters, he has authored three books. These include Spanish So White: Conversations on the Inconvenient Racism of a 'Foreign' Language Education (2023). He is also the co-author of Aquí se habla: Centering the Local and Personal in Spanish Language Education (2025) as well as Language, Identity and Justice: The Anthropolitical Worlds of Ana Celia Zentella (2026). Some suggestions of topics and their artistic representations include: identity, responsibility, and justice represented in literature, art, film, and other forms of popular media, including social media influence of film and literature on the public and private sphere reassessing the purpose and value of language teaching expressions and perceptions of trauma in response to injustice justice in utopian fictional worlds addressing and expressing identity in the language classroom questions of identity in literature, film, the arts, and other popular media responsibility issues in production and reception of artistic expressions responsibilities associated with researching and representing cultures apart or in comparison to our own the broader influence of imaginary worlds created in film, literature, the visual arts, and other forms of media on real political and personal justice language and linguistic-related topics concerning identity, responsibility, and justice other topics Please submit a proposal (of no more than 250 words) for a single paper or a full panel (max. of 3 presentations) on the conference webpage. We can only accept online submissions. Please contact Margit Grieb (grieber@usf.edu) if you have any questions.

items.fullDescription: The rise of the superhero is one of the most significant cultural developments of the twentieth and twenty-first centuries. Since the debut of Superman in Action Comics #1 (April 18, 1938), superheroes have evolved from colorful comic-book figures into powerful global symbols that shape conversations about politics, morality, identity, technology, gender, race, mythology, trauma, and resistance. What began with the imaginative vision of Jerry Siegel (writer) and Joe Shuster (artist) has expanded into a worldwide phenomenon spanning comics, film, television, literature, gaming, digital media, and academic discourse.

items.fullDescription: At many universities, learning communities foster connectedness and belonging among students. At their best, they promote the perspective that learning is a collective activity in which knowledge is constructed through relationships with peers, professors, and communities, bringing together diverse voices and interdisciplinary perspectives. They provide a welcoming environment that eases the transition to college and provides a foundation for a peer network of academic support (Schreiber & Valle, 2013).

items.fullDescription: Call for Papers: Literary Gardens: Cultivation, Movement, and Modernism An International Online Conference | February 12-13, 2027 | Online sponsored by The Elizabeth von Arnim Society in conversation with The Literary Garden: The Cultivation of Plants & Gardens in Narratives Stephen and Peter Sachs Museum, Missouri Botanical Garden The Elizabeth von Arnim Society invites paper proposals for an international online conference on literary gardens, held in conversation with the Missouri Botanical Garden exhibit The Literary Garden: The Cultivation of Plants & Gardens in Narratives (Sachs Museum, May 2026-March 2027), curated by Nezka Pfeifer. Inspired by the exhibition's wide-ranging exploration of plants and gardens, this conference will consider gardens as spaces of literary cultivation, movement, and modernity. Gardens are never simply settings: they are imagined spaces, sites of labor and care, refuge and restoration, social and cultural exchange, but also places of exclusion, transgression, and imperialist pilfering. Plants, people, texts, ideas, and botanical knowledge move through them. Gardens can therefore illuminate modernism's preoccupation with mobility, displacement, belonging, transformation, and the relationship between the human and more-than-human worlds. The conference centers on modernism, broadly conceived, including fin-de-siècle precursors and modernism's later extensions and legacies. We are particularly interested in women's garden writing, including that of Elizabeth von Arnim, as well as the ways gardens participate in transnational literary and cultural networks. We welcome work on African American, Caribbean, diasporic, queer, Indigenous, and other perspectives that complicate and expand histories of modernism and the literary garden. We warmly encourage you to share this call with colleagues, graduate students, and independent scholars Keynote Speakers: Nezka Pfiefer, curator of The Literary Garden: The Cultivation of Plants & Gardens in Narrativesat the Sachs Museum, Missouri Botanical Garden Karina Jakubowicz, author of Gardens in the work of Virginia Woolf: Nature, Modernity, and the Politics of Space (2026 Edinburgh UP) We welcome proposals on subjects including, but not limited to: Cultivation and Modernist Cultures Elizabeth von Arnim and the literary garden Fin-de-siècle garden writing, including Oscar Wilde and Gertrude Jekyll Women, gardens, and modernist cultural production, including Elizabeth von Arnim, Virginia Woolf, Katherine Mansfield, H.D., and Edith Wharton Gardens as spaces of artistic, literary, and intellectual exchange War, Healing, and Remembrance The healing garden: refuge, restoration, remembrance, and renewal Peace gardens and gardens of reconciliation in the aftermath of war Gardens, illness, disability, care, and the body Gardens, Labor, Identity, and Space Gardens, labor, class, domestic service, and foodways, including Agnes Smedley and Zora Neale Hurston Gardens, gender, sexuality, queer identity, and the body, including Vita Sackville-West and Beverley Nichols Gardens as spaces of hospitality, community, and cultural production Comparative and translation studies of literary gardens Gardens, archives, botanical history, museums, and exhibitions Movement, Migration, and Belonging Plants, people, texts, ideas, and botanical knowledge in circulation Gardens, migration, diaspora, exile, and the imagination of home Cultivation, transplantation, naturalization, displacement, and belonging Gardens, empire, colonialism, and postcolonialism African American modernism and the garden, including the Harlem Renaissance, Anne Spencer, and Black cultural networks Caribbean and transatlantic modernisms, including Alejo Carpentier and Claude McKay Global and transnational modernisms, including Mário de Andrade Gardens, Plants, and Modernist Form Gardens and modernist poetry, including T. S. Eliot and Sara Teasdale Gardens in fiction, including gothic, speculative, fantasy, mystery, and children's literature Gardens, plants, and the more-than-human: monstrous flora, sentient gardens, and speculative botany Writing in the garden: composition, retreat, and creative practice Ecocriticism, plant studies, and botanical modernisms Gardens, books, illustration, and modernist print culture Submission Guidelines Please submit an abstract of approximately 250 words for a 20-minute paper, or for a full panel (3-4 papers) 250 words per speaker. Include a short biographical note (100 words) for each speaker. Submit through our submission form: forms.gle/pqbJjueSge3pAFoL9 by November 30, 2026. items.fullDescription: Overview | South Mediterranean University, Tunisia Hybrid Format: In-person and Online Participation The SMU Conference on AI-Era Teaching: Innovative Pedagogy and Reimagined Classrooms will take place at South Mediterranean University, Tunisia. This research oriented event brings together scholars, educators, instructional designers, and researchers to explore evidence-based pedagogical innovation in technology-mediated and AI-enhanced learning environments. This conference provides an international platform to present academic research, foster interdisciplinary dialogue, and advance collaboration on the future of teaching and learning in the AI era. The 2027 SMU Conference, themed "AI-Era Teaching: Innovative Pedagogy and Reimagined Classrooms," examines how AI and emerging educational technologies reshape instructional design, classroom engagement, assessment, and learning ecosystems. Key focus areas include measurable learning outcomes, ethical and inclusive AI integration, pedagogical quality assurance, and student competency development in hybrid and digital environments. We invite researchers, practitioners, instructional designers, and graduate students worldwide to submit original research, empirical studies, and case studies on innovative pedagogy, AI-enhanced instruction, learning analytics, engagement strategies, and inclusive practices.
