items.fullDescription: Living with the Wild: Wildlife, Civilization, and the Trouble of Coexistence University of Catania, 1-3 March 2027 Abstract deadline: 30 November 2026 The final conference of the WILD-CONNECT project, Wildlife Circulation and the Enactment of Civilization in Diachronic Perspective, invites contributions exploring how relations between the "wild" and the "civilized" have been shaped across historical, political, and cultural contexts. The conference approaches these categories as historically produced and mutually constitutive, and examines how their boundaries are continually renegotiated through institutions, practices, imaginaries, and material forms of life. We welcome contributions from anthropology, history, political ecology, environmental humanities, and related fields addressing wildlife circulation, control, transformation, and reintroduction, as well as the interconnected processes of dewilding and rewilding. Possible topics include domestication, conservation and ecological restoration; colonial and postcolonial wildlife governance; sovereignty, borders and wildlife circulation; everyday encounters with wildlife; scientific, legal and economic classifications of living beings; and the unintended consequences and limits of wildlife governance. The conference will feature keynote contributions by Vanessa Manceron (CNRS), Marcy Norton (University of Pennsylvania), and Erik Gómez-Baggethun (Norwegian University of Life Sciences). Accepted papers will be circulated among participants in advance, and contributions presented at the conference will be considered for inclusion in a collective volume or a special issue of an international journal in environmental humanities. Living_with_the_Wild_Call Please submit: an abstract of 300-400 words; a short biographical note of 100-150 words; institutional affiliation, if any, and contact details. Submissions should be sent to mara.benadusi@unict.it and lorenzo.coccoli@unict.it. Deadline : 30 November 2026 Notification of acceptance : 2 January 2027

items.excerpt: EUROPEAN SHAKESPEARE RESEARCH ASSOCIATION Congress, Shakespeare and Form: 'To set a form upon desired change' Bangor University, Wales, 27-30 July 2027 CALL FOR PAPERS : Seminar 9, Forms of Shakespeare's Diplomacy Convenors: Nathalie Rivère de Carles (Université Toulouse Jean Jaurès), France & Helen A. Hopkins (Birmingham City University, UK...
items.fullDescription: EUROPEAN SHAKESPEARE RESEARCH ASSOCIATION Congress, Shakespeare and Form: 'To set a form upon desired change' Bangor University, Wales, 27-30 July 2027 CALL FOR PAPERS : Seminar 9, Forms of Shakespeare's Diplomacy Convenors: Nathalie Rivère de Carles (Université Toulouse Jean Jaurès), France & Helen A. Hopkins (Birmingham City University, UK) This seminar investigates Shakespeare's diplomacy as a set of theatrical, political, and cultural forms: embassies, intelligence networks, ceremonial encounters, negotiated speech, translation, performance, heritage display, and later uses of Shakespeare as cultural capital. It will explore: · how diplomacy within Early Modern plays depends on forms: letters, reports, oaths, staged audiences, theatrical entertainments, curatorial narratives, and embodied performances of civility or threat · how drama stages the fragile procedures by which states, courts, and individuals form relations across difference · how playing companies have performed and/or participated in diplomacy from the early modern era until now (performing for ambassadors, negotiating patronage, censorship, audience reception, and transnational theatrical exchange, operating as cultural intermediaries through international festivals, touring productions, education programmes…) · formal and informal ambassadorship from early modern times until now, and the models of negotiation generated through varied uses of Shakespeare's works and cultural capital · how Shakespeare becomes an object of heritage diplomacy: curated through archives, museums, anniversaries, diplomatic/commemorative monuments, exhibitions, festivals, and touring productions that present him as a shared cultural inheritance while often reproducing hierarchies of nation, empire, race, gender, and class · how plays and institutions produce diplomatic knowledge: teaching audiences to read gestures, decode equivocation, evaluate testimony, and imagine political community beyond national borders The discussion will move from early modern diplomatic forms to Shakespeare's afterlives in official cultural diplomacy, public diplomacy, soft power, and heritage policy. Attention will also be given to deformation: failed negotiations, distorted information, imperial appropriation, and the conversion of cultural prestige (soft power) into political force (as cooperation or coercion). The wider aim is to reassess "Shakespearean diplomacy" as both an early modern practice of relation-making and a modern instrument whose global circulation may enable conversation, domination, or critique. In this way, we engage with the discourse around the decolonisation of Shakespeare. This process will therefore be treated not as the rejection of Shakespeare, but as a method for interrogating the colonial uses of the "Bard," recovering plural performance traditions, and rethinking heritage as a contested diplomatic space. By bringing together approaches from literary criticism, theatre history, performance studies, critical heritage studies, gender studies, race studies, and new diplomatic history, the seminar asks whether Shakespearean drama merely reflects diplomatic culture or actively theorises it. Abstracts (250-500 words) should be sent to both nrivere@univ-tlse2.fr and helen.hopkins3@bcu.ac.uk by 4th December 2026 Acceptance notification: 16th December 2026. Details about the Congress can be found here: https://www.bangor.ac.uk/sah/the-european-shakespeare-research-association-esra-2027

items.title: Hong Kong Temporalities
items.location: Online · Chinese University of Hong Kong
items.excerpt: [Call for Abstracts] A Hong Kong Studies Virtual Symposium 21-22 January 2027 | Online https://bit.ly/4hGfW8y Organised by Hong Kong Studies, this two-day symposium invites papers from across the humanities and social sciences that explore time and temporality in relation to Hong Kong's cultural, historical, technological, social and political imaginaries...
items.fullDescription: [Call for Abstracts] A Hong Kong Studies Virtual Symposium 21-22 January 2027 | Online https://bit.ly/4hGfW8y Organised by Hong Kong Studies, this two-day symposium invites papers from across the humanities and social sciences that explore time and temporality in relation to Hong Kong's cultural, historical, technological, social and political imaginaries. Hong Kong has long been a city peculiarly conscious of time. Its modern history has been narrated through beginnings and endings, leases and deadlines, arrivals and departures, anniversaries and countdowns. 1997 became an anticipated future long before it became history; 2047 likewise exists simultaneously as date, horizon, projection and cultural imaginary. Yet Hong Kong's temporalities extend far beyond these emblematic dates. They can be found in memories of vanished places, family histories and memoirs, experiences of migration and exile, changing generations and languages, speculative and science-fictional futures, technological acceleration, artificial intelligence, and everyday experiences of waiting, repetition, anticipation and change. The symposium asks: what forms of time have shaped Hong Kong and its cultural imagination? How are its pasts remembered, forgotten, recovered or reinvented? How do memoir, literature, cinema, art and popular culture create alternative relationships between past, present and future? What temporalities emerge through migration, diaspora, exile and return? How do generations inhabit historical time differently? What happens to experiences of time under conditions of rapid political, urban and technological transformation? How might artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies alter our understanding of memory, prediction, authorship and futurity? And what can science fiction and speculative practices tell us about Hong Kong futures that have been anticipated, deferred, foreclosed or not yet imagined? We welcome papers addressing topics including, but not limited to, countdowns and deadlines; history and historiography; memory and forgetting; memoir and life writing; nostalgia and post-nostalgia; futurity and anticipation; science fiction and speculative fiction; utopia and dystopia; technology and technological change; artificial intelligence and algorithmic time; digital memory and archives; ageing and generational time; migration, diaspora, exile and return; colonial and postcolonial temporalities; urban transformation and disappearing spaces; everyday rhythms, waiting and repetition; acceleration and rupture; haunting, spectrality and afterlives; alternative histories and counterfutures; and temporality in literature, cinema, music, visual art, performance and popular culture. By bringing these approaches into conversation, the symposium seeks to consider Hong Kong as a site of intersecting temporalities, where remembered pasts, contested presents and multiple possible futures continually reshape one another. We invite contributions from scholars at all stages of their professional development, as well as independent scholars, writers, artists, filmmakers, critics, curators, educators, technologists, and other cultural practitioners whose work engages with Hong Kong and questions of temporality. In addition to traditional academic papers, the symposium welcomes short presentations or informal talks that approach Hong Kong temporalities through creative, professional, personal, or interdisciplinary perspectives. Please submit an abstract of 300-500 words, along with a short third-person biography (approx. 150 words), compiled in a single Word document. Submissions should be sent to hkstudiesjournal@gmail.com by Friday 4 December 2026. Following the symposium, selected papers (6,000-8,000 words) will be considered for publication in future issues of Hong Kong Studies (Open Journals Hub).

items.fullDescription: Call for Chapters: One Stitch at a Time: Telling Stories, Archiving Histories, and Threading Narratives of Resistance and Rebellion through Embroidered Art and Needlecraft For thousands of years, embroidery and embroidered work have been used as a mode of visual storytelling and of documenting national or cultural histories. From the 12000 years-old fiberwork found in the Guitarrero Cave, to twine textile artwork of the Peruvian Norte Chico civilization of 2500 BCE, the thousands of years old Chinese silk thread embroidery, the decorative thread arts of the Indus Valley Civilization of 3000 BCE, the ancient Egyptian needlework of 1300 BCE, the Bayeux Tapestry of Norman conquest, and the thousands of years old embroidery and quilt work of the indigenous communities across the North and South Americas, human civilizations have woven and embroidered their histories and cultures and have archived everything for future generations. Embroidery has also functioned as a powerful trope of resistance narrative and rebellious vision. Marjorie Agosín's iconic book, Tapestries of Hope recounts how Chilean women used embroidery and textile art as tools of resistance and rebellion during Pinochet's dictatorship. More recently, Kirstie McLeod's collaborative project "The Red Dress" brings together the needlework, voices, and stories of 380 individuals from 51 countries. Collectively, their embroidered experiences on a single red dress, across a range of expertise, positions, and languages, testify to human rights concerns around the world. In the context of underprivileged women from the global South, embroidery and needlework have been a source of financial freedom and a platform for women's social bonding and personal expressions. For example, cottage industries in Bangladesh, India, and many other South and East Asian countries have mobilized economically impoverished women into an active workforce and have turned embroidery and needlework into a booming business. In literature and media, embroidered works also provide intense narrative power. Adrienne Rich's "Aunt Jennifer's Tigers" and Rosa del Valle's tablecloth in Isabel Allende's The House of the Spirits, are two such examples. Embroidery has provided a pertinent motif for re-presenting folklore, myth, and collective memory in many countries, such as Bangladesh and India, where women's acts of illustrating folklores, personal loss and pain in quilts or narrating the mythical stories of the Ramayana and the Mahabharata through needlework are an essential part of their national and cultural history. Textile arts, embroidery and needlework function as narrative technologies that initiate individual, social, and political involvement. It invokes memory and provokes individuals to make or break myths regarding nation, narration, gender, identity, and/or human existence in the age of artificial intelligence. Against this extensive backdrop of embroidery as a narrative technology, we invite abstracts for a collection tentatively titled One Stitch at a Time: Telling Stories, Archiving Histories, and Threading Narratives of Resistance and Rebellion through Embroidered Art and Needlecraft. Tentative topic list for the paper (but is not limited to): Archiving history through embroidery Embroidery as narrative technology Embroidery as a trope of Agency and/or Identity Embroidery as a narrative of political resistance Embroidery as Storytelling Embroidery and human rights or social justice Embroidery and activism Embroidery and/in literature Embroidery and/as cultural identity Embroidery and/as visual narrative Embroidery and ecocriticism Myth, memory, and embroidery Retelling myth and re-presenting identity Women and embroidery Please send us your 150 words abstract with 3 key words and a 50-word bio by December 10, 2026. If accepted, we will request for the completed essay (minimum of 7000 words) by June 30, 2027. The anthology is expected to be published by a university press in the US. Looking forward to receiving your abstract at fayeza.hasanat@ucf.edu , cc farrah.cato@ucf.edu Sincerely, Dr. Fayeza Hasanat and Dr. Farrah Cato English Department University of Central Florida

items.fullDescription: Volume 6: Immersion and Emergence in the Fantastic (Fall 2027) Immersion is a key concept in the fantastic. From the 3D worlds of Avatar to the in-depth lore of The Lord of the Rings, fantastic narratives thrive on the idea of immersing us in worlds so detailed that we feel as if we are really there. Fantastic worlds often come with their own detailed maps, histories, languages, and cultures, creating the illusion of being a real place. Media industries invest heavily in producing technologies of immersion, such as 4D cinema or VR games. Immersion is one of Henry Jenkins' "Seven Core Principles of Transmedia Storytelling", while Mark J.P. Wolf distinguishes between physical immersion, as in a theme park ride, and conceptual immersion, in which audiences are mentally absorbed by the imaginary world, often to the extent of crowding out the real world. In psychology, this state has been called "narrative transportation" (Brock and Green 2000) with researchers attempting to create a scale that measures the feeling of immersion and the techniques that help generate this state. However, immersion is also a problematic metaphor as it assumes the audience desires complete absorption into another state. For Viktor Shklovsky or Bertolt Brecht, immersion was a prelude to estrangement, where distance from the fictional world was essential for aesthetic effect. Reception practices also raise doubts about whether immersion is the desired goal of audiences. Technologies for greater sensual immersion, such as 3D and VR, have not proven as popular as a theory of immersion would suggest. Merja Polvinen has argued that the theory of narrative transportation ignores the "double vision of fiction" (2017), the capacity of audiences to appreciate a storyworld and its aesthetics simultaneously. If appreciation of how Game of Thrones breaks with fantasy genre conventions is an intrinsic aspect of its success, how is this to be reconciled with the idea of pure immersion? Another complication is when the fantastic enters the real world. Henry Jenkins pairs immersion with "extractability," the ways in which audiences take aspects of the narrative universe and deploy them in reality, such as activists dressing up as handmaids from The Handmaid's Tale in order to advocate for reproductive rights. As elements of fantastic worlds bleed into our world, they complicate the metaphor of immersion. Consider the development of quidditch as real-life sport: is this immersion in the world of fantasy or the emergence of the fantastic into the real? The pairing of immersion and emergence suggests another possibility, that true immersion in a fictional world only happens when the fictional world generates emergent properties that are not contained within the text. Imagining the Impossible invites articles on issues of immersion and emergence in relation to the fantastic. Possible themes include: Theoretical approaches to immersion and emergence Immersion and estrangement Immersive techniques in fantastic storyworlds Immersive technologies and their implications for worldbuilding Extractability and emergence in the reception of the fantastic Fan practices that blend immersion and emergence Analysis of specific texts where immersion or emergence are textual features Length 5000-8000 words, Chicago style (in text), please keep notes to a minimum. Illustrations are welcome, 300 dpi at print size, .jpg. Authors are responsible for all illustration copyrights. Deadline for Volume 6 A 500-800 word abstract on December 11, 2026. A first draft article by May 1, 2027, to be published Fall 2027. The finished article should include 125-150 word abstract and 5 - 7 keywords. Articles will be double blind peer-reviewed, edited and published online as they are submitted to the journal. Please send proposals and questions to the editorial team. Editorial team Stephen Joyce, Aarhus University, sjoyce@cc.au.dk Christian Mehrstam, University of Gothenburg, christian.mehrstam@lir.gu.se Per Israelson, Stockholm University, per.israelson@littvet.su.se

items.fullDescription: Social Inclusion, peer-reviewed journal indexed in the Social Sciences Citation Index and Scopus, welcomes new and exciting research papers for its upcoming issue "Inclusive Diversity in European Education: From Policy Frameworks to Classroom Practices," edited by Roberto Baelo Álvarez, Alessandro Bergamaschi, and Anna Elia. Submission of Abstracts: 1-15 December 2026 Submission of Full Papers: 15-30 April 2027 Publication of the Issue: June/December 2027 About the issue: Contemporary European societies are characterised by an unprecedented degree of diversity (linguistic, cultural, ethnic, religious, and socioeconomic), challenging the foundations of traditional educational systems. The concept of superdiversity, which moves beyond binary majority-minority frameworks to account for the complex intersectionality of identities and trajectories, reflects the lived reality of classrooms, schools, and universities across the continent. However, educational policies and pedagogical practices have often lagged behind this transformation, generating tensions between normative aspirations for inclusion and the structural conditions shaping everyday educational contexts. This thematic issue brings together interdisciplinary scholarship examining how educational systems across Europe and beyond are responding, or failing to respond, to the challenges and opportunities posed by diversity. Drawing on sociology, educational science, political science, and intercultural studies, the issue addresses four interconnected dimensions: the normative and policy frameworks governing diversity in education; the social implications of superdiversity for educational communities, particularly the tension between demands for equality and differentiation in everyday school situations; the pedagogical approaches, teacher education strategies, and curricular innovations aimed at fostering inclusive learning environments; and the perspectives of key actors, including students, educators, institutions, and civil society. Finally, the issue aims to critically examine whether inclusion can be considered a new paradigm for understanding social cohesion, alongside established models such as multiculturalism and assimilationism, and their respective contributions to the educational field. The issue welcomes original research, systematic reviews, and theoretically grounded contributions that engage with multiculturalism, intercultural education, diversity management, social cohesion, and inclusive educational practice in formal and non-formal settings across all educational levels. Comparative, cross-national, and transdisciplinary perspectives are particularly encouraged, as are contributions documenting good practices and innovative approaches. By bringing these conversations into dialogue, this issue advances scholarly understanding and evidence-based policy reflection on one of the most pressing challenges facing European and global educational systems today. Instructions for authors: Authors interested in submitting a paper for this issue are asked to consult the journal's instructions for authors and submit their abstracts (maximum of 250 words, with a tentative title) through the abstracts system: https://www.cogitatiopress.com/app/socialinclusion/abstracts When submitting their abstracts, authors are also asked to confirm that they are aware that Social Inclusion is an open access journal with a publishing fee if the article is accepted for publication after peer-review (corresponding authors affiliated with our institutional members do not incur this fee). Open access: Readers across the globe will be able to access, share, and download this issue entirely for free. Corresponding authors affiliated with any of our institutional members (over 100 institutions worldwide) publish free of charge. Otherwise, an article processing fee will be charged to the authors to cover editorial costs. We defend that authors should not have to personally pay this fee and encourage them to check with their institutions if funds are available to cover open access publication costs. Further information about the journal's open access charges can be found here: https://www.cogitatiopress.com/socialinclusion/about/editorialPolicies#publicationFees Abstracts welcome until 15 December 2026.

items.fullDescription: In her book Bodyminds Reimagined , Sami Schalk asks us “What might it mean to imagine disability differently?” (2) Her work, situated in the exploration of black speculative fiction, engages with (dis)ability studies and black feminism to gesture toward a reimagining of what Margaret Price termed the ‘bodymind’, a concept predicated on “the enmeshment of the mind and body.” (5) How might this enmeshment be understood in the context of chronic conditions, themselves experienced as a direct result of climate change and biomedical violence? Is the planet - made sick by extractive capitalism and anthropogenic action as Shukla, Settee, Lincoln and others claim - now existing in a state of (dis)ability?

items.fullDescription: Beginning in the nineteenth century, the world witnessed the emergence of national movements that advocated the construction of states founded upon the historical and cultural identity of peoples, as well as upon their independence and strategic autonomy. This wave, which manifested itself most prominently in the European revolutions of 1848, the so-called "Springtime of the Peoples," produced a long-term historical impact - according to the principle of the longue durée - that influenced world political history in the decades that followed. This phenomenon was of enormous importance in the Western political sphere, having its precursors in the American Revolution and in the political epic of South American Bolivarianism, and gaining momentum from 1848 onward with the emergence of a whole series of European national movements. With the First World War, and with the promotion by Woodrow Wilson and the United States of the principle of "self-determination of peoples," the same idea experienced a revival which, through Turkish Kemalism and the formation of the Chinese nationalist movement, extended into the non-Western world. Non-Western forms of this type of movement, in turn, had important precursors in anti-colonial movements, which, like European national movements, sought to secure independence and autonomy for broad sectors of the world subjected to foreign domination of an economic and extractive nature. During the twentieth century, the idea of national independence assumed various ideological and political forms, eventually giving rise to different theories of national autonomy and sovereignty, such as Mao Zedong's "Three Worlds Theory." At the same time, the rise of communist revolutions and of the world socialist camp revitalized this political idea, generating new formulations of theories of national revolution. With this call for papers, we intend to collect contributions on the theme of national revolutions in the West and the East, considered both from a theoretical perspective - by examining the political thought of the authors who promoted these movements, as well as the movements themselves - and from the perspective of the relations among these movements and the elaboration of a political theory of coexistence among these political projects. We also intend to focus on the theories and practices of these movements from the perspective of international relations, both by analyzing national revolutions within the international context, in diplomatic and strategic terms, and by addressing the theoretical elaboration of an international order founded upon national independence. A non-exhaustive list of topics that may be addressed includes: Jacobinism and the emergence of the idea of national revolution in Europe The American Revolution and the national-revolutionary paradigm Bolivarianism and national revolution in Spanish America 1848 and the transformation of the national idea in Europe Mazzini and the theory of nationalities The Italian Risorgimento and its relationship with the great powers Bonapartism and national revolutions Self-determination of peoples and the international order after the First World War Kemalism and the Turkish national revolutionù The Soviet Revolution and the issue of nationalities Chinese nationalism and national revolution in the thought of Sun Yat-sen Nationalism and anti-imperialism in anti-colonial liberation movements Mao Zedong and the theory of national revolution National revolution and internationalism in Marxist and communist thought National sovereignty, the balance of power, and the international order National identity and international relations theory National movements and the opposition to a bipolar and unipolar world National movements and anti-colonial struggles in Africa Arab nationalism and movements for emancipation in the Middle East Indian nationalism and the struggle for independence National and revolutionary movements in twentieth-century Latin America Nationalisms in Southeast Asia and the dissolution of the colonial empire Proposals should contain a title, a brief summary or abstract of between 300 and 400 words, the author's email address, and a brief five-line CV. Proposals must be sent to the email address nationalrevolutionsintheworld@gmail.com The deadline for submitting proposals is December 31, 2026. Accepted proposals will be announced starting January 31, 2027, and editorial instructions for preparing the book chapter will be provided. The deadline for submitting the final version of the chapters will be a date to be determined in the first quarter of 2027. items.fullDescription: The Dark Lord Sauron, the titular Lord of the Rings in Tolkien’s magnum opus, plays many roles and takes many forms throughout The Lord of the Rings, The Silmarillion, and the rest of Tolkien’s Legendarium, and even more in the various adaptations and reimaginings that have since emerged. Over years of varying interpretations, Sauron has evolved into a figure of vast significance. From his early depictions as a looming, disembodied threat to his more recent portrayals as a visually captivating "sexy" villain in contemporary pop culture, Sauron’s image has undergone a transformation, revealing much about changing attitudes toward power, corruption, and desire.

Speaking from vastly different parts of the world, there was an unmistakable sense of a planet slipping beyond available comprehension and unplugging us from work and life routines. As wars in the Middle East expand and fires spread from apartment blocks reduced to rubble to bombed oil refineries and shipping corridors, profound geopolitical, personal, even psychic rifts leave us grasping for the language and feel of the moment, the falling apart of things, the zeitgeist of an endangered now.

items.title: Animal Studies Across Disciplines
items.location: Arizona State University · Arizona State University
items.excerpt: Animal Studies Across Disciplines Symposium April 7th-April 9th 2027 Arizona State University Many scholars argue that we are now living in a new geological epoch-the Anthropocene-a name chosen to encapsulate an irreversibly transformed planet due to the rapid expansion of human populations, increasing exploitation of animals and natural resources, and pe...
items.fullDescription: Animal Studies Across Disciplines Symposium April 7th-April 9th 2027 Arizona State University Many scholars argue that we are now living in a new geological epoch-the Anthropocene-a name chosen to encapsulate an irreversibly transformed planet due to the rapid expansion of human populations, increasing exploitation of animals and natural resources, and pervasive pollution. The effects of the Anthropocene have been caused by only a small percentage of the world's population, yet those living in the Global South disproportionately suffer the consequences. The Anthropocene, then, is just as much a social problem as it is an environmental issue. Despite the centrality of animals to planetary health, however, nonhuman life often remains peripheral to discussions of climate and environmental sustainability, even as industrial agriculture drives deforestation and carbon emissions, species extinction destabilizes ecosystems, and the increasing emergence of zoonotic diseases-Covid-19 and Hantavirus among them-reveals the profound interdependence of human, animal, and environmental health. At the same time, dominant responses to environmental crises, which made possible the conditions of crisis in the first place, tend to privilege scientific discovery and technological innovation while neglecting the cultural narratives, entrenched biases, and networks of power that shape human-animal relationships.. To that end, imagining more just and hospitable futures requires new interdisciplinary approaches that recognize animals and interspecies relations as critical to collective flourishing and environmental sustainability. The Animal Studies Across Disciplines Symposium will bring together scholars, artists, students, animal professionals, and community members across the humanities, social sciences, and natural sciences to discuss animals and multispecies futures. The symposium is designed not only as a scholarly gathering, but as the start of a long-term collaborative network capable of shaping future research, public humanities work, community partnerships, and environmental dialogue. The inaugural Spring 2027 Symposium will center on the keyword "care," inviting participants to analyze how different disciplines, professions, and communities define and mobilize care in relation to animals, multispecies justice, and environmental stewardship. In doing so, the Symposium will evaluate practices of protection and responsibility alongside the violences and inequalities that shape life across species. For example, how might a humanities scholar, veterinarian, ecologist, or activist understand and practice care differently, and what might each learn from the knowledge, methods, and questions of the others? How might regional, place-based, and communal forms of knowledge offer different ways of understanding our relationships and responsibilities to animals? How is care negotiated when the welfare of an individual animal comes into conflict with the preservation of a population, species, or ecosystem? What might care mean for animals such as insects, whose small size, vast numbers, and frequent classification as pests or disease vectors complicate familiar practices of care? How do animals care for themselves, one another, and members of other species, and what might these practices teach us about caring for each other and the more-than-human world? The Symposium invites participants to consider what becomes possible when different ways of knowing and relating to animals are brought into conversation, and how such exchanges might expand our understanding and practice of care across species. Possible topics include: Regional approaches to Animal Studies and human-animal relations (e.g. desert ecologies, southern studies, the arctic, etc.) Global and transnational approaches to Animal items.title: Derrick Bell and the History of Africana Philosophy
items.excerpt: The Journal for the New Narratives in the History of Philosophy (JNNHP) invites submissions for its special on Derrick Bell and the History of Africana Philosophy, to be published in Fall 2027. Derrick Bell, the founder of Critical Race Theory, produced one of the most innovative, insightful, and transformative ideas in the 20th century. His philosophical...
items.fullDescription: The Journal for the New Narratives in the History of Philosophy (JNNHP) invites submissions for its special on Derrick Bell and the History of Africana Philosophy, to be published in Fall 2027. Derrick Bell, the founder of Critical Race Theory, produced one of the most innovative, insightful, and transformative ideas in the 20th century. His philosophical insights continue to challenge how western liberal nations contend with questions of civil rights, human rights, immigration, policing, and education. Recent conservative attacks focused on Critical Race Theory (CRT) in the U.S, Canada, and England assert, albeit erroneously, that CRT is a Marxist and communist ideology that seeks to supplant western values and the ethos of liberal democracy. Contrary to these fallacious attacks, Bell's textbook Race, Racism, and American Law is amongst the first law textbooks to give a comprehensive view of how racism shaped the development of American law and race relations. In this regard, CRT draws heavily on a tradition of Africana philosophy from slavery through the 20th century. It challenges, not only the supposed neutrality of U.S. law, but also the universality of western political ideals, and U.S. law as egalitarian. For example, Bell engaged Frederick Douglass's critiques of natural law theorists and abolitionists who read the American Constitution as a slave document. For Douglass, the Constitution is an economic contract that robs slaves of their labour and property rights. Drawing on Douglass' critique, Bell interrogated how economic interests have structured American law as an instrument for white class interests over Black claims for justice from slavery through the 20th century. Similarly, Bell engaged W.E.B DuBois's reading of American democracy that underscored how U.S. law in the 13 colonies suppressed African revolts while upholding slavery. Such legal resistance to African acts of liberation, Dubois argued, created paradoxes for American democracy and shaped how the legal system understood the Black freedom struggle. Following Dubois' analysis, Bell explored how the law is an ineffective tool for racial remediation when it comes to addressing social injustices that confront Black life. Bell also engaged Malcolm X's critiques of the Reconstruction era civil rights and 1960 civil rights amendments as pyrrhic victories. This inspired Bell to think about how civil rights function as symbolic victories while ensuring racism is a permanent fixture of American democracy. Given Bell's extensive engagement with 18th-20th century Africana philosophy, this special seeks to consider Bell's work within Africana philosophy. As such, the special welcomes essays that focus on Bell's work as philosophical historiography and inquiry into Black life and its relation to democracy as part of the long tradition of Africana philosophy. The special seeks contributions that address the following themes: Derrick Bell as a philosopher of Black history. Derrick Bell as a philosopher of Black legal theory. Derrick Bell and the Black Nationalist and the Black Radical Tradition. Derrick Bell as a philosopher of Black Education. Derrick Bell as a philosopher of contemporary society and issue of civil rights. Essays must be submitted to https://journal.lib.uoguelph.ca/index.php/nnhp/about/submissions Deadline for Essay Submission: January 7th, 2027. Papers will be considered after January 7th, 2027. The Co-lead Guest Editors for this Special are Drs. Dalitso Ruwe (Queens University), Adebayo Oluwayomi (West Chester University), Andrew Soto (Hartnell College). For questions about the Special, please contact: derrickbellspecial@gmail.com JNNHP is an open-access online journal committed to publishing papers on underrepresented figures or themes in the history of philosophy, both Western and non-Western traditions, from the ancient period to the mid-20th century. JNNHP accepts papers in English and French. Papers should be no more than 10000 words. JNNHP also seeks to highlight relevant translations, archival work or new editions of primary texts in progress. We will publish selections from such works, with critical notes and contextual introductions.

items.excerpt: CALL FOR PAPERS Affective Worlds: Emotions and Aesthetics in Afro-Descendant Women's Writing International Conference 24-25 May 2027, Vrije Universiteit Brussel (Belgium) Format: in person Language: English Link to the CfP : https://clic.research.vub.be/afropemotions-international-conference The conference explores the role of affect, emotions, and aesthe...
items.fullDescription: CALL FOR PAPERS Affective Worlds: Emotions and Aesthetics in Afro-Descendant Women's Writing International Conference 24-25 May 2027, Vrije Universiteit Brussel (Belgium) Format: in person Language: English Link to the CfP : https://clic.research.vub.be/afropemotions-international-conference The conference explores the role of affect, emotions, and aesthetics in the rich and diverse body of work published in the twentieth and twenty-first centuries by women writers of African heritage from African, European, Caribbean, and other diasporic contexts. The event examines how affect and emotions shape both the sociopolitical dimensions of Afro-descendant women's literature and its narrative and aesthetic practices across multiple linguistic, cultural, and historical contexts and through fiction, poetry, and drama. By often exploring issues of displacement, marginalisation, systemic oppression, colonial legacies, trauma, cultural memory, and environmental change, Afro-descendant women authors present affect as a site of self-awareness, resistance, community formation, and political imagination, while articulating it through narrative form, language, imagery, and other aesthetic strategies. The conference brings together established and early-career researchers working at the intersection of different fields, including affect studies, African and African diasporic literary studies, comparative literary studies, feminist and queer studies, postcolonial and decolonial studies, trauma and cultural memory studies, and the environmental humanities. While acknowledging theoretical distinctions between affect and emotion, particularly those developed in affect theory by scholars such as Tomkins (1962) and Massumi (2002), the conference welcomes literary criticism informed by diverse affective frameworks, such as cognitive and narratological perspectives on affect (e.g. Hogan 2003, 2011), sociopolitical approaches to affect and emotions (e.g. Ahmed 2004; Berlant 2011), and affective ecocriticism (e.g. Bladow and Ladino 2018). We invite papers exploring affect and emotions in Afro-descendant women's literature written in English, French, German, Italian, or other languages. Topics may include but are not limited to: Affective relations, transnational belonging, and diasporic identities Migration, displacement, and affective literary geographies Affect and gender, race, class, and sexuality Queer affects Affect, narrative form, and aesthetics Affect, language, multilingualism, and translation Emotions, trauma, and memory Collective affect, solidarity, and community formation Eco-emotions and environmental change Emotional responses to injustice, inequality, and systemic oppression Affect, embodiment, and resistance SUBMISSION GUIDELINES Please send proposals for 20-minute papers in English to Dr. Isabella Villanova (Isabella.Villanova@vub.be) and Prof. dr. Elisabeth Bekers (Elisabeth.Bekers@vub.be). Proposals should include: an abstract (max. 250 words), with up to 5 references, preferably in Chicago style; 5 keywords; a short biographical note (max. 100 words) Deadline for Proposal Submissions: 10 January 2027 Notification of Acceptance: 10 February 2027 Selected papers may be considered for publication in a special journal issue. items.fullDescription: Call for Proposals The editorial and scientific board of the journal Co-herencia invites researchers, professors, and scholars affiliated with national or international institutions to submit proposals for thematic issues/dossiers, and to apply to serve as Guest Scientific Editors for Volume 25, Issue 48 (covering the period January-June 2028). Presentation and Scientific Scope of the Journal Co-herencia Co-herencia is an indexed scientific journal, published biannually, under Diamond Open Access with a CC BY 4.0 license, and edited by the School of Arts and Humanities at EAFIT University. Indexed in major international databases such as Scopus (Arts & Humanities, Q2 SJR), Co-herencia ensures methodological rigor, double-blind peer review, and high ethical publishing standards. The journal is published in Spanish, English, and Portuguese. Published without interruption since 2004, the journal aims to serve as a forum for interdisciplinary discussion on the contributions of the humanities and the arts to the shaping of a thoughtful, critical, and deliberative community. Its scope and thematic axes are concentrated mainly on: Literary Studies: Literary theory; Literary genres; Classical tradition; Hermeneutics; Canon, criticism, and history of literature in the Americas; Writing and orality; Translation; Reception; Literary creation; Semiotics; Editing studies; Journalism and literature; Applied literature. Philosophical Studies: Critical theory and social philosophy; Ethics; Political philosophy; Aesthetics; Epistemology; Philosophy of science and technology; Philosophy of mind; Cosmology; Philosophy of language; Argumentation theory; Rhetoric; Phenomenology; Philosophical hermeneutics; Ontology; Conceptual analysis; History of philosophy. Historical Studies: Historiography; Theory and philosophy of history; Methodology of history; Intellectual history; Conceptual history; Cultural history; Social and political history; History of knowledge; National and Latin American history; Global history; Colonial history; Memory and history; Historical geography and cartography; Imagination, speculation, and historical narratives. Arts: Mediality, transmediality, and intermediality; Creative industries; Musicology; History of music; Material and visual culture; Curatorship and museography; Sociology of the arts; Interartistic relations; Avant-gardes and artistic movements; Canon, criticism, and history of the arts in the Americas. Humanistic Studies in Dialogue with the Social Sciences: Critical discourse analysis; Plain language; Digital humanities; Cultural studies; Research-Creation; Philosophical and historical anthropology; Human geography; Environmental humanities; Medical humanities; Digital humanities; Public humanities; Qualitative analysis of quantitative methods; Clinical sociology; Studies on violence, peace, and reconciliation; Communication studies with a humanistic approach; Gender studies. Requirements for Submitting Proposals In keeping with international editorial best practices in the field of Arts and Humanities (diverse impact, editorial exogamy, international outreach, and analytical rigor), proposals submitted by candidates for guest editors must be presented in a single document (PDF or Word), written in Spanish, English, or Portuguese, and must include, in detail, the following five sections: Title of the thematic issue: it should be concise, clear, conceptually strong, and reflect the central problem to be addressed. Thematic presentation and theoretical grounding (500 to 1,000 words): propose a conceptual delimitation and a definition of the object of study, the core question, or the problematizing axis of the dossier. The proposal should also detail the disciplinary or interdisciplinary frameworks, indicating how the theme and approach engage with the journal's scientific scope. Justification and academic relevance (500 to 1,000 words): include a synthesis of the state of the art and a clear account of the novelty and relevance of the proposal within the contemporary debate in the arts and humanities. This section should ideally state the potential impact and interest the issue will generate within the international research community. Scientific biography of the prospective guest editors: a team of two to three guest editors with diverse institutional affiliations is recommended. For each team member, please indicate: full name, current institutional affiliation, highest academic degree, ORCID iD, and a summary (max. 300 words) of their research lines, ongoing projects, and recent publications in the thematic area of the proposal. List of prospective authors and articles: as evidence of the commitment to attracting original manuscripts, this section of the proposal must list between 3 and 6 potential or pre-invited authors of recognized standing or relevant emerging trajectory for the thematic issue. For each anticipated contribution, please provide: the author's full name, institutional affiliation, tentative article title, and a brief abstract (100-200 words). All manuscripts resulting from the call for the selected proposal must undergo double-blind peer review. Guest editors commit to actively participating in the preselection of manuscripts, suggesting qualified reviewers, and drafting a presentation/introduction for the dossier. Timeline for the Open Call and the Editorial Process Opening of the call for thematic issue proposals: September 1, 2026. Deadline for submission of thematic issue proposals: January 10, 2027. Evaluation of proposals by the scientific board and notification of results: January 25, 2027. Public launch of the call for the selected proposal: January 31, 2027. Deadline for submission of articles for the thematic dossier: May 31, 2027. Peer review and revision process: June-November 2027. Early publication of revised articles: October 2027-January 2028. Copyediting, XML-JATS markup, and digital layout: November 2027-February 2028. Official publication (Vol. 25, No. 48, January-June 2028): February-March 2028. How to Submit Proposals Complete proposals must be submitted electronically to the journal's official email (co-herencia@eafit.edu.co) or processed through the Co-herencia journal's OJS (Open Journal System) platform, attaching the document (PDF or Word) with the required information, using the subject line "Application for Thematic Dossier Vol. 25-48 - [Short title of the proposal]." Contacts for Further Information Editorial team of the journal Co-herencia: coherencia@eafit.edu.co Editorial assistant: Liam Agudelo Calle lagudeloc@eafit.edu.co Editor-in-chief: Andrés Vélez-Posada avelezp6@eafit.edu.co

items.fullDescription: CALL FOR PAPERS First International Congress in Humanities - Texts, Images and Communities: "Body, Age and Gender" Org. HUM-TIC Research Group, University of Madeira, 17-18 June 2017 The way in which the body, age and gender shape human experiences is one of the most pressing challenges facing contemporary societies. Today, more than ever, there is a need to build fairer, more equitable and sustainable communities, which are in a state of continuous development and adaptation and which face limitations and obstacles. Some of these are long-standing and deeply rooted, whilst others are new and not very well known. A multidisciplinary approach to the cultural and social constructs of the body - and the multiple levels at which it functions as a generator of meaning - is therefore imperative. The proposed lines of research, both in their contemporary context and in terms of their cultural and historical foundations, fall within the core mission of the Humanities Research Group - Texts, Images and Communities (HUM-TIC). This event fosters free, informed discussion, driven by dialogue across the Humanities. This is the first International Congress organised by the HUM-TIC Research Group, Faculty of Arts and Humanities at the University of Madeira. It is an in-person event, which will take place at the Colégio dos Jesuítas, at the University of Madeira's Rectorate building in Funchal. The conference aims to explore one of HUM-TIC's main thematic areas - Body, Age and Gender - from a dialogical and transdisciplinary perspective. In this context, proposals of a theoretical or empirical nature, including case studies, are welcome across the Humanities. These may include, among others, Art, Communication, Culture, Design, History, Linguistics, Literature, Psychology and Sociology. Discussion Topics (some suggestions): - Discourses, narratives and representations of the body, age and gender. - The body, space and territoriality: real, symbolic and imaginary places. - Rethinking the Human: AI and representations of the body, age and gender. - Aesthetics of the body, beauty and ugliness, the monstrous and the abject. - Building Self and the Other in different cultural contexts. - Stages of life: representations, experiences and intergenerational relationships. - Double standards of ageing in a consumer society. - Embodiment: inner and outer, personal and social, physical and idealised. - Body and gender: sexuality, emotions, ethics, violence. - Myths, stereotypes and imagined representations of the body, age and gender. - Ecologies of the body and environmental humanities. - Gender-based violence in the digital sphere. - The manosphere and social media impact. - Intersectionality and multiple forms of discrimination. - Gender, natural disasters and climate change. Abstract Submissions: - Submission deadline: 15th January, 2027 - Working languages: Portuguese, English, Spanish - 20-minute Paper/ Panel (up to three papers): Microsoft Forms https://forms.cloud.microsoft/pages/responsepage.aspx?id=21zvRr7bJE6SsSdesroEW_Wv92T_NzBPkLLdceU3SMlUMkRYQjNBQllBTlhIT1BCRTlMQlFLWkJUMS4u&route=shorturl - Notification of acceptance: 15th February, 2027 - Conference email: 1cong.ch2027@mail.uma.pt Registration Fees: - Registration fee: €80 - MA and PhD. student registration fee: €40 - UMa lecturers and researchers registration fee: €40 - Non-speaking participants (with certificate of attendance): €10 Registration Deadlines: - Speaking participants: 30th April, 2027 - Non-speaking participants: 18th June, 2027 Location: Colégio dos Jesuítas Reitoria da Universidade da Madeira Rua dos Ferreiros, 9000-082 Funchal Madeira, Portugal Publication: Selected papers will be published in a peer-reviewed volume. Details on deadlines, guidelines, and reviewing process will follow. items.title: Black Is...Black Is: Story as Construction and Celebration of Identity
items.location: Howard University · The Gregory J. Hampton Graduate English Student Association at Howard University
items.excerpt: In his seminal and final film Black Is…Black Ain't , the documentarian Marlon Riggs utilizes a pot of gumbo to articulate his thesis that Blackness necessitates an identity built on multiplicity, complication, and depth (Riggs 1995). Such a vision contests and destabilizes narratives depicted within the film that sought to limit Black identities an...
items.fullDescription: In his seminal and final film Black Is…Black Ain't , the documentarian Marlon Riggs utilizes a pot of gumbo to articulate his thesis that Blackness necessitates an identity built on multiplicity, complication, and depth (Riggs 1995). Such a vision contests and destabilizes narratives depicted within the film that sought to limit Black identities and identifications, and it cuts against the second half of his title, which suggests Blackness in terms of negation, evasion, and minimization. His articulation becomes not just an evocation of Black identifications but a creation of what a Black identity can be. Riggs continues a conversation with Ralph Ellison, Ama Ata Aidoo, Toni Morrison, Stuart Hall, and centuries of international Black thought. By doubling down on the "is" and considering contradictory, harmonious, and contrapuntal accounts of the many ways Blackness is and can be, the Gregory J. Hampton Graduate English Student Association hopes to join this dialogue with its March 25-26, 2027 conference. We invite papers that contemplate how storytelling produces and shapes Black identities as much as it narrates them, forming, revising, and improvising senses of self and community. This conference also does commemorative work. We are honoring the career of Dr. Jimisha Relerford, a graduate of our program and member of the Howard community who passed recently. Her dissertation broke critical ground in its study of Black women's satire. We thus encourage the submission of papers about Black satire, especially Black women's work in the genre. Writers such as Leone Ross, Danzy Senna, Fran Ross, and Zadie Smith, all of whom were discussed in Dr. Relerford's dissertation, use satire to comment on and transform notions of Blackness. We hope to continue Dr. Relerford's project by reflecting on how storytellers work within this genre to talk about identity. We additionally encourage studies of Afrofuturist and speculative Black texts in reference to our organization's namesake, a pillar in Afrofuturist study. In addition to recognizing the intellectual impacts of Drs. Relerford and Hampton, this conference serves as a milestone, marking the tenth conference our organization has hosted in honor of Black literary study. Given Black academia and HBCUs's influence on identity and storytelling around it, we also welcome papers pondering scholarly impacts on identity as seen in criticism, productions, and protest. We additionally invite papers in the following areas that intersect with identity and identification study in story: African Studies African-American Studies Caribbean Studies Disability Studies Ecocriticism and Ecopoetics Diaspora, Ethnicity, and Migration Studies Food Studies Hip Hop Humor Literary History Protest and Rhetoric Queer Studies Television and Film Theater and Performance To submit a paper or panel to our conference, please email an abstract of 250-300 words to gesasecretary@gmail.com no later than January 15, 2027. In your email include your name, affiliation, contact information, and a brief biographical blurb.

items.fullDescription: The Negative Journal is Calling for Papers for its third issue, co-edited by Dr Julie Reshe (editor-in-chief) and Dr Aaron Aquilina (guest editor). This is a general call for papers that also invites a special cluster on queer negativity. Call for Papers: General Issue There are many names for negativity: pessimism, nihilism, antinatalism, misanthropy, cynicism… sometimes absurdism, solipsism, or even mysticism, in certain senses. Some academic pursuit that teases out unique nuances among these terms would be - as are all pursuits - worthless. But expanding and conjoining these terms with more common parlance (depression, apathy, disappointment, suffering, meaninglessness) allows us, at bare minimum, to sketch our existence in a manner that makes legible and listens to these negative experiences rather than seeking to extinguish them through the fictions of therapy, companionship, hope, or love. This is not about being suicidal, at least not wholly. In the words of E.M. Cioran, '[w]e do not rush toward death, we flee the catastrophe of birth, […] source of every infirmity, every disaster' (The Trouble with Being Born). That place of non-being preceding our existence continues to haunt us throughout life, if we are unhappy enough to be attuned to it. Life is revealed, then, as 'death lived in postponement', and the void within makes of us the living dead, the being-not-being (Aaron Aquilina, The Ontology of Death). With these last remarks, and despite the proliferation of negativity's designations, one can quickly see how language begins to falter and fall into incomprehensibility; and perhaps not having the words for negativity is the most articulate anyone can be. Our horrified muteness is not merely some contemporary resignation in the face of 'global climate change, natural disasters, the energy crisis, and the progressive extinction of species world-wide' (Eugene Thacker, In the Dust of this Planet). Suffering has always been here, whether it is our own human condition or the pelicans' choking on plastic bottle caps. Depression, taken as a mode of (non-)being rather than reduced to a treatable illness, thus 'becomes a mode of knowing, a way of perceiving, of being touched and wounded by the world's wounds' (Julie Reshe, Negative Essays). This more-than-individual suffering only continues to manifest the negativity that thought acknowledges as its burden, arguably realised continually throughout history (Seneca and P.W. Zapffe come to mind). In light of this, the Negative Journal calls for papers that address negativity rather than pave the way for some illusory emancipation. Contributions might extend the thought of philosophical pessimists, inhabit the despair evident in literature and art, explore modes of non-being and un-becoming, or locate negativity in apophatic spaces beyond philosophy, psychoanalysis, and language. Work that interrogates negativity's limits, exclusions, political uses, and uneven distribution-as in Afro-pessimism or as per J. Logan Smilges's Crip Negativity-is equally welcome. The Negative Journal aims to provide a locus for these discussions, which are all too often deemed unspeakable. Special Cluster - Queer Negativity Additionally, this issue of the Negative Journal invites contributions towards a special cluster on queer negativity. The association of queerness with the death drive-that core negativity-is by now well established. Thinking through the consequences of this association in tandem with BAEDAN's anonymous editors, we come to realise that 'queer negativity […] means nothing less than the destruction of the civilized world' and its quiescent citizens. Queerness is figured, here, as a deadly anti-politics of the social and psychic alike, a void at the heart of it all. This act of connective thinking, however, is far from complete; indeed, it is even more urgent while late capitalism's assimilationist politics squeeze us harder than ever until we fit into 'intelligibility's mandate and the correlative economy that regulates what is ''legitimate and recognizable"' (Lee Edelman, No Future). Queers are encouraged to ally with the proponents of life on pain of perishing. The vigilant questions at the heart of this special cluster, then, are as follows: what constitutes the intersections of living queer and living death? How do queerness and negativity collude outside the domain of neoliberal homonormativity and its optimistically organised selves? One way would be to foreground the irruptions of various modes of death, rendering superfluous any attempt at positivist meaning-making out of queer subjectivity (to some extent or other, thinkers such as Michel Foucault, Judith Butler, Jeffrey Weeks and José Esteban Muñoz are proponents of this). That is, understanding how one can not participate in the warm embrace of 'the cult of difference' (Leo Bersani, 'Is there a Gay Art?'). And with figuring death's thwarting of "meaning" and "progress", of "community" and "generations" and "futures", come inquiries of the temporal privileges denied to those who insist on emptiness, unfixability, and death in the now not later. The positive time of social order can so easily be read as "straight time", after all (cf. Elizabeth Freeman, J. Halberstam, and others). Standing aside from the space of the polis and the time of life, what remains? Queer inchoate subjects, inarticulate and traumatised by life, humiliated and always-othered (…but somehow, always there…). Maladapted monsters, really: at best defined by mutations and gendered chimerism, at worst by viruses and the failure to participate in some grand narrative of reproductive evolution. These broken figures may be glimpsed in the history or the arts: what of them? What kind of pessimistic queerness, living through all sorts of deaths, can be read in novels, films, and other art forms in ways that are congruent with shoring up one's despair at life? But instead, perhaps, one should just laugh, for that is another way of fundamentally pulling the rug out from under those who deny life's disaster. Whether we shake with mirth or sobs, queerness no more pushes us towards desiring annihilation than acknowledges death's constant unworking of the self and its bonds. And speaking of desire: when considering selfhood against those charlatans that promise to fill the void, how is the scale that weighs sex and relations of un/knowing tipped one way or the other (cf. Oliver Davis & Tim Dean)? Too often for comfort, '[t]ransgressing limits [of sexuality] is to do with a vague notion of inclusiveness rather than active contravention', an affirmation rather than negation (Jonathan Dollimore, Sexual Dissidence). How, then, to wilfully pervert not just sexual practices but the tyrannical myth of happiness, which seeks to suffocate both negativity and queerness? In the end, more questions quibble in the corner: is queerness merely a layer on top of being that is always suffering? Or is it the case that, if queerness is another modulation of pessimist negativity, it is queerness itself that hurts? Submission Abstracts of no longer than 300 words (along with brief biographical notes) should be sent to julie.reshe@gmail.com and aaron.aquilina@um.edu.mt by 15th January, 2027. Submission emails should be headed by 'Negative Journal Issue 3 Submission' or 'Negative Journal Issue 3 - Queer Negativity'. Accepted papers extending the thoughts of this Call should be no longer than 4000 words, and less conventional and/or creative-critical forms are encouraged. Full pieces will be expected no later than by 1st June, 2027. For those seeking consideration for the queer negativity cluster, topics can include but are not limited to: · Queer negativity and/at the limits of psychoanalysis; · Depressing readings: queer literature, queer art more generally; · Queer hauntings, queer horror: wolf-men and chimeras hiding in the closet; · Queerness as posthuman, proto-human, less-than-human; · Failure, laziness, futility, hollowness, apathy, asexuality, refusal; · Negational laughter: camp, drag, gallows humour, absurdism, and queer irony; · Impossibilities: the language/silence of queerness; · Anti-social projects: queerness, anti-politics, anarchy; · Queer pessimism: queerness and Arthur Schopenhauer, Emil Cioran, P.W. Zapffe, Eugene Thacker, Philipp Mainländer, and similar; · Trans* identities and negative subjectivity; · Queering science: apoptosis, entropy, decay, extinction, and destructive plasticity; · Queerness and forms of death (suicide, retirement, illness, madness, etc.); · The negative heart of queer sex and desire; · Temporality and queer negativity; chrononegativity; · Queerness as anti-natalist in several ways; · Play as negative queer modality; · Queer responses: saying no to queer theory and queer theorists. Note: Work selected for the queer negativity cluster could potentially also be considered for a future edited volume with Negative Press (https://www.negativepress.ie/).

items.title: Frames and Framing: Constructing Meaning in Literature, Linguistics, and Translation
items.location: Faculty of Al-Alsun (Languages), Ain Shams University
items.excerpt: Every act of communication, interpretation, and representation is an act of framing. In literary analysis, a “frame” might define genre, direct narrative perspective, or position a text within a historical moment. In linguistics, frames organize semantic understanding, govern pragmatic interaction, and underpin metaphor. In translation and interpreting, f...
items.fullDescription: Every act of communication, interpretation, and representation is an act of framing. In literary analysis, a “frame” might define genre, direct narrative perspective, or position a text within a historical moment. In linguistics, frames organize semantic understanding, govern pragmatic interaction, and underpin metaphor. In translation and interpreting, frames are negotiated, shifted, and sometimes shattered in the movement between languages and cultures. They are the selective filters that highlight certain elements while relegating others to the background, the conceptual structures that allow us to categorize, interpret, and communicate complex realities.

items.fullDescription: The Asian Studies section is currently accepting paper and panel proposals for the 69th Annual Conference of the World Social Science Association. The conference will be held at the Hilton Denver City Center in Denver, CO from March 31st through April 3rd. The Asian Studies section welcomes research on the historical, cultural, social, and political aspects of the Middle East, South Asia, Southeast Asia, Pacific, and East Asia. Previous panels have explored Asian immigrant women's participation management, governance in China, contemporary Japanese digital culture, and feminist readings of the Bh?gavata Pur??a. We encourage innovative and critical approaches that address contemporary and historical issues. The Asian Studies section is particularly eager to include the voices of graduate students and early-career scholars. This is an excellent opportunity for emerging researchers to share their work and engage with a broader academic community. The WSSA also holds several competitions and awards, including cash prizes for undergraduate and graduate papers. Winners of the John Wicks Dissertation Paper Award are eligible to receive a prize of $250 (USD) and the refunding of registration and conference fees. Winners of the Bert & Phyllis Lamb Prize in Political Science will receive partial or full reimbursement of travel costs and a $1,000 (USD) prize. The deadline for paper abstracts and panel proposals is January 15th, 2027. Early registration for the conference and discounted registration fees end on November 30th, 2026. Virtual participation in the conference is permitted; however, additional registration fees are required. In-person participation is highly recommended. Please visit the WSSA conference page for further information or to submit a paper or panel proposal at https://www.wssaconference.com/ Please direct any questions concerning the Asian Studies section to Dr. Barbara Greene at greene-barbara(AT)Jissen.ac.jp

items.fullDescription: AI & Antiquity: Journal of Teaching and Technology in Ancient Studies invites contributions for its first Special Issue, Playing Antiquity: Video Games, Teaching and Historical Knowledge, to be published in June 2027. Video games have become one of the major environments through which students and wider audiences encounter the ancient world. Yet their significance for Ancient Studies extends beyond questions of historical accuracy. Through mechanics, rules, maps, narratives, economies, political systems, and player choice, games transform particular interpretations of Antiquity into interactive and playable systems.

Hailed as “the most influential Westerner to write about China since the 13th century’s Marco Polo”, Pearl S. Buck not only introduced Chinese literature and culture to global readers through her literary writings, but also participated actively in transnational cultural dialogue, humanitarian engagement, and the shaping of international understandings of China.

items.excerpt: Special Issue Website: https://www.mdpi.com/journal/literature/special_issues/B781Q58SAM Dear Colleagues, This Special Issue of Literature will collect essays addressing the reception, influence, adaptation, or incorporation of literature from the Greco-Roman world into later theatre, film, and television. The Greeks and Romans pioneered a wide range of p...
items.fullDescription: Special Issue Website: https://www.mdpi.com/journal/literature/special_issues/B781Q58SAM Dear Colleagues, This Special Issue of Literature will collect essays addressing the reception, influence, adaptation, or incorporation of literature from the Greco-Roman world into later theatre, film, and television. The Greeks and Romans pioneered a wide range of performed literary styles like tragic and comic drama, or epic and lyric poetry, as well as developing extensive mythic story networks and what we now recognize as formal histories, etc. Some of these works remain among the most influential and beloved writings ever produced by humanity. Because Greco-Roman literature is so culturally powerful and beloved, receptions and uses of it have occurred continually since the Greco-Roman era itself, in myriad different ways. This Issue seeks articles focused on performed receptions, exploring the cultural and artistic politics of how Greco-Roman material is brought to life for viewers, either on stages or screens. The recent controversies about casting and "historical accuracy" with Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey film remind us of the power and perils of live performance in the evocation of classics, so the articles for this Issue will interrogate the weight of and responses to classics' cultural authority. The Special Issue aims to provide current scholarly arguments about the role and ongoing power of Greek and Roman literature in theatre, film, television, or other performed media, consistent with the broader aims and scope of Literature. Purposefully taking a broad lens, the Issue seeks essays focused across time periods (e.g., medieval to the present), different national or regional performances/arts, and across media in order to bring together the most comprehensive body of essays possible. Potential topics include, but are not limited to: Theatrical or performed adaptation of or allusions to Greek and Roman literature within the Greco-Roman world. Medieval European or Middle Eastern reworkings and influence of Greco-Roman poetry or drama. Renaissance or Enlightenment re-conceptualizations of classical works. Re-writings, reworkings, artistic depictions, stagings, etc., of Greek or Roman literature for popular audiences (including Nolan's recent film). Global receptions and performances of Greco-Roman literature for postcolonial or comparative literature purposes. Feminist performed engagement with and critique of classics. Dr. Phillip Zapkin Guest Editor Manuscript Submission Information Manuscripts should be submitted online at www.mdpi.com by registering and logging in to this website. Once you are registered, click here to go to the submission form. Manuscripts can be submitted until the deadline. All submissions that pass pre-check are peer-reviewed. Accepted papers will be published continuously in the journal (as soon as accepted) and will be listed together on the special issue website. Research articles, review articles as well as short communications are invited. For planned papers, a title and short abstract (about 250 words) can be sent to the Editorial Office for assessment. Submitted manuscripts should not have been published previously, nor be under consideration for publication elsewhere (except conference proceedings papers). All manuscripts are thoroughly refereed through a double-anonymized peer-review process. A guide for authors and other relevant information for submission of manuscripts is available on the Instructions for Authors page. Literature is an international peer-reviewed open access quarterly journal published by MDPI. Please visit the Instructions for Authors page before submitting a manuscript. The Article Processing Charge (APC) for publication in this open access journal is 1000 CHF (Swiss Francs). Submitted papers should be well formatted and use good English. Authors may use MDPI's English editing service prior to publication or during author revisions. Keywords: Greek Roman literature reception adaptation studies classics

items.fullDescription: Call for Papers | CJHS Volume 3 (2027) The call for papers is now open for the third volume of CJHS , scheduled for publication in December 2027. Deadline for submissions: June 30, 2027 Contact email: commentarium@mail.uma.pt All submissions will undergo double-blind peer review. CJHS is an open-access scholarly journal, published annually, dedicated to research in the field of the Humanities - particularly in Culture, Literature, Linguistics, Communication, History, and Philosophy, as well as related areas. Interdisciplinary in nature, it welcomes original articles and critical reviews in Portuguese, English, Spanish, French, and Italian. Book reviews may be submitted only in Portuguese or English. For more information, please visit the CJHS Journal website: https://commentarium.web.uma.pt/index.php/journal Editor-in-Chief Joaquim Pinheiro Editorial Board Inês Tadeu Luís Pimenta Lopes Rui Carlos Fonseca Vanessa Cesário ------------------------ Universidade da Madeira Faculdade de Artes e Humanidades Departamento de Línguas, Literaturas e Culturas
